Current approaches to training quadruped robots are restricted to specific localities and
require substantial preparation, including carefully designed starting positions, precise
starting orientations, and pre-programmed motion patterns. We contend that this should
not be the case. We have developed an evolutionary method for generating individualized
gait patterns in a quadruped robot based on an analytic model of the robot's dynamics.
This trajectory creator is highly adaptable and produces a limitless number of feasible
gait patterns, significantly expanding the quadruped's ability to navigate various
environments and obstacles. When combined with a standard model-predictive-control system,
the evolutionary creator enables the smooth execution of complex tasks like walking around
blocks and climbing up slopes, which would be impossible with pre-defined patterns. The
method's efficiency was further enhanced by incorporating a focused reinforcement learning
technique, which significantly reduces the time required to create a usable gait pattern. The
result is a highly automated system that quickly creates a variety of functional gait
patterns, enabling more sophisticated quadruped behavior. Details about the method and our
results are available online. Technical information about the method and our findings can be

The behavior of super-massive black holes in their active, luminous state has been extensively studied, yet little is known about their behavior during outbursts. A unique observation of the low-intensity active galaxy, NGC\ 7213, using high-resolution Chandra X-ray, allows us to examine Fe XXVI K-alpha line emission and nearby interstellar absorption, revealing that this absorption is significantly lower than predicted by standard models. Considering that special conditions must be affecting the observed Fe XXVI lines, we looked at Fe XXV lines for further insight. The resulting analysis indicates that Fe XXV has a higher temperature than expected and also has lower interstellar absorption levels. Two models explaining this data are presented - the 'hot wind' model and the 'two-component cooling model'. The hot wind model postulates that this decreased absorption is a result of hot plasma originating from the black hole, sweeping away cooler gas. The two-component cooling model proposes that the decreased absorption is a result of a cooler gas component originating from the black hole's accretion disk, which affects the observed Fe XXVI and Fe XXV lines. Both models can explain the observed data, though the hot wind model is more consistent with previously collected data. Furthermore, both models can be applied to other active galaxies, which may offer further insights into their behavior. Closed-loop systems like spacecraft and industrial processes often benefit from a linear controller when their dynamics can be accurately represented by a linear model. However, linear models don't account for nonlinear effects, which can lead to significant performance losses. One way to improve this is through an optimal regulator, a model-based control method that yields the best performance when fully informed. Since perfect model accuracy is often unrealistic, we explored a method to adapt the optimal regulator to account for measurement errors without relying on system parameters. This parameter-independent solution was approached using a reinforcement learning technique, which was applied in a simulation-based learning process. Despite not requiring the Euler-Lagrange equations, our method still benefited from their underlying structure. We compared the efficiency of this two-step learning process to other model-free reinforcement learning methods, finding it to be significantly more effective when considering computational cost. Ultimately, this discovery suggests that even in the absence of system parameters, the optimal regulator structure can still be utilized to facilitate efficient learning. As such, this research presents a model-free approach to reconfiguring the optimal regulator, which is applicable across a range of systems and learning scenarios. Keywords: Reinforcement learning, Model-free, Linear and nonlinear systems, Predictive control.

The SiD Detector is one of the two detector options being considered for the future ILC. Although the detailed design of the SiD Detector has been established, this study will present alternative ideas for the inner tracker's design. Due to the substantial cost associated with the detector, as well as the inherent technical risks, it is crucial to ensure the detection capabilities of the detector without the most challenging aspects of the design. To achieve this, we will demonstrate a simplified design for the SiD Inner Tracker that reduces the inner tracker's cost and technical complexities while maintaining its overall sensitivity. This design integrates a silicon tracker with a tungsten comb design for precise momentum measurement and efficient particle tracking. Notably, the tungsten combs serve both as targets for beam luminosity measurement and a part of the silicon tracker, thereby utilizing the particle beam's internal measurement without an additional luminosity detector, which reduces costs. With approximately 8 m in length, between 0.4-0.6 T magnetic field strength, and with inner and outer radii of the tracker at approximately 1.3m and 4.3m respectively, the silicon tracker tungsten comb design for the SiD Detector has been replaced. This modified design utilizes a silicon tracker tungsten comb system with 5 combs spaced equally along a 5.66m combined length at 0.4T magnetic field, with inner and outer radii of 1.3m and 4.3m, to achieve precise momentum measurement and efficient particle tracking. This concept has been compared with the current SiD Detector design through the use of the REPLAY simulation software. Notably, the track finding efficiency for hadrons remained at 90%, with an innermost point finding efficiency of 95%, as the detector's design was modified to incorporate five tungsten combs along the length of the tracker. This has been achieved with five more acceptance points along the length of the tracker compared to the current SiD Detector design. Furthermore, the innermost point tracking efficiency for electrons remained at 99%, as the detector's design was modified to incorporate the silicon tracker tungsten comb design. This has been achieved with improved precision and increased sensitivity in the measurement of the weak magnetic field and the charm mass due to the extended length of the tracker. This has been achieved with reduced detector volumes and increased luminosity, allowing for the observation of rare events at a luminosity of 5.9 x 10^34 cm^-2s^-2. Road detection is a critical component in both self-driving vehicles and map development, with existing methods, however, struggling to accommodate diverse scenarios such as construction zones, red-zone roadblocks, and roads with periodic patterns. A new framework, called ReAD, has been designed with the capacity to detect irregular patterns of roads at a large scale. ReAD starts by dividing the global map into local regions and then dynamically assigning a direction to each segment based on the most consistent road orientation found within that segment. These assigned directions are then used to calculate a stability value for each segment, with segments exhibiting significant differences from the overall average road orientation considered irregular. Through both manual and automated testing, ReAD has been found to significantly outperform other detection methods. For example, when testing roads with construction zones, ReAD achieved an accuracy rate of 94.5% using human annotation, far surpassing other methods. Additionally, when using automated Ground Truth, ReAD reached an accuracy rate of 88.4%, representing a notable improvement over other methods. ReAD's performance in detecting periodic road patterns reached an accuracy rate of 92.6%, also surpassing other methods. Even when accounting for noise during testing, ReAD maintained an accuracy rate of 91.6%, cementing its value as a reliable and efficient road detection method. Vector data, such as point clouds, can be used to enhance accuracy while deep learning methods can be leveraged for automatic map development to expand the framework's capabilities. When incorporating these additional capabilities, ReAD's value was further demonstrated, with the capacity to detect road patterns, construction zones, and roadblocks from point clouds. Moreover, ReAD can be used for automatic map development, with and without the use of point clouds. A comparison of ReAD's performance using just GT data to its performance using point clouds revealed that its accuracy rate improved by 3.1%, demonstrating the effectiveness of its capabilities. A self-designed dataset, called the RCD, has been developed with diverse road patterns to support the training of ReAD's deep learning model. The RCD, consisting of 160 images, was used to test and refine ReAD before comparing its performance to other road detection methods. Notably, when testing roads with construction zones using the RCD dataset, ReAD achieved an accuracy rate of 94.5%, far surpassing other methods. The goal is to determine the extent to which the pion's form factor affects the anomalous magnetic moment of the muon. Furthermore, a comparison among the three approaches and experimental data is conducted to validate the respective methods. Additionally, a state-of-the-art calculation of the pion's electromagnetic form factor within the Vainshtein-Inomata-Zhirov diagrammatic theory is presented. Lastly, a discussion on future directions involving Bethe-Heitler processes and pion radiative decay is mentioned. The underlying work is part of a broader study on the muon's anomalous magnetic moment that also investigated the pi mu atom. The abstrakt solution aims to create a comprehensive abstract representation of computer code, independent of its specific programming language. This abstract representation is designed to be language-agnostic and encompasses two components: (1) a syntactic view capturing the code's structural features and (2) a semantic view that incorporates code modifications to enable reasoning and bug detection. Our abstract code model comprises nine components, covering code regions, control flow, data structures, array indices, pointer operations, string interactions, taint states, numeric computations, and context-dependent information. Each component of the abstract representation is accompanied by a formal definition, and we have formally established the relationship between code's concrete and abstract representations. Moreover, we have effectively applied the abstrakt solution to both procedural and object-oriented code bases, utilizing the generated abstract representations to implement various bug detection tools. To facilitate efficient abstract representation creation, we have developed fast, automatic code analysis tools based on advanced parsing and semantic analysis techniques. These tools can analyze even large code bases within minutes, and we have successfully tested them on over 43 billion lines of code. Our abstract representation has been validated through extensive experimentation, and we have formally demonstrated its effectiveness in detecting a broad range of software bugs. Furthermore, we have implemented a feature set for abstract code models that encompasses over 700 distinct bug characteristics, and we have applied this feature set to detect previously identified bugs in widely used software systems. To promote the adoption of our abstract representation, we have released the accompanying source code, as well as detailed documentation, under an open-source license. Additionally, we have established a website providing ongoing support and showcasing the continuous evaluation of our abstract representation on constantly evolving code snapshots. Finally, we have formally proposed and implemented a formal framework for specifying software verification conditions using abstract predicates and verification diagrams. This formal framework has been successfully applied to detect software bugs in multiple contexts. In summary, our abstract representation offers a comprehensive solution for analyzing computer code, encompassing a deep understanding of code regions, control flow between them, and the interactions of code components, as well as the code's semantic context. This abstract representation is characterized by robust formal definitions and has been effectively applied to both procedural and object-oriented code, utilizing the generated abstract representations to implement innovative bug detection tools. Based on this abstract representation, we have developed a feature set for abstract code models that encompasses over 700 distinct bug characteristics and have effectively promoted its adoption through open-source software releases and related services. The relationship between a galaxy's mass and extend of its dark matter halo is examined using two datasets, which allow for consideration of multiple galaxy types and redshifts. By looking at how this relationship changes over time, researchers discover that spiral and elliptical galaxies follow the same mass-to-sphere radius rule, regardless of whether the galaxy is an early-type spiral or a passive elliptical. It's hypothesized that a galaxy's mass-to-sphere radius increases due to active supernovae that make the halo larger and more massive, leading to a longer rotation period for spiral galaxies. This theory is supported by observations showing that the majority of early-type spirals at higher redshifts have larger, more massive halos than those at lower redshifts. On the other hand, supernovae have little effect on the mass and size of massive, fast-rotating galaxies like the Milky Way. These massive galaxies, including local ellipticals and those with large black holes, have a more stable structure and are less likely to change as the supernovae rate decreases with time. It's suggested that this change in supernovae rate is the key factor that transforms disk galaxies into stable, passive halos. Additionally, it's proposed that the core-collapsed galaxies, including many local ellipticals, may have initially been massive, rotating galaxies like those found at higher redshifts, with lighter, more extended halos that then became heavier, more stable ones. This is consistent with earlier research indicating that galaxy evolution is linked to their dark matter halos. Furthermore, it's suggested that supernovae that make a galaxy's stars more numerous also make its halo more extended, and that this extends to active galaxies that are similar to the passive ellipticals. Finally, it's discovered that the mass of supermassive black holes at higher redshifts is associated with both the mass of their host galaxies and their dark matter halos, indicating that galaxy evolution is associated with its dark matter halo. While using photometry from stars to monitor the atmosphere's optical depth has been around for decades, recent breakthroughs in technology have revitalized this method, particularly for measuring aerosol optical depth. We discuss the underlying principles of the approach and present an overview of the latest developments in photometry-based aerosol measurement techniques. These advancements have enabled ground-based measurements of aerosol properties with high spatial resolution and have facilitated the retrieval of long-term aerosol data records, along with corresponding products that can be accessed freely through online repositories. These products are now being utilized in various applications, including climate modeling and constraining model parameters by comparing data with simulated observations, as required by future climate change experiments. We also report on ongoing research aimed at using lunar photometry as an alternative method to obtain accurate measurements of aerosol optical depth. This method is particularly significant when taking data during eclipses or in regions with limited sunlight, allowing for inter-comparability of results and validating the retrieved aerosol data at specific heights. We outline plans for integrating aerosol measurement capabilities into networked ground-based telescopes, along with data sharing and product dissemination, as part of the CLIMA ground-based astronomy network. CLIMA is equipped to handle these tasks and is now in a prime position to contribute to this field, aided by the upcoming ATLAS project that will be operational at the ATLAS A1 facility in Northgrastern University, UK. The CLIMA network and ATLAS A1 facility will both play vital roles in advancing aerosol measurement technology and its various applications. Ultimately, the goal is for ground-based telescopes to play a key part in obtaining critical aerosol data over land and water, as well as in urban and natural environments, contributing to global aerosol data records and informing critical environmental policies. We present GGLasso, a Python library designed to perform graphical model estimation using Lasso, Ising, and Gaussian maximum likelihood methods. The library includes functions for node degree thresholding, edge sparse regularization, graph reconstruction, and performance metric calculation. The tensor computation technique employed by GGLasso enhances the package's performance on GPU-based systems. The package's performance on CPU-based systems is attributed to its efficient multi-threaded design. The library has been validated using various benchmarks, including (i) a synthetic dataset of known network structure, and (ii) real-world single-cell RNA-sequencing data. The results demonstrate the package's performance and accuracy, which surpasses existing alternatives. We have simulated the distribution of electrons that would result from these models around the TW Hydrae low-mass star and future radio observations have the capacity to verify these predictions. We have simulated the distribution of electrons that would result from both photoevaporation and MHD disk wind models, taking into account different masses and widths of the disk. According to the photoevaporation model, a 10 mJy signal at 1 GHz should be observable with a spaced baseline radio telescope such as the Next Generation Very Large Array (NGVLA). In contrast, the MHD disk wind model yields a signal that is too strong to be observable with such a telescope. However, if we scale the mass of the disk that is affected by photoevaporation to 0.01 M⊙, the predicted observables converge and a signal of around 10 mJy could be expected. In both cases, future radio observations have the potential to verify these predictions and help to resolve the uncertainty surrounding these models. Additionally, the models that take into account the disk's density and electron fraction yield similar results to each other and a signal of around 10 mjy could be expected. In contrast, the magnetized wind model yields a stronger signal than the wind model. DWIFOB is based on a dynamically weighted forward-backward algorithm that continuously adjusts its proximity operator weights to accelerate convergence. By using a weighted proxy instead of the standard forward-backward approach, DWIFOB offers improved robustness to stabilization parameters and enhanced convergence speed in suitable conditions. Furthermore, DWIFOB can be implemented using a block-Coordinate Forward-Backward algorithm, which reduces computational complexity by fixing most variables while updating a subset of them. We also provide a globally converent version of DWIFOB by incorporating a regularization term and propose an implementable variant of the algorithm. Finally, we demonstrate the effectiveness of DWIFOB through numerical examples and highlight its advantages in terms of convergence speed and robustness compared to established methods. Additionally, DWIFOB is compatible with parallel computing and can be used to solve large-scale optimization problems. We provide C code for our results.

In this research, we examine the issue of assigning frequencies and selecting beamforming patterns for transmitting data to multiple groups of devices in millimeter wave communication systems. To increase the efficiency of communication, we divide the assignment of frequency and beamforming into separate problems. For beamforming, we develop a novel encoding scheme called hybrid encoding, which reorganizes the base beams into lower rank structures and identifies the primary modes that convey the most information. This is accomplished without access to the channel state information, relying solely on the eigenvalue decomposition of the effective channel covariance matrix. Through simulations, we show that our proposed method outperforms standard hybrid beamforming in terms of total information transferred to all groups. Furthermore, we address the conflict between interference and missing signals by formulating an optimization problem and proposing a solution that maximizes the total information transferred to all groups. Our method also demonstrates better performance compared to traditional approaches. Simulation results show that our solution efficiently balances interference reduction and signal acquisition. Additionally, we discuss the extension of our research to include non-oracular channel state information. Notably, our approach is compatible with various mmWave standards, including IEEE 802.15.3D. Simulation results verify that our proposed method achieves superior performance across different channel models and device group sizes. Furthermore, we analyzed the computational complexity of our approach and found it to be more efficient than traditional methods. While existing research focuses on safeguarding model data, our study addresses the underexplored issue of safeguarding user inputs during the data extraction process in FL. We develop a novel, efficient protocol called Federated Extraction Protocol (FEP) to protect these inputs. However, existing FEP protocols have significant communication overheads, hindering efficiency. This research focuses on developing efficient real-time distributed algorithms for coordination among nodes in Content-Centric Networks, utilizing Name Data Networks (NDN) based computing. As applications on networks utilizing NDN grow, the challenge persists in optimizing node communication. Our work addresses this issue by designing algorithms for dynamic coordination that effectively utilize information available through NDN's forwarding elements, specifically request rates and service times. These algorithms are proven optimal by established measures, including mean response time and mean queue length, and demonstrated through numerical analysis and realistic simulations, which show significant improvements in performance and scalability compared to conventional methods. Notably, our proposed approach exhibits better mean response times and smaller queue lengths as node service times and arrival rates increase. These results provide crucial insights for designing high-performance computing systems on NDN-based networks. Furthermore, the source code for reproducing the figures in this study has been made available. Additionally, a novel NDN-based distributed computing framework, known as \textit{DeCFC}, has been developed and demonstrated through experiments. This framework effectively utilizes DeCFC to successfully demonstrate dynamic coordination of complementary service components. The experimentally verified DeCFC framework has been successfully applied in a use case involving video encoding, and has been made available for public use. The source code for DeCFC can be accessed at: https://github.com/zhengwupc/DeCFC.git. This research has been partially supported through grants from NSFC (No.61971045, 61971046). We examine the exponential stability of a beam on a star-shaped graph with multiple branches, where each branch has a constant density and the beams are initially displaced and then given a localized velocity in the same direction. Despite the infinite number of branches, the stability properties can be understood through a finite model, which is the Euler-Bernoulli equation for a beam with multiple degrees of freedom. However, the constant density assumptions lead to non-optimistic exponential stability rather than optimal stability. If the density parameters are allowed to vary, the stability properties become optimal, which is a more complex and less non-constant model. Consequently, the optimal stability requires a more intricate energy estimate than what is specified by the Euler-Bernoulli model. Notably, the stability properties are not uniformly exponential across all times, which is primarily due to a resonance phenomenon where the system displays quasi-periodic behavior. Specifically, the system exhibits a specific time scale where the energy is quasi-periodically bounded, which is a combination of the L^2 integral time scale and a rapidly oscillating time scale given by the eigenvalues of the beam. Therefore, designing an energy estimate that captures both time scales is crucial to understanding the stability properties. Ultimately, the stability properties can be generalized to other beam models with variable density and may be extended to other types of beams, such as those subject to external forces or beams in free space. Additionally, the results can be generalized to other types of star-shaped graphs with varying connectivity. Lastly, the research can be extended to other problems in both theoretical and applied mathematics, which may also be relevant to other fields such as physics and engineering. Additionally, the results can be useful in developing control strategies for beam structures. In the quark-meson model with a specific type of symmetry breaking, we analyze whether inhomogeneous phases can occur with a specific type of symmetry. Our research reveals that as pion mass increases, regions where these inhomogeneous phases can occur decrease, however we found they can still occur with a pion mass that reflects the natural world. The instability of this inhomogeneous matter primarily occurs within one particular interaction type, while it's not favored in another type. The structure of this inhomogeneous matter varies depending on the quark chemical potential and pion mass. Unlike more complex systems, this inhomogeneous matter has a simpler structure. We were able to demonstrate that as pion mass increases the size of this inhomogeneous region decreases in size and it's not favored when a certain type of interaction isn't present. Lastly we calculated the mass of this inhomogeneous matter and found it's lower than more complex systems matter. 

Keywords: Inhomogeneous phases, Compact stars, Chiral nuclear phase transition, Quark-meson model.

Utilizing ternary chemical potential phase diagrams and phonon spectrum analysis, the authors demonstrate that compounds formed by combining cadmium or mercury with thallium and tellurium, specifically CdTl$_4$Te$_3$ and HgTl$_4$Te$_3$, exhibit stability. Through theoretical calculations, the authors identify these materials as belonging to a new class of strong Topological Insulators characterized by a non-trivial Z$_2$ topological signature and a remarkably large gap of approximately 3.24 meV in the bulk. This classification confers the materials with unique surface states, featuring Dirac and Rashba bands that the authors also compute. Notably, the pressure-dependent behavior of these materials was found to undergo a topological phase transition at 0.46 GPa for CdTl$_4$Te$_3$ and 0.20 GPa for HgTl$_4$Te$_3$, prompting a heightened demand for further experimental research to verify these predictions. Based on their results, the authors suggest that these materials possess the requisite conditions for supporting ultrafast Zener tunneling-induced charge transfer across their thallium atomic plane. This potential charge transfer was shown to occur when the interplane distance is minimized under 0.46 GPa in CdTl$_4$Te$_3$ and 0.20 GPa in HgTl$_4$Te$_3$. This property could possibly give rise to exceptionally high carrier concentrations. Additionally, the authors propose that these materials exhibit a unique property where the effective mass of electrons and holes displays opposite directional variation under pressure. This unique behavior, coupled with their predicted tolerance to pressure, makes the materials a promising lead in developing the new class of large band gap topological insulators under high-pressure conditions. In many domains, optimizing design or operating parameters according to multiple goals necessitates weighing these goals against one another, often encapsulated in an utility function. Despite the utility function's central role, it remains uncommon for it to be given an explicit, human-readable form; more often, it is learned through data or, conversely, is provided by a subject matter expert (SME) but remains tacit, unreachable to computational methods. We propose employing SME-provided, non-explicit utility information – in the form of rankings or intervals of equivalence – and demonstrate its effectiveness in learning utility functions through data for parameter optimization tasks with multiple objectives. Our approach surpasses traditional methods that rely solely on performance data, while also accommodating the input of SME-supervised, explicit utility learning tasks. Utilizing pairwise comparisons from SME knowledge enhances optimization results, and we show these improvements to be significant when comparing them to results from purely data-driven optimization. Moreover, our utility learning framework facilitated the first known successful optimization of a multi-objective ray tracing application, yielding superior performance under various utility functions. Our framework and accompanying code are available at https://github.com/amie-group/UtilityLearn. In a study on tunable Dirac points within a two-dimensional non-symmorphic lattice arrangement, researchers found that adjusting the symmetry of a lattice structure enabled the creation of multiple Dirac points. By applying band mapping techniques, it was determined that increasing the size of the lattice cell reduced the number of Dirac points. Furthermore, investigators discovered that adjusting the relative rotation and translation of the lattice layers influenced the location and distribution of Dirac points along the Brillouin torus. Additionally, the possibility of achieving flux-induced topological phases was noted, and the relationship between tunable Dirac points and non-symmorphic symmetry was emphasized through a generalized star-of-David lattice model. Finally, the connection between Dirac points and symmetry-protected Dirac points was identified, and the potential for observing Dirac points through scanning tunneling spectroscopy was considered. The proposed ideas provide a framework for controlling quantum topology in solid-state materials and artificial materials.

A optical atom trap, integrated with an etched silicon chip, serves as the foundation for an innovative microtrap design that offers a compact and robust setting for precise manipulation of single atoms. Furthermore, the design enables detection capabilities along three axes and enables the integration of a pyramidal structure for enhanced light collection efficiency in optical photon detection. This groundbreaking design has opened the door to innovative technologies for single-photon and single-atom processing. Monomers are initially identified through analysis of molecular weight and composition data, and then used to develop candidate polymers. Our approach is rooted in a comprehensive least squares formulation that relies on a square coefficient matrix, an over-constrained norm, and optimal singular value decomposition (SVD) for solution determination. By addressing potential rank issues through relevant feature 'rank' estimation, we can efficiently obtain optimal camera resection solutions. Our method does not necessitate any specialized calibration coefficients, merely requiring standard linear regression calculations to determine the optimal solution. Furthermore, we analyze and address the problem of derived camera poses not corresponding to the original observed features, which is particularly evident in low-rank situations. Our method has been thoroughly evaluated against existing resection techniques on numerous datasets, indicating notable performance improvements, from enhanced robustness to superior feature localization accuracy, especially with sparse and noisy datasets. Moreover, we investigated the application of our approach to existing self-calibration techniques and discovered that incorporating our proposed method yields improved results. Our code is freely accessible at https://github.com/JulianWeidner/completeLeastSquares. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive dataset, dubbed the 'Rank Estimation Game', at https://github.com/JulianWeidner/rankEstimationGame to facilitate the development of novel rank estimation techniques. The effect of disorder on one-dimensional interacting electron systems is of great theoretical interest due to the diverse range of outcomes, which can lead to insulating, localized, or semimetallic states. A random singlet state, characterized by localized spins, may arise when disorder prevails over interactions. Using numerical cluster and variational methods, we examine the interplay of disorder and interactions in one-dimensional Hubbard chains. Our results indicate that strong interactions can bypass the onset of a random singlet phase and instead lead to a transition from a metallic to an insulating state. To understand the phase diagram's insulating region, we employed the concept of a spin liquid with a gapped Fermi surface, supported by the observation that the Luttinger parameter remains at a value of n_q=1. We also demonstrate that the nature of the wave function making up the insulating phase changes at the point where the interaction strength meets the disorder strength. Furthermore, using numerical cluster diagonalization, we were able to analyze the effects of interactions on the single particle density of states and the pair field correlations in the presence of disorder. Our findings indicate that interaction-induced transitions can be distinguished from those resulting from disorder. We also observed that the pair field correlations in the random singlet phase display features characteristic of conformal field theories. The system's ability to form pairs in the presence of interactions, despite disorder, is particularly noteworthy. Our research uses the Luttinger parameters to characterize the different phases of the system. We have extended the application of Luttinger parameters to include interactions that violate particle number conservation, and we have carried out a detailed analysis of Luttinger parameters within the variational wave function used in our study. This involves a systematic expansion of the wave function around the critical point of a underlying quantum field theory that is both particle and number conserving. Our study shows that Luttinger parameter-based reductions can accurately capture critical behavior as well as noncritical phases, and that interactions that break number conservation can be effectively treated within the framework of Luttinger parameters. We have found that Luttinger parameters remain effective even when interactions violate number conservation, and that they can effectively describe the behavior of strongly interacting systems that are both particle and number conserved. We have demonstrated that Luttinger parameters provide a clear, easily interpretable means of describing the different phases of strongly interacting systems, and that they can be used to accurately predict key properties such as the transverse magnetic susceptibility. Through experiments, particularly using robotic manipulation tasks under partial oversight, we demonstrate that our hierarchical Bayesian model facilitates efficient learning of preferences and achieved better results compared to state-of-the-art baselines. Additionally, our method effectively handled diverse rewards and achieved state-of-the-art performance when applied to tasks with explicit annotations. Notably, our approach enabled learned policies to generalize across various preferences expressed through different reward functions. We also conducted evaluations in unregulated scenarios, demonstrating that our method can adapt to new preferences found through follow-the-regularizer objectives without the need for expert supervision. A video showcasing our method's capabilities is available at https://youtu.be/7xkIkrx8B1k. Code has been made available at https://github.com/alimanghokro/CFR-PRL. Furthermore, we establish the equivalence between the existence of a strong small loop transfer domain and the existence of a finite ramification degree for subgroups of the fundamental group. Finally, we provide an illustrative example in the realm of finite etale covers. (Translated from the original Russian article cited below.)

Recent advancements in deep reinforcement learning have led to superior performance in complex control tasks. Nonetheless, despite these achievements, several difficulties persist in deep reinforcement learning. Notably, it is challenging to ensure robust policies are discovered that cope with diverse situations and small changes in the environment. In addition, deep reinforcement learning policies often exhibit instability when applied to new tasks, even those that are similar to those experienced during training. To tackle these limitations, we present a novel method that decouples learning policy actions and predicts the subsequent state, thereby enabling the transfer of learned skills to related tasks. We evaluate our approach by comparing it to established state-of-the-art controllers on two intricate robotic systems. In comparison, our proposed method exhibits improved performance across both systems. Specifically, it results in increased efficiency and enhanced robustness to variable environments. Furthermore, it demonstrates the ability to transfer learned skills to new tasks more effectively. This study is the second in a series focusing on the mass distribution of black holes across various sizes, spanning from the mass of stars to supermassive entities. It specifically explores the development of supermassive black holes and uses data from observational studies of active galaxies to construct a mass distribution model. To account for the rapid growth of supermassive black holes in the early universe, a separate mechanism is introduced and shown to be supported by both theoretical and observational evidence. To determine the mass distribution of black holes in galaxies since the universe's formation, a mass distribution model is developed and applied using data from the SDSS-IV/BRIGHT galaxy sample. It is found that the model accurately fits the observed data and that the distribution of supermassive black holes in galaxies is uniform and influenced by a component requiring less black hole mass that is significant at a 3-sigma level. Further analysis is needed to confirm this finding. It is hypothesized that the rapid growth of black holes in the early universe may be linked to primordial star formation and the presence of dark matter in a smaller radius in the centers of galaxies. This hypothesis is based on previously proposed models and observations, and it is suggested that the observed mass distribution of supermassive black holes is the result of a combination of factors including stable, less-rapid growth over long periods of time, and the effect of galactic mergers in shaping the final mass of the black hole. It is concluded that it is possible for supermassive black holes to reach masses far exceeding their growth rates, and that this is consistent with current data and a mass distribution model. Additionally, it is proposed that the largest black holes of all may be the result of a distinct physical process, and that a mass gap between intermediate and supermassive black holes may be a real phenomenon that requires further study. Finally, a mass distribution model for all sizes of black holes is presented, and it is shown that it accurately fits observational data and that it is possible for black holes of all sizes to follow a universal mass distribution that is consistent from the smallest black holes in stars to the largest black holes in the universe. A next step in this research will be to further develop this model using data from galaxy distributions and the growth rates of black holes over long periods of time. Over the past thirty years, preprints have undergone significant development and become an essential component of the scientific publishing system. This article provides an overview of the history and growth of preprints, analyzing trends and correlations based on data from the largest preprint archive, arXiv, over the 1991-2020 period. The results show that preprints have become increasingly popular and widespread over the decades, with some fields such as physics and mathematics consistently using preprints since the early 1990s, and biomedical research emerging in the early 2000s. The benefits of preprints include accelerated publication speeds, with fields like physics and biology experiencing publication times that are significantly shorter than predicted, and in other fields significantly longer than predicted. The consequences of preprints also extend to research outcomes, with critical studies and high-impact publications more likely to originate from preprints. Ultimately, the impact of preprints has led to substantial changes in research communication, from support roles to central positions, and has led to the current state in which nearly three-quarters of scientific researchers rely on preprints as a significant component of scientific literature. The future implications and challenges of preprints, including self-expression, self-organization, and self-sustainability, are also discussed. Binary matrix datasets are widespread in scientific research and analyzing them often leads to straightforward statistical examination using parametric models, such as testing for random uniformity or comparing groups using nonparametric approaches like permutation tests. Yet, researchers may find themselves facing a pressing issue: the concern that observed matrices might be overly regular, potentially influencing their findings and making them inconsistent with theoretical predictions. To address this, we introduce a novel framework for testing random uniformity in binary matrices that accounts for their structural symmetry. This involves measuring the number of distinct matrix configurations that result in the same counts of ones and zeros as the observed matrix, a concept that can be efficiently explored using a binary search algorithm. Our method enables researchers to easily derive p-values or critical values for statistical tests, including those related to comparisons between groups and assessing uniformity. To facilitate this analysis, we also introduce a device for rapidly generating binary matrix configurations in a systematic manner, thereby significantly reducing computational time. The proposed method is demonstrated on artificial and real datasets, showcasing its practical applications in statistical research. To ensure transparency and replicability, we include the implemented R code in the supplementary materials. This work is a continuation of our previous investigation on testing random uniformity in binary matrices, which found that observing too many matrix configurations is a more significant issue than seeing too few. To accommodate this, we modify our approach to focus on the higher quantiles of the matrix configuration count distribution, thereby requiring only minor adjustments to existing methods. Notably, when examining the lower quantiles, our approach mirrors the spirit of permutation tests, while the upper quantiles evoke ideas related to higher-order statistics. Our novel framework is a fresh perspective on permutation testing that is both more versatile and efficient. To exemplify the versatility of our method, we illustrate its application to various research hypotheses that go beyond comparing groups, including assessing whether a binary matrix is uniformly random under a different set of marginal totals, thus extending our framework to include novel research directions. This work is originally to appear in [Biometrics]. Supplementary materials and R code for this work and our previous investigation can be found at https://github.com/c4stats/uniformity_tests. Through both theoretical and experimental investigations, the relationship between the planting interval, the optical bandwidth, and the resonator decay rate has been studied. This latter characteristic is understood as a subgroup being made up of individuals who, given the subgroup's inclusion, fully comply with its requirements. Quantization has garnered significant interest due to its capacity to reduce the computational burden and storage requirements without incurring a decline in performance. One key aspect that sets quantization apart is its ability to improve model generalizability, a phenomenon that has gone largely unexplained. To bridge this knowledge gap, we develop a theoretical framework that REVEALS how quantization enhances generalization. By constructing binary weight neural networks (BNNs) and deriving their neural network knowledge (NK) tensor, we establish a direct connection between the binary weight quantization and the NK tensor's dependence on the training data. Specifically, we demonstrate that converting weighted networks (WNs) to BNNs leads to an NK tensor with smoother characteristics off-the-shelf, resulting in generalization performance improvements. To test our theory, we developed the Quantization Improved by Generalization (QIG) algorithm, which artificially creates an NK tensor with similar smoothing properties in WNs during the training process. Our findings show that QIG yields superior results across various benchmark datasets. Moreover, our research offers innovative methods for enhancing model generalizability through binary weight quantization. A comprehensive investigation of our findings and the relevant code is available at https://github.comhydrabug/quantization-improved-by-generalization. A system's entropy, completely determined by its quantum connections, changes smoothly when systems combine or separate. We apply this principle to examine the connection between conformal field theories and extremal surfaces in a higher-dimensional, curved space. We suggest that this relationship forms a consistent, self-contained framework known as the holographic entropy prism, allowing for new relationships between different entropies of a system. We also represent key features of the prism, such as duality, dominance, and monotonicity, using algebraic and topological properties. The principles governing the prism's behavior emerge from the underlying quantum connections and the extremal nature of the surfaces. These principles remain effective across a wide range of environments and system types, even when interactions fade and in cases of multiple branchings. The prescription for calculating entropy based on extremal surfaces becomes a reliable tool for understanding intricate systems. We represent this framework geometrically as a convex polytope, whose facets correspond to conformal field theories and describe the entropy prism. This approach generalizes to higher dimensions of entropy, representing more complex systems. The methods used here can be applied to study the connection between entropy and geometry in complex systems. Building on the framework by Pyne and Schafer Namekage, our approach generalizes to models defined by any simple algebra with invertible 'crossing matrix'. We apply this method to the XXZ model, using it to derive a formula for the crossing vector in the S1XXXH chain, previously published in [P. Pyne, B. Schafer Namekage, arXiv:2102.04191]. We also extend the method to uniform tensor products of higher-dimensional irreducible modules. Furthermore, we outline the potential adaptation of our method to models involving non-abelian anyons. We verify the accuracy of our crossing vectors through direct computation in specific cases and by proving that our formula satisfies the universal crossing equation. We also relate the crossing vector to the algebra's Galois action, which we illustrate using the XXZ model. We conjecture that this relation holds universally. like stabilization techniques that utilize previous iterations. This research 
investigates five diverse stabilization methods - including self-excitation, 
back-propagation, delay, logical operations, and adaptive learning rate - across 
a range of recovery algorithms. Our performance metrics, encompassing both static 
and dynamic sparsity, reveal that stabilization yields significant improvements, 
with back-propagation and adaptive learning rate exhibiting the greatest effectiveness 
in various environments. Moreover, utilizing stabilization with inadequately designed 
performance-promising algorithms leads to substantial recovery performance improvements, 
ultimately resulting in superior outcomes. This research also includes a readily-useable 
code repository for replicating the presented results. Additionally, an interactive 
visualizer enables users to customize and observe the recovery process. Experimental 
data indicates that standardized stabilization across algorithms produces consistent, 
high-quality results, further validating the efficacy of stabilization in compressed 
sensing. Numerical experiments demonstrate the potential for stabilization to 
significantly enhance compressed sensing recovery, highlighting considerable 
performance improvements and potential for more advanced techniques. Our findings 
also emphasize the value of future research in compressed sensing stabilization.

Formulas for calculating the point spread function (PSF) of combined images 
and the update rule for image deconvolution using the maximum likelihood principle 
are provided. The linear PSF of a combined image is determined by taking a weighted 
average of the individual PSFs, with weights proportional to the flux 
constrained so that the sum remains unity. For nonlinear images, the PSF is 
calculated as the derivative of the nonlinearity model. Based on this, 
an iterative algorithm for deconvolving images is derived, effectively reducing 
noise and preserving pixels with high signal-to-noise ratio. The method can 
be applied to a range of image deconvolution tasks and is particularly useful 
for preserving bright pixels during the deconvolution of noisy images. 
Furthermore, it is demonstrated that this method is equivalent to a linear 
deconvolution applied to an image with its bright pixels clipped. 
Consequently, the method is compatible with conventional deconvolution 
techniques and can be used as either a pre-or post-processing step. 
Ultimately, the method is shown to be effective in removing smoothing from 
images without relying on an a priori knowledge of the PSF. 
Additionally, it is possible to utilize this method for estimating the PSF 
when it is unknown, in which case it can be estimated based on the difference 
between original and deconvolved images. The method is provided as Python 
software, specifically the clippdecon module of PySPE, and is illustrated 
using examples involving Hubble Space Telescope images. Lastly, it is noted 
that this method holds general applicability beyond image deconvolution and 
can be utilized in a broader range of deconvolution tasks.

Despite the potential of quantum computing, widespread adoption is hindered by the lack of reliable quantum error-correcting techniques and robust quantum fault-tolerance protocols. Our study bridges this gap by developing the first traditional verification method for quantum computations prone to errors. Building on a graph homomorphism framework, our protocol uses a self-testing quantum circuit to accurately determine the outcome of a noisy quantum computation, doing so with a linear time complexity of O(π). This represents a significant advancement over previous approaches, which had a quadratic complexity of O(π^2). Furthermore, our method has been successfully implemented in a hardware environment. Additionally, we investigated an alternative approach involving quantum error-correcting codes, but discovered it to be less effective due to the enormous size of supporting circuits, rendering them unfeasible for practical use. Conversely, our proposed solution reflects the trade-offs between reliability, efficiency, and complexity more accurately. Moreover, while there is no absolute threshold for qubit noise that renders quantum computations unreliable, our experiments suggest that the current level of noise in existing hardware significantly hampers the reliability of quantum computations, contaminating the results with considerable error rates. Nevertheless, our protocol remains capable of correcting a limited number of errors even in such scenarios, thereby facilitating the development of reliable quantum computing despite existing noise levels. Lastly, we explored various forms of traditional verification, ultimately recommending the use of measurement-based circuits, which offer enhanced flexibility and redundancy. This study provides a comprehensive understanding of the underlying noise dynamics and presents a feasible solution for practicing quantum computing in the present, offering reliable results while accounting for both measurement and computation errors. Additionally, our protocol presents an effective means of comparing and evaluating quantum circuits, offering a straightforward method for verifying and contrasting the behavior of distinct circuits, which can be extended to support hybrid quantum-classical algorithms as well. Ultimately, this study presents a practical approach for applying quantum fault-tolerance principles in the context of traditional verification. Additionally, we investigated the feasibility of developing a quantum fault-tolerance tool, but discovered that a crucial aspect of such an approach, the process of verifying quantum circuits, remains unsolved. This study presents a comprehensive solution to this problem, enabling the reliable computation of quantum circuits despite the presence of errors, which can be constructed from a quantum triple circuit. Furthermore, we established a novel approach to traditional verification, providing a linear-time complexity solution and offering an efficient means of comparing and evaluating quantum circuits, which can be extended to support hybrid quantum-classical algorithms. This study offers a practical understanding of the underlying noise dynamics

Generating cell shapes randomly to mimic cell development behavior in embryo regions has been achieved to some extent, but training a single universal model to generate all cell types across different species with high precision is still a significant challenge. Most current methods rely on cell shape summaries, such as centroid, orientation, and cell edge maps, to create a conditional shape profile that a single universal model can learn. These shape representations work relatively well for generating the global shapes of cells but often fall short of capturing the intricate details of cell membranes. In our study, we utilize implicit neural representations to model the membrane of a single cell type and achieve significant improvements over existing methods in terms of fidelity. We argue that membrane maps are insufficient for capturing the shape profile of cells and that a conditional neural network would be required for each cell type. To overcome this limitation, we applied robust testing to find the optimal resolution for neural radiance fields (NeRF) models that can generate cell shapes up to 10 grid points in each direction. Our results reveal that these models achieve sub-micrometer accuracy in generating cell shapes, outperforming existing methods. Additionally, we found that reducing the sampling density of cell shapes improves the models' robustness to noise and hard coding, allowing us to achieve 0.78 similarity scores for generated cell shapes without requiring training data. We observed similar results when using spherical harmonic coefficients to represent cell shapes, but with reduced robustness. We do note, however, that these advances come with a significant cost, as our NeRF models require 7.7 GB and spherical harmonic representations require 5.1 GB of memory, making them impractical for training universal cell shape models that can learn from a small number of cell shapes. Consequently, we were unable to train a single universal model for all cell types. Instead, we were able to train four models for distinct cell types - fibroblasts, muticellular cluster cells, polarized cells, and stem cells - and achieved 0.78 similarity scores for generated cell shapes. Our methods do note that reducing the sampling density of cell shapes improves the models' robustness to noise and hard coding. Consequently, we were able to generate cell shapes under extreme conditions, such as high densities and extreme densities, and observed cell division behaviors that matched the training data. Our implicit neural representations of cell shapes have potential applications in the development of video games that simulate realistic cell behavior for educational purposes. Two primary theories, grid cell and place cell, explain spatial cognition with grid cells providing location representation through regularly spaced cells activated at varying frequencies according to the cell's location, and place cells which form associative maps learned from navigation experiences. This theoretical framework suggests that specific neural connections strengthen based on shared activity during associated experiences. To evaluate this model, a simple place cell model was implemented using reinforcement learning to accumulate a cognitive map through repeated navigation in a virtual environment. The results indicate that even without external spatial information, a place cell map can develop consisting of distinct locations associated with particular situations. The corresponding grid cell model displayed regularly activated cells corresponding to the place cell locations. The significant correlation observed between the magnitude of the cell's activity and its distance from the corresponding place cell suggests a strong relationship. Notably, when parts of the grid cell map were compressed into the place cell space, the corresponding place cell magnitudes demonstrated increased correlation. This finding implies that a compressed grid cell map can effectively reconstruct an uncompressed cognitive map. Concurrent transmission based wireless systems have gained significant attention due to their ability to increase throughput, reduce latency and enhance reliability in resource-constrained wireless environments. This class of systems can operate within, outside of, or or concurrently with traditional serial transmission based wireless systems, thus enabling a higher degree of spatial diversity. As a result, these systems typically possess more complex multi-input multi-output (MIMO) characteristics and greater capabilities for concurrent data transfer over multiple channels. This paper provides an in-depth examination of the underlying theory behind these systems, as well as commonly employed transmission techniques in MIMO-based wireless applications. Additionally, the paper reflects on existing research in the field, highlights real-world implementations of these architectures, and proposes a comprehensive wireless architecture that incorporates the magic of superposition. Finally, the paper discusses promising research directions in the area of concurrent transmission based wireless systems. This comprehensive study is tailored to meet the needs of students, instructors, researchers and engineers working in the field of concurrent transmission based wireless systems. This work delves into the geometric analysis of spectrogram level sets to derive generalizations of established spectrogram properties. Building on previous research, we extensively examine the properties of these level sets, including their dimensions, behaviors, and distribution. Our research provides a new mathematical framework for understanding spectrogram level sets, leading to a method for accurately estimating their Hausdorff dimension. This work culminates in an approach for scrutinizing spectrograms, enabling the extraction of meaningful information about signals via level sets. 

In the supplement, we explore the connection between our spectrogram level sets and a widely utilized signal analysis technique based on Levi-Civita differentiation. This connection establishes a method for integrating our dimension estimation approach with Levi-Civita differentiation, potentially yielding improved signal estimation and retrieval. 

Signal spectrograms are a powerful tool for analyzing signals, providing a geometric perspective that underpins numerous signal processing techniques. Spectrograms can be expressed as level sets of the spectrogram function, allowing for the application of stochastic geometry and subsequent estimation of the spectrogram level sets' Hausdorff dimension. 

Our method involves two main approaches - direct and indirect - for spectrogram level set analysis. The direct approach focuses on level sets and expresses the spectrogram as a combination of different dimensions. The indirect approach examines the geometric structure of these level sets, distributing them via polynomial chaos. Both methods enable the detection of signals with coprime components, characterized by distinct dimensions. 

Notably, the direct approach estimates the spectrogram level sets' Hausdorff dimension, incorporating information about their structure. The indirect approach, on the other hand, employs polynomial chaos to transmit signals via level sets and explores their geometric distribution via stochastic analysis. 

Ultimately, both methods enable the scrutiny of spectrograms, extracting information about signals via level sets. 

In the supplement, we establish a connection between the geometric structure of spectrogram level sets and Levi-Civita differentiation, a technique that underpins signal analysis and propagation. By integrating our dimension estimation approach with Levi-Civita differentiation, we potentially obtain improved signal estimation and retrieval. 

It is worth noting that combining our methods with Levi-Civita differentiation may offer a more accurate signal analysis and retrieval technique, encompassing spectrogram level sets and Hausdorff dimension for signal propagation. 

This work, along with the included supplement, presents a geometric analysis of spectrogram level sets, generalizing established properties and providing a new framework for scrutinizing spectrograms, enabling the extraction of information about signals via level sets.

We've developed a reliable universal method to identify and analyze dynamic patterns of chimera and synchronization in neural networks using a chaostheory-based approach. This method leverages long-term temporal behavior characterized by the network's Lyapunov spectrum, determining stability through a straightforward estimation of local linearized instability thresholds. Applying this technique to various disordered networks, regardless of their overall connectivity pattern, has allowed us to accurately detect and distinguish between chimera, synchronized, and asynchronous states. Furthermore, our method indicates the existence of distinct quantitative relationships between the degree of disorder and the emergence of chimera states, which could be useful for creating novel chimera-based information processing systems. An in-depth implementation of this method on a particular class of active-lateral interaction networks has revealed the presence of a unique state that transitions between chimera and synchronized behaviors due to varying parameters, showcasing the efficacy of our approach. This method is freely available as an open-source software tool. Despite its potential applications in neuroscience, this report does not aim to provide a deep understanding of chimera states in neuroscience but rather focuses on the development and testing of our proposed method. Additionally, we emphasize that our analysis is confined to long-term temporal behavior, differing from common techniques that concentrate on short-term transient dynamics. To our knowledge, this paper initiates the first application of chaostheory to spiking neural networks, along with an extensive validation against numerical integration of the original differential equations. Consequently, our results are robust and not prone to observational instability issues that can occur when analyzing finite approximation trajectories. In essence, our approach provides a robust, accurate, and long-term evaluation of the network's behavior. A crucial consideration is that our method uses a specific dynamic behavior described by the network's Lyapunov spectrum, which might not be directly accessible through numerical integration. However, we've successfully verified that our method can accurately identify this behavior from easily obtainable time series data, confirming the reliability of our approach. Nonetheless, our technique is confined to evaluating stability during the asymptotic late stages of transients, which might not accurately represent early dynamic network behavior influencing spiking neuron tolerance to parameter disturbances. An open-source software tool is available to investigate the outcomes presented in this study, incorporating an extensive example demonstrating how our method identifies a chimera state in a model of active-lateral interaction networks. Research into El Ni\~no's two primary flavors - East Pacific and Central Pacific types - has become a significant focus in climate variability studies. Recent investigations further distinguish a third, North Pacific, flavor, though more systematic exploration of this variant and its global spatial and temporal impacts in comparison to the other two flavors has been lacking. This research seeks to rectify this by analyzing the characteristics of all three flavors in terms of their impact on global precipitation patterns. The results reveal that the Central Pacific and East Pacific flavors exhibit distinct regional markings in precipitation variability. The Central Pacific's low seasonal rainfall is mirrored in the opposite hemisphere during the non-active season, whereas the East Pacific's low seasonal rainfall is accompanied by heightened rainfall in Australia and reduced rainfall in South Africa. Conversely, the North Pacific's low seasonal rainfall is most pronounced in Russia and less so in Australia and South Africa. Notably, all three flavors present differently timed high seasonal rainfall patterns. The analysis indicates that each flavor's influence on precipitation variability is distinctly signaled in the North Pacific by the preceding season's rainfall in the case of the North Pacific, the same season's rainfall in the case of the East Pacific, and the following season's rainfall in the case of the Central Pacific. Consequently, monitoring these seasonal rainfall patterns in the North Pacific can provide early warnings of upcoming changes in precipitation, whether an active or a passive season. Lastly, this research also identifies potential indicators of each flavor in the critical South Pacific region, the understanding of which could further complement existing research into using sea-level and temperature data to identify this flavor. The research does, however, caution against relying solely on these indicators, as they can be interswift - meaning they signal the end of one flavor while hinting at the onset of another. The research does, however, propose that these indicators may hold value when combined with other research techniques. Lastly, this research does point out that the research does not address how to identify the beginning of a flavor, simply focusing on easily identifiable signals during and after their active periods. To each multiplicative linear logic proof structure, we can apply two distinct transformations: "removal" and "cut-elimination". This paper delves into the broader implications of these two transformations, demonstrating that they can be streamlined into a single, more fundamental one. Additionally, we show that if a particular multiplicative proof structure has no cuts, cut-elimination becomes a trivial operation. Moving on to the semantic level, we define how these transformations translate to the interpretation of proof structures through ordered monoids, establishing that the semantics remains invariant under these transformations. Finally, we illustrate the relevance of these results to the concept of equivalence in multiplicative proof structures. In particular, we prove that equivalence is an equivalence relation that can be determined solely by examining the structure of the base proof structure, devoid of any cuts. This allows us to formulate a novel notion of equivalence for proof structures with cuts, which we find to be consistent with the traditional notion for cut-free structures. Lastly, we investigate the specific case of MLL with exponential markers, demonstrating that the outcome remains valid in this more comprehensive system as well. Due to space constraints, some of the key concepts and specific theorems have been omitted from this abstract and are instead presented in the accompanying appendix. Furthermore, since the target audience is primarily composed of computer scientists, we have endeavored to simplify the presentation and incorporate an introductory section that provides a concise overview of multiplicative linear logic proof structures and the key concepts necessary for understanding the main results. These concepts are essential for fully grasping the proofs, which we assume will be provided in detail in an upcoming technical report. It has been demonstrated that the electron-phonon and spin-phonon interactions are not only influenced by local environments but also by the momentum of the electrons and holes involved. Momentum-dependent interactions lead to dynamic effects that vary according to the wave vector of the electrons, resulting in distinct temporal characteristics. In extrinsic momentum-dependent interactions, these dynamics are primarily determined by the rate at which the wave vector changes, whereas in intrinsic interactions, dynamic behavior is influenced by both the wave vector and the momentum relaxation time. Finite momentum-dependent interaction lifetimes can give rise to dynamic electron-phonon and spin-phonon interactions that persist for tens of femtoseconds, even in the presence of momentum relaxation. Our understanding of dynamic electron-phonon and spin-phonon interactions will enable the accurate modeling of ultrafast electronic processes and enable the manipulation of charge, spin, and orbital characteristics on an analogous timescale to thermal relaxation. Furthermore, we have shown that dynamic electron-phonon interactions can be inferred from spin-sensitive experiments without the need for independent electron-phonon coupling calculations. Additionally, we have demonstrated that the rapid dynamics of extrinsic spin-phonon interactions can result in the transfer of spin from holes to electrons, an process that can occur on an atimescale comparable to thermal relaxation and may lead to long-lived spin transfer persisting beyond thermal equilibrium. Our theoretical framework incorporates both extrinsic and intrinsic spin-phonon interactions, allowing us to characterize the dynamics of spin transfer through dynamic electron-phonon and spin-phonon interactions. Our theoretical results are applicable to semiconductors and semiconductor devices such as quantum wells, and can be extended to nanostructures and 2D materials like transition metal dichalcogenides. Additionally, we have shown that the concepts outlined can also be applied to superconductors where the electron-phonon interaction plays a crucial role in the mechanism by inducing pairing. In superconductors, the breakdown of the BCS state can occur on a femtosecond timescale due to the momentum-dependent electron-phonon interaction, resulting in a momentum-dependent critical time. Furthermore, we have demonstrated that the critical state can be restored on an analogous timescale to thermal relaxation through the decay of quasiparticle distributions. However, incorporating satellite imagery into industrial flow processes is complicated due to the need for precise image analysis. A feasible solution involves using proposed methods to streamline this process. By integrating spectral image processing and physics-based modeling, the likelihood of errors can be minimized. To further streamline operations, machine learning algorithms can be used to create predictive models that learn patterns in wildfire data and account for its variability. Consider a scenario where multiple individuals share their location data with a service provider, who intends to learn about the distribution of locations for a specific group of people. For instance, a delivery or ride-sharing company might collect location data for its drivers and want to understand the general distribution of their drivers' locations to improve the service. To protect the privacy of these individuals, the service provider uses a location tracking method based on an anonymous privacy fund. This fund works by rewarding users for sharing location data while maintaining confidentiality through a stochastic aggregation process. Prior studies focused on analyzing the impact of reward structures and transmission policies, but did not account for the fact that location data is typically collected under specific prior distributions. To address this gap, we developed methods to model and apply various probability distributions associated with location data collection. Our results show that using these probability distributions can significantly improve the accuracy of inferences the service provider wants to make, while also providing a framework for designing more effective reward structures and transmission policies. Furthermore, our research enables the service provider to accurately estimate the parameters of these probability distributions at any level of accuracy, and verify whether the learned inferences match the intended probability distributions. To demonstrate the practical value of our findings, we also compared different methods for estimating the parameters of these probability distributions, including traditional statistical methods and machine learning algorithms, and showed that location data collectors can achieve nearly the same level of accuracy with as little as 10% of the computational resources required by these methods. Finally, we presented a metric for measuring how effectively the service provider's goals are achieved, and showed that using location data under specific probability distributions can result in a level of accuracy that is up to 200% better than other methods. Based on these findings, we identified design rules for reward structures and transmission policies that enable the service provider to achieve a level of accuracy that is up to 120% better than other methods. To facilitate practical applications, we also implemented these design rules in open-source software. Additionally, we presented a framework that can determine whether the service provider's goals align with individuals' expectations and demonstrated how this framework can be used in a data-driven approach to design reward structures and transmission policies that better match individuals' expectations. Lastly, we identified a point at which the service provider's goals and individuals' expectations converge, thereby alleviating concerns about the service provider's motives when participating in location data sharing. Building on previous work, where a directed graph equivalent of the Ricci curvature was developed based on the Chung Laplacian, this note focuses on characterizing the lower Ricci curvature bound in terms of heat diffusion. We discovered that the heat diffusion process near the initial time can be described using a generalized heat equation, whose solution is related to the directed graph's spectral properties. Notably, our findings indicate that the heat transfer distance is proportional to the square root of the time, and that the concentration of measure phenomenon occurs. This result is supported by two equivalent statements describing the growth rate of heat measures and directed entropies of ball sets. These findings demonstrate that the heat measures' growth rate is analogous to that of ball sets' directed entropy, and that both are related to the square root of the time. Consequently, the concentration of measure phenomenon is evident, and its consequences include the determination of the critical exponent and the establishment of a limit theorem for the normalized entropy of ball sets. We also determined that the exponent is related to the combination of the largest eigenvalue of the directed graph's transition matrix and the curvature bound. Moreover, two properties were proven - the monotonic increase of directed entropy within a given time frame, and the convergence of normalized entropy to zero as the radius approaches zero. These results were used to establish the concentration of measure phenomenon and the convergence of normalized entropy. Furthermore, two properties were found - the monotonic decrease of entropy outside a given time frame, and the convergence of normalized entropy to one as the radius approaches infinity. These results were used to determine the limit of normalized entropy as the radius approaches infinity, and to establish the concentration of measure phenomenon. We also found that the limit of normalized entropy as the radius approaches infinity is a function of the curvature bound and the time. Furthermore, two properties were identified - the maximum directional growth rate of heat measures and the maximum directional growth rate of ball sets.
