The effectiveness of programmable electrostatic phase plates in improving resolution in transmission electron microscopes is well established. However, there are concerns about how they will affect image measurement accuracy, especially in high-resolution structures. To address these doubts, researchers used simulations to determine if a programmable phase plate could also act as an aberration corrector in a transmission electron microscope. To this end, they designed an computational model of an electron microscope that includes features like spherical aberration, a weak beam and high-resolution hole array. By applying various programs to the phase plate to eliminate built-in aberrations, researchers were able to demonstrate that it is possible to eliminate spherical and astigmatism aberrations through numerical adjustment of the phase plate. Once these primary aberrations were corrected, the microscope's resolution significantly improved and remained stable even when small amounts of primary aberrations returned. Surprisingly, the findings indicated that the accuracy of structure measurements in the electron Fourier transform did not decrease; in fact, it remained stable at a level higher than 100 millionths, regardless of resolution. This suggests that even with very high-resolution images, structural measurements can be trusted. Based on these results, the possibility of using a programmable phase plate not just for improving resolution but also for correcting optical aberrations in high-resolution electron microscopy appears feasible. This knowledge could also be applied to other areas such as optical microscopy. Furthermore, the study indicates that the true potential of phase plates has not been fully utilized and that they may be capable of more advanced functionality than previously thought. Additionally, the study lays the foundation for the use of numerical phase plates in high-resolution imaging and suggests that even minor additional functionality features could significantly enhance the performance of high-resolution electron microscopes. This could be particularly beneficial for 4D electron cryo-microscopy, cryo-electron tomography, and other high-resolution imaging techniques. Furthermore, the study suggests that these concepts could be applied to optical microscopy with the use of spatial light modulators. The fundamental Universal Approximation Theorem states that a feedforward neural network with one hidden layer can approximate any continuous function with arbitrary precision, given sufficient regularization. Despite this theoretical foundation, implementing neural networks in practice remains complicated by the need for manually selecting the number of hidden layers, number of neurons in each layer, activation functions, and a learning rate for backpropagation. To streamline neural network implementation, our research develops a novel, automated structure-finding method that leverages the Universal Approximation Theorem and eliminates the need for manual hyperparameter tuning. By employing a novel, gradient-free algorithm based on evolutionary principles, our approach identifies the optimal neural network configuration for a specific task with minimal computational overhead. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed framework achieves superior generalization performance and outperforms traditional hyperparameter tuning methods. The implementation is freely accessible via the NN-UAT GitHub repository. Additionally, we present an online demo showcasing the framework's capabilities. Key findings of our study have been embedded into a executable report, allowing readers to reproduce our results using the provided code. Crucially, our work preserves the theoretical underpinnings of the Universal Approximation Theorem, distinguishing it from existing evolutionary neural network research. Furthermore, we investigate the link between our approach and nonconvex optimization, addressing a previously overlooked critical problem in neural network research: the lack of theoretical guarantees for evolutionary methods. The theoretical underpinnings of our work are based on two novel contributions, a Convergence Theorem and a Structural Bias Correction, which have been formally established and proven. The latter is shown to be inferior to our proposed estimators, which are also found to be robust against outliers, performed well across various sample sizes, and predominantly outperformed the influence function estimator.  Notably, in the presence of missing data, our proposed estimators exhibited improved performance relative to the same estimators applied to complete data.  The research findings were validated through numerous tests, including comparisons based on mean squared error, normalized bias, and specific quantile regression analysis. Our study examines the relationship between head-mounted display distortions and user discomfort in Virtual Reality. We developed a tool to measure field of view distortions on VR users and applied it in an experiment involving 120 participants. The participants experienced various levels of distortion while engaging in a stimulating game and provided comfort ratings based on their perceptions. The results reveal that user discomfort is strongly associated with distortion levels, even when the distortion affects the field of view. However, user performance in the task remained unaffected by distortion levels. Furthermore, we discovered that users tend to rate their comfort more negatively than expected based on measurement errors. Interestingly, compression of the field of view, rather than distortion itself, is a key factor that contributes to discomfort. Conversely, we found that users are more tolerant of distortion that affects the side fields of view. Our research highlights the importance of consideration and potential mitigation strategies for compression and calibration-related distortions in VR development. Additionally, we provide insights on how to refine VR systems by exploiting user tolerance of certain types of distortion. Our research has implications for designing more comfortable VR experiences and contributes to the development of self-calibrating VR systems that minimize distortion-related problems. The code for our research is publicly available, allowing other researchers to verify and replicate our results. Time-efficient approaches to autocomponent analysis are crucial for processing large amounts of real-time data in edge AI systems. Research has focused on the fast calculation of autoregression components, but automatic feature extraction components require more complex calculations. We present a new, efficient algorithm, M-ar-K-Fast, for calculating both autoregression and feature extraction components from mixed-order models. The method is based on the principle of minimizing component variances with constraints on model order and efficiency. We derive analytical formulas for calculating components under given model orders and develop a forward search approach to dynamically determine optimal feature extraction component orders. Experimental results demonstrate that M-ar-Fast determines component models accurately and achieves significant improvements in calculation efficiency, outperforming existing methods by up to twofold. Additionally, M-ar-K-Fast retains key strengths of existing methods while enhancing their computational efficiency. The study includes code implementations and dataset recommendations for future research. M-ar-K-Fast represents a forward-thinking approach to autocomponent analysis and paves the way for widespread adoption in real-time edge AI applications. We've developed a speedy computation of skewed spherical harmonics, enabling quick analysis of the bispectrum in cosmology. The ability to quickly examine non-trivial configurations of angular momentum and momentum transfer is crucial for comparing cosmological simulations with observations from the cosmic microwave background and galaxy surveys, a process that's currently slow and hindered by limitations. We've created an algorithm that calculates skewed harmonic coefficients approximately $5000$ times faster than the standard method, using only $10-20$ percent more resources. We've also adapted this algorithm to compute approximations of skewed harmonic coefficients with an accuracy of $10^{-6}$ in just a few milliseconds. We've incorporated both methods into the HEALPix library to speed up the comparison of simulated signals with different cosmological models, including signals from the cosmic microwave background and galaxy surveys, a process that's currently too slow with current methods. We've validated our new method by comparing its results with the exact method, checking that the differences in calculated bispectra are less than the measurement errors, and have seen that the new method takes significantly less time to compute without sacrificing accuracy. We believe our new method will enable researchers to make the most of recent and forthcoming data from the cosmic microwave background and galaxy surveys, a total of $1.4$ million times faster than the standard method. As artificial intelligence becomes more practical, protecting it from malicious attacks has become a pressing concern. The concept of adversarial robustness has emerged, referring to the ability of a machine learning model to perform well even when given intentionally false inputs. However, current methods for enhancing a model's robustness typically rely on numerical estimates and do not provide any assurance that the added uncertainty will remain stable under future use. In this study, a formal framework for incorporating adversarial robustness into Bayesian inference is introduced. A mathematical proof shows that incorporating a margin of uncertainty into the model's training will indeed result in a broader predictive distribution over future test inputs. The researchers then apply this theory to the training of deep learning models, achieving a significant reduction in test accuracy losses while gaining assurance that the expanded uncertainty will remain stable. Moreover, the researchers find that utilizing this trained uncertainty can lead to more informed decision-making in high-stakes applications by providing a greater prediction range. Finally, a verification procedure is proposed to confirm that the model's increased robustness translates to a deeper understanding of the learning process. The researchers successfully verify the theoretical conclusions on a diverse set of image classification datasets and demonstrate that the model's expanded uncertainty holds constant even when subject to intense attacks. Furthermore, the researchers show that incorporating this uncertainty leads to more prudent decision-making, thereby establishing a new connection between predictive uncertainty and adversarial robustness. The researchers hope that this formalized approach will facilitate the development of machine learning algorithms that not only perform well but also possess a new and important aspect of adversarial robustness. This study investigates the effects of various dimensionality reduction techniques on hyperspectral image classification. Different methods were applied to the famous Indian Pines dataset using a prominent deep learning algorithm and six popular supervised classification algorithms. Our analysis compares the reduced-dimensional datasets based on pixel similarity and the computational requirements of the techniques. Our findings show that certain methods like LeNet can benefit from dimensionality reduction, while others like VGG16 are unaided by it. Additionally, using a deep learning method for classification may render dimensionality reduction unnecessary. Our study highlights the suitability of Linear Discriminant Analysis for reducing hyperspectral data using LeNet. Interestingly, principal component analysis and self-organizing maps, which are based on different principles, yielded similar results. Furthermore, our research demonstrates that undersampling the hyperspectral response can lead to improved classification performance when paired with suitable machine learning methods. Ultimately, our study underscores the importance of carefully selecting dimensionality reduction techniques for hyperspectral image classification, considering both the method and the associated algorithm. Compressing NLP models with minimal computational resources has become a crucial objective. Unlike typical model compression methods, which evaluate the accuracy of classification models on synthetic data after decompression, this research examines the efficacy of various compression techniques on real-world data without decompression. By comparing the accuracy of authentic data under different compression parameters, this research demonstrates that some established compression methods like Tensor-Train and Tensor-Contract may not always be suitable for NLP models. Interestingly, the random pruning method surprisingly yielded comparable results to the top-performing model in some cases. Ultimately, this research suggests that the effectiveness of model compression techniques should be re-evaluated by utilizing authentic data and a more precise metric, as measuring relative error proves more reliable than evaluating classification accuracy. The process of exciton condensation leads to phase transitions in solids. To better understand this, researchers are developing ab initio methods that combine theoretical techniques with approximate solutions to describe the complex behavior of electrons in solids. Two such methods, ab initio GW and ab initio dynamical mean-field theory, are used to investigate the exciton condensation in titanium diselenide (TiSe2). When applying the ab initio GW approach alone, it fails to capture the experimental temperature at which the phase transition occurs. However, by combining it with the ab initio dynamical mean-field theory, researchers were able to reproduce the experimental results and gain insights into the role of correlations and excitons in the phase transition. This combination of approaches can be applied to various problems, including the exciton condensation in dense quasiparticle systems. Additionally, the technique has potential applications in the search for exciton condensates in monolayer and thin-film systems of TiSe2. Furthermore, the methodology can be used to investigate phase transitions in other materials, such as trigonal TiTe2, which may also provide opportunities for discovering new exciton condensates. On the other hand, using the ab initio GW approach alone, researchers were able to identify some crucial features of the phase transition in TiSe2 that are challenging to capture through other theoretical methods. Moreover, by applying the ab initio GW approach with a dynamical vertex approximation, researchers were able to identify key features of the phase transition in TiSe2 that are difficult to capture through other theoretical methods. To analyze the impact of external magnetic fields on novel symmetries in superconductors, we use a rotating frame to describe Cooper pairs with non-trivial angular momentum in the presence of a nematic interaction that breaks rotational symmetry. In the case of a triplet Cooper pair with zero momentum in the neighborhood of a four-fold symmetry point, we find that the Cooper pairs develop a magnetic response that is proportional to the square of the external field. This results in the Cooper pairs exhibiting spontaneous magnetic polarization when in contact with a marginally unstable mode that facilitates pairing. Furthermore, the critical temperature of the superconductor decreases in proportion to the square root of the external field. In the event that the external field induces a symmetry breaking that a neighboring superconductor exhibits, we find that the Cooper pairs develop a novel response that scales in inverse proportion to the external field, with the critical temperature increasing in direct proportion to the external field. In both scenarios, the behavior of the triplet Cooper pairs is distinguished from that of ordinary superconductors, with the triplet Cooper pairs exhibiting an unconventional response that is not observed in ordinary superconductors. We propose a new research paradigm for setting training objectives in machine learning. Unlike standard regularization techniques that solely restrict the model's capacity, our approach, minimax engaged learning, also imposes constraints on the data. This dual minimax framework in ML draws on concepts from game theory and we demonstrate that it can be effectively implemented through the use of Bregman divergence functions. Notably, our research reveals that models trained using this paradigm exhibit enhanced generalizability when compared to similarly constrained models using standard regularization. Moreover, our results show that the optimal game-theoretic solution correlates positively with L1 regularization, and we provide theoretical and empirical justifications for this observation. To facilitate the practical application of our model, we have developed a Python library that enables researchers to test minimax engaged learning on a variety of problems. Our study also includes an examination of the impact of diverse loss functions and data constraints, and we verify that the benefits of our training paradigm extend to models deployed in inference mode. To date, our smallest model trained using minimax engaged learning has achieved a top-1 accuracy of 80.2% on the CIFAR-10 dataset, surpassing previously published results. Furthermore, our research includes an in-depth analysis of how different game-theoretic values, specifically Nash equilibrium and maxmin optimization, translate to ML training objectives. Our study demonstrates that maxmin optimization training, although suboptimal in theory, yields models with generalizable properties. To illustrate the applicability of our training paradigm in real-world contexts, our researchers also employed minimax engaged learning to build a binary image classifier from Wikipedia pages. The system was trained using a dataset comprised of binary images derived from Wikipedia pages, and our results show that the resulting model can achieve a top-1 accuracy of 80.2% using the Accuracy@k metric. Our study provides a theoretical and empirical understanding of the minimax engaged learning paradigm, and we hypothesize that the benefits of this training objective have the potential to benefit a broad range of machine learning tasks. The minimax engaged learning library, along with our research findings, have been made available for download at https://github.com/gatech-ai/minimax-ml. Our website at http://www.gatech.edu/ml/minimax also provides additional resources and context for our study. Extended versions of this research have been published in arXiv:2101.02846 and arXiv:2006.15755. Related research can be accessed via the following DOI: 10.53469.

To study the evolution of musical styles, we analyzed the informational complexity of songs from the Great Society Song Database, spanning nearly five decades. Our analysis considered how musical arrangements changed over time, including variations in tempo and meter. We used a complexity measure derived from the works of Kolmogorov and Chaitin to calculate the complexity of individual songs and represented it graphically through a frequency distribution. Finding that the complexity distribution was not normally distributed, but rather skewed to the left, we applied a mathematical function to model it. Our results showed that the complexity of songs released in the 21st century was greater than those released in the 1960s, indicating an increase in musical arrangements. Furthermore, correlating our data with data from the Library of Congress and US Census Bureau, we found a positive relationship between musical complexity and societal factors such as urbanization and access to education. These findings are consistent with the theories of Konrad Lorenz and Steven Pinker, suggesting that social changes contribute to the development of musical styles. We validated our analysis by applying it to two other cultural phenomena: literature and human languages, observing similar correlations between cultural complexity and societal factors. Ultimately, our study demonstrates the effectiveness of quantitative methods in analyzing cultural evolution and provides a framework for further research into the development of musical styles. Additionally, our analysis highlights the importance of considering the inherent characteristics of cultural systems and the interconnectedness of societal factors when studying cultural evolution. Ludics is a mathematical framework for concurrent interaction that is also a proof-theoretic framework. It is closely related to the Girard's linear logic proof-net approach and can be visualized through a device called the 'glossary'. Traditional Ludics focuses on'marked' proofs, whereas 'unmarked' Ludics is an extension that facilitates a more direct connection between proofs and interactive systems. In this paper, we re-examine the core concepts of unmarked Ludics and develop a new interpretation for unmarked proof-nets, based on a flow table-like structure known as a 'harmony'. This harmony reflects the flow of 'names' that can be established during a computational process and it is revealed through a series of static analysis steps. One key insight is that the concepts of focus, choice, and focus transfer, which are significant in linear logic and Ludics, can be re-characterized as reflecting the emergence of names at different points in time. Ultimately, this paper is motivated by the hope that the harmony view of unmarked Ludics can serve as a useful tool for analyzing and understanding the behavior of computational systems. Furthermore, this paper is a condensed version of the author's doctoral dissertation. 

Note that the original dissertation contains further developments, including an extension of the harmony interpretation to a higher-level functional programming language based on unmarked linear logic. Moreover, this paper is primarily a tutorial-style introduction to unmarked Ludics and it is hoped that the concepts and techniques discussed here can also be of value to researchers working in related areas. Finally, this harmonic view of unmarked Ludics may also be of interest to researchers in other related research streams, such as stateful program logic. 

An associated technical report is available at arXiv:2201.05242. This paper has been published in Transactions of the Royal Society of South Africa, volume B2, issue 1, and a preprint version can be found at arXiv:2103.05731.

The Average Treatment Effect (ATE) is a causal parameter that can be estimated in a dataset with covariate information, and its nonparametric identification equation involves an average function of covariates for specific individuals. When there are numerous covariates and no underlying structure, implementing this equation using neural networks has become a preferred approach. However, the lack of a well-established method for standardizing these networks on individual data points has been a limitation. Researchers suggest using standardized neural networks to estimate the ATE, and through simulations using real datasets, the proposed method has been tested and compared to alternative treatments. Additionally, the theoretical underpinnings of this method have been established by proving its consistency and the asymptotic normality of its estimator under specific conditions. Under these conditions, the rate at which the estimator converges to the true ATE can be determined. Researchers have also provided codes for the methods discussed in this study. Through the proposed methods, the challenges presented by high dimensions of covariates and the nonparametric estimation of treatment effects have been addressed. Researchers have demonstrated that the ATE and CTE can be standardized efficiently using neural networks, and the findings of this study can be utilized in numerous applications where these parameters are crucial, such as in marketing and clinical research. Researchers have observed that the Standardized Neural Network (SNN) and the Standardized Augmented Neural Network (SANN) methods display exceptional performance in estimating the ATE and CTE compared to other parametric methods. A typical strategy for modelling extreme events involves considering occurrences beyond a high threshold as events of a non-homogeneous Poisson process. Our method relies on a straightforward analytical transformation that can be applied both in and out of a Bayesian context. To validate this new approach, we perform simulations on synthetic data and compare it with alternative methods on real-world data from rainfall and stock market returns. Airborne transmission risk in confined environments like buses is complexly affected by various factors like airflow patterns, occupant positioning, and the dynamics of respiratory particles. Predictive models for disease transmission on urban buses often utilize straightforward approaches, assuming uniform air circulation and equal exposure risks everywhere on the vehicle. However, there's limited scientific evidence to support these methods. In an attempt to improve transmission risk assessment, our study focuses on the airflow patterns in urban buses using computational fluid dynamics (CFD). The findings of our research indicate that exposure risks are not consistently distributed throughout the urban bus. In contrast to previous transmission risk assessment models, our research indicates that certain positions may carry lower risks of transmission. Therefore, it's advised that these risks are reconsidered in future transmission risk assessment models. Additionally, our study introduces a simplified framework that can be used by non-experts to estimate exposure risks and calculate the transmission risk on an urban bus. The accuracy of this framework has been validated against the detailed airflow simulations. Furthermore, our study explores the impact of modulating airflow by the bus's front grille and windshield on exposure risks. Based on these simulations, our study proposes several enhancements that can significantly reduce exposure risks. Specifically, these modifications include increasing the size of the grille to at least 380x150 mm and ensuring that the windshield has a lower edge at or below 150 mm from the top, with a minimum of 520 mm between the top of the windshield and the roof of the bus. The incorporation of these designs could considerably lower the transmission risk on urban buses. Lastly, our study includes recommendations for further research based on the complex airflow patterns in urban buses identified during our study. These potential research areas could be exploring the influence of turbulence on exposure risks or the collection and analysis of field data to complement our research. Detailed methods and detailed results are available online. Illustrations, videos, and interactive 3D visualizations have also been made available for this research at the link below: https://github.com/Calculo-UIO/Urban_Bus Exposure_Risk_Assessment/blob/main/index.html. Additionally, detailed airflow simulations have been uploaded to the research container at the following link: https://coclow5.container.shinyapps.io/urban_bus_raw_data/. Furthermore, the uploaded container includes sample user data, along with 3D visualizations and other related resources. Additional research considerations have also been uploaded at the following link: https://calculateduo-washington.github.io/Urban_Bus_Exposure_Risk_Assessment/index.html. Additional research

This study focuses on the $\beta$-decay characteristics of $^{135,137}$Te isotopes, specifically examining their atomic masses, $\log ft$ values, and the relative strengths of the $\beta$-delayed $\gamma$-transitions. The theoretical estimates were generated through large-scale shell-model computations by utilizing two different Hamiltonians: the MNV18 one-body Hamiltonian and the corrected MNV18 Hamiltonian which accounted for higher-order Pauli corrections. The results were then compared with the experimental data, revealing that the corrections brought the theoretical $\log ft$ values into closer agreement with the experimental results for both $^{135}$Te and $^{137}$Te. The applied theoretical framework demonstrated a satisfactory level of agreement with the experimental data, with an average $\log ft$ error of 0.06 for both isotopes. Furthermore, the study identified potential $\beta$-delayed $\gamma$-transitions that were previously overlooked in previous experiments. The theoretical $\log ft$ values indicated that $\beta$-only transitions should have higher $\log ft$ values compared to the previously calculated ones. To validate the theoretical $\log ft$ calculations, the theoretical $\log ft$ values were corrected to match the experimental double-beta decay energy $E_\beta^{(0\nu\beta\beta)}$. The applied correction resulted in $\log ft$ error reductions of approximately 0.10 and 0.13 for $^{135}$Te and $^{137}$Te, respectively. To further refine the theoretical $\log ft$ values, the shell-model spacing was re-evaluated at specific points corresponding to the $\log ft$ values of 5 and 6, which led to the attainment of theoretical $\log ft$ values in closer agreement with the experimental results. The applied corrections brought the theoretical $T_{1/2}$ within closer agreement with the experimental results. Moreover, the theoretical $\log ft$ values enabled the determination of the $\log ft$ values associated with previously overlooked $\beta$-delayed $\gamma$-transitions. To achieve this goal, the theoretical $\log ft$ values were plotted in descending order, which facilitated the tracking of the previously overlooked transitions. A double auction is the most widely used trading mechanism despite being criticized for not being able to determine whether the equilibrium is reached. Our research presents a new method for determining whether a double auction reaches equilibrium by analyzing and comparing bid and ask price lists. Our algorithm can confirm equilibrium in specific cases and provide approximate results for others. To resolve issues with double auctions having too many solutions, we've developed a novel and unique demand and supply function. These functions enable a direct comparison of bid and ask price lists and make it possible to determine if an equilibrium is reached without relying on the revealed preference approach. To improve the uniqueness of solutions, we've also developed a new trading mechanism. Our research applies validated numerical methods to analyze and compare the performance of double auctions and other more recent trading mechanisms. These numerical methods enable the determination of the largest possible revenue for a seller and the lowest possible cost for a buyer. Our study shows that double auctions are not suitable for a single valuated market and can result in inferior outcomes compared to more recent mechanisms. However, double auctions perform best in multi-valued markets, and their properties make them suitable for large-scale applications. These findings are validated through numerical analysis and comparisons with other established mechanisms. This study delves into analyzing the structure of nonexpansive functions on discrete time periodic graphs. Significant progress has been made in understanding the composition of periodic functions, particularly when one component is nonexpansive. In contrast, the decomposition of a nonexpansive function into periodic components remains an understudied area. We focus on two main objectives: first, to establish a new decomposition theory for nonexpansive functions at the graph level, and second, to extend this framework to stochastic processes and a specific class of Lévy processes. This research not only enhances our understanding of nonexpansive functions but also facilitates the development of unique ergodic theorems. Unique conditions are identified to ensure the convergence of a nonexpansive process to a unique ergodic solution. Our work further demonstrates that these findings can be applied to both geometric and non-geometric graphs. Moreover, the theorems derived from our decomposition theory are exemplified through relevant real-world applications, such as stochastic process analysis and piecewise deterministic Markov processes. These examples illustrate that our results can be utilized to solve complex problems in various fields. Additionally, the proof of our primary theorem relies on our previously developed inverse theorem for nonexpansive functions. This inverse theorem has far-reaching implications and multiple uses. Furthermore, the theorems presented in this research are corroborated by numerous examples and counterexamples, providing valuable insights. Notably, the counterexamples showcased exhibit anomalous behavior while their nonexpansive components exhibit ergodic behavior, demonstrating that our findings are precise and uncover previously unknown properties. Lastly, the research offers a sketch of a potential approach to generalize our findings to a broader functional analytic setting. This potential generalized framework is rooted in the properties of nonexpansive multivalued functions. In conclusion, this research expands the knowledge of periodic decompositions and nonexpansive functions, yielding novel and precise theorems that break new ground in the field. These theorems exhibit sharp conditions, exemplified through various examples and counterexamples. Moreover, the research offers to translate these theorems to stochastic processes and Lévy processes, facilitating novel ergodic theorems with precise and unique conditions. In modern research on data-driven systems, a primary focus lies on developing accurate models from limited and noisy data. The dynamic mode decomposition (DMD) technique plays a key role in analyzing complex data sets and extracting meaningful insights. Nonetheless, critical drawbacks exist within the original DMD methodology: it yields a sparse equation representation and an optimal solution is not guaranteed. In addition, when applying DMD to high-dimensional systems, a key issue arises with regard to dimensionality constraints. To address these challenges, a novel optimization framework called LANDO has been developed. LANDO generates a dense equation representation and ensures optimal results can be achieved. Moreover, LANDO includes an efficient regularization method that enables reduced-dimensional modeling of high-dimensional systems. A major strength of LANDO lies in its ability to derive a kernel version, which facilitates the application to partial information and uncertain data. Experimental results on various systems have demonstrated the effectiveness of LANDO. A related work on the application of DMD has also been contributed through the development of KLANDO. KLANDO includes two primary versions, namely LANDO-GP for nonlinear systems and LANDO-SP for partial information systems. KLANDO achieves state-of-the-art performance in its respective categories. Valuable directions for future research have also been identified. Furthermore, the developed techniques have been successfully applied to the analysis of a solar wind time series and a planetary gear system. Relevant codes have been publicly posted on the GitHub platform. URLs for access to this resource are provided. LANDO and KLANDO offer novel solutions to the challenges inherent to DMD, thereby serving as valuable tools for data analysis. They can be utilized within numerous domains, including aerospace, civil engineering, geophysics, geology, medicine, power systems, robotics, meteorology, and transportation. These domains may employ these techniques to improve performance and gain deeper physiological and system understanding. In summary, the primary objectives of this research were to address the sparse equation and optimality limitations in DMD, as well as to develop a regularization method for reduced-dimensional modeling of high-dimensional systems and a kernel version that accommodates partial information and uncertain data. data from the chess.com community, allowing for a comprehensive examination of the
complexity and relatedness of openings utilizing complexity metrics and similarity
measurements. Furthermore, predictions on chess.com have been evaluated using
advanced machine learning techniques, highlighting the correlation between complexity
metrics and performance outcomes. Results showed that higher complexity is linked to
poorer outcomes, indicating a straightforward cause-and-effect relationship between

analysis to organize chess openings based on their connections, and explores the
significance of specific opening strategies, such as controlling the center of the
board. Ultimately, this research provides a solid foundation for future studies on
chess openings, grounded in statistical analysis of a large, diverse dataset.

Various theoretical models attempt to explain the origin of millisecond pulsars (MSPs). To further elucidate the direct transformation of neutron stars (NSs) from white dwarfs (WDs), particularly through accretion-induced collapse (AIC), researchers have been interested in identifying WDs that are destined to evolve into MSPs. The primary goal of this study is to determine fundamental parameters of MSP-producing WDs that undergo AIC, such as mass, radius, and core temperature. Using advanced computer simulations, researchers have modeled WD evolution to identify AIC progenitors. The results show that fundamental parameters of these WDs, such as mass, radius, and core temperature, can be accurately calculated by applying specific laws. The findings of this research are consistent with observed data and provide valuable insights into WD evolution. The parameters obtained can help researchers identify potential MSP progenitors among observed WDs, thereby providing crucial evidence to support the WD AIC theory. The derived parameters also have the potential to improve the understanding of population synthesis, radio pulsar, and X-ray binary star phenomena. Additionally, these parameters may aid researchers in identifying magnetar candidates and providing the necessary conditions for black hole formation. Lastly, these parameters may help researchers better understand the causes of supernova explosions using the double-degenerate AIC scenario as a reference. This allows for a thorough classification of non-local characteristics in such systems. The study further investigates non-local dynamics in the context of polymer-like chains and establishes a theoretical framework for developing Euler-Lagrange equations in differential equations involving non-local functions. The findings are then validated with practical examples. Lastly, the paper explores the dynamics of a classical particle in terms of non-local characteristics. The research contributes to the understanding of non-local mechanics by clarifying the concepts of functional form and temporal-spatial dependencies. The study is a crucial precursor to developing a comprehensive theory of non-local mechanics. Ultimately, the paper lays the groundwork for a thorough analysis of continuous media based on non-local characteristics. The theoretical framework has been successfully applied to a range of problems in condensed matter physics, including polymer-like chains and a classical particle. Three-dimensional objects can be conveyed through virtual reality freehand
sketches, allowing users to convey complex shapes and avoid language barriers.
However, this technique faces challenges in capturing the sketch's intent
due to the discrepancy between the sketch's 3D shape appearance and its 2D
representation. To overcome this limitation, our approach focuses on linking
the sketch's 2D fragments to its corresponding 3D shape appearance through
semantic segmentation and 3D shape alignment. To facilitate this process,
we introduce a new dataset, known as VR-Drawing, comprising 360-degree 3D shapes
and freehand VR sketches rendered in four different lighting conditions.
Our experiments demonstrate that by incorporating the sketch's 2D fragments to
its 3D shape appearance through semantic segmentation and 3D shape alignment,
our approach outperforms state-of-the-art shape retrieval techniques. The
proposed framework and the VR-Drawing dataset are now available for public
access at https://openresearch.louisville.edu/. This research was supported

A significant issue in current research on reinforcement learning is the lack of a clear understanding of how experiments are conducted effectively. To address this limitation, we have developed a quantitative method to measure the effectiveness of a learning task by evaluating the learning process's end goals. In our study, we utilized this approach to identify the features of reinforcement learning tasks that facilitate successful learning. Using a large dataset of reinforcement learning tasks, we analyzed the correlation between the characteristics of the tasks and their learnability. Through this analysis, we discovered that effective motor learning is influenced by tasks that require exploration of the task environment, precision in movement execution, and the incorporation of visual information. These findings provide valuable insights for designing learning tasks that promote skilled behavior. Additionally, our research has several applications, including generating realistic video games and simulating complex robotic tasks. The impact of our research could be seen in areas such as robotic training and the development of autonomous vehicles. We plan to deepen our understanding of effective motor learning by investigating how to apply our findings to more complex learning tasks involving 3D environments. We anticipate that our research will facilitate the creation of challenging training simulations that model real-world robotic tasks precisely. Furthermore, our approach has the potential to be utilized in the testing and validation of autonomous vehicle learning methods. We expect that our underlying evaluation methodology will be of considerable use to the robotics and autonomous vehicle communities. We are currently working on extending our method to evaluate learning tasks in three-dimensional environments. We anticipate that our research will contribute substantially to the development of efficient reinforcement learning algorithms. Vibrant Poincaré symmetry is obtained by extending the Poincaré algebra with four commuting coordinate-dependent boosts. This enhanced algebra can be achieved in various ways, each corresponding to different irreducible representations of the Galilean algebra. By selecting a representation with scalar properties, the resulting action mimics Einstein's gravity theory when coupled with Gibbons-Wiltshire term. An invariant Lagrangian for massless particles, excluding ghosts, can also be derived from the vibrant Poincaré algebra. This Lagrangian yields the conventional Poincaré invariant action for massless particles. Conversely, a novel action for massive particles, invariant under the vibrant Galilean algebra, can be obtained by discarding the conventional mass term. This new action may serve as a candidate for particle theory in a Newtonian limit. Moreover, a vibrant Pauli-Sobolev algebra leads to a Lagrangian for a spin-1 particle that thwarts gauge fixating, as its vibrant gauge transformations remain invariable under the Pauli-Sobolev transformation. Finally, a vibrant Nilpotent algebra in two dimensions generates an invariant action for a massless d=2 particle, which has a novel characteristics distinct from the conventional massless d=2 particle. This research may provide fresh approaches to fundamental theory, particularly in gravity and particle physics. It is hypothesized that a vibrant symmetry might be a crucial paradigm for generalizing theories in curved spacetimes and non-invariant algebras. Additionally, this research may be of significant interest in the fields of non-invariant general relativity and generalized theories in curved spacetimes. We have developed four new upward planarity techniques that can solve sequential or parameterized problems related to upward embedding, link drawing, and combinatorial embedding with some restrictions. Our methods can be applied to various problem variants such as Full Upward Planarity, Planarity with Structure Preserving Embedding, and Outerplanarity. Specifically, we have found efficient parameterized algorithms for Full Upward Planarity and Planarity with Structure Preserving Embedding, and established a parameterized technique for Link Drawing with the guarantee of no 2-chain. Interestingly, we discovered that Outerplanarity does not have a satisfactory parameterized algorithm. Our techniques can be applied to various problem variants with guarantees. Moreover, we propose a new concept called "sequentiality degree" to evaluate the feasibility of combining techniques in upward planarity. This degree helps us to determine which techniques can be combined effectively. Our experimental evaluations have shown that the obtained results are encouraging. Furthermore, we have applied our parameterized techniques to establish new parameterized tricoloring algorithms for Full Upward Planarity and Planarity with Structure Preserving Embedding. Additionally, we found an efficient parameterized algorithm for Link Drawing without 2-chain. Lastly, we propose new sufficient conditions for Outerplanarity. These conditions could be useful in solving the problem in a parameterized approach. Our work contributes to extending the applicability of parameterized techniques in graph drawing and planarity problems. The source code of our experimental evaluations is available online.

Image-based goal-oriented navigation is a challenging task in robotic research. To overcome this, robots are typically provided with a map or a set of reference images that they can navigate to. However, managing and selecting relevant previous experiences (memories) becomes a limiting factor in achieving this. Current techniques either disregard existing memories or view them as a hindrance. We present a new method called MemoNav, which effectively incorporates memories in visual navigation. MemoNav treats memories as spatially-oriented data sources and proposes two main functions: 1) eachening memories to be relevant to the current navigation task, and 2) selecting a subset of optimized memories that maximize navigation performance. We demonstrate MemoNav's efficacy through comprehensive testing of viewpoint manipulation and goal-directed navigation tasks and showcase its superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art techniques. Additionally, we provide insights into MemoNav's performance by analyzing its navigation success rate and memory optimization quality. We also offer theoretical justification for MemoNav's design and showcase its practical effectiveness. MemoNav is now available under an open-source license at https://github.com/ChenZheng123/MemoNav. We hope this technology will contribute to the advancement of visual navigation research. This abstract discusses our thorough investigation of a dynamic system where each entity acts according to a local replacement rule that is influenced by its neighbors. Regardless of the initial conditions or the specific replacement rules applied, the entity dynamics always result in stable equilibrium states. Additionally, we demonstrate that the equilibrium state achieved depends only on the specific network topology and the replacement rules employed. To further analyze the dynamics, we develop and apply mathematical tools, such as the transfer operator's spectrum, to understand and predict collective behavior. Finally, using numerical simulations and theoretical models, we investigate how different network topologies affect collective behavior and observe that the dynamics can exhibit significant variations depending on the specific equilibrium state achieved. We examine the relationship between distinct methods of systematically generating sets of local operators through growth operators and perturbative series. Our research focuses on a variety of scenarios, including whether different methods produce the same set of local operators and whether there are multiple valid methods of growth operator construction. We also explore how much information about the underlying QFT is captured by a single growth operator. Interestingly, our findings indicate that different methods of growth operator construction are mutually informative and can be used to recover one another. However, we are unable to determine if they are mutually equivalent. Furthermore, while a single growth operator does provide valuable insights, it is generally not sufficient for fully characterizing the QFT. Ultimately, our study suggests that combining multiple methods of growth operator construction is a effective way to thoroughly map out the local operator structure of a QFT. We illustrate the applicability of our analysis using the $O(N)$ model as a practical example. Interestingly, our work suggests that growth operator construction can serve as a effective diagnostic or 'probe' for testing whether a given quantum field theory is consistent with the principle of maximum entropy. The detailed steps required to decompose an operator into its constituent components also hold potential for growth operator construction in manageable, finite-time processes. These findings stem from our observation that the decomposition process is inherently data-driven and can be applied using real-world data to generate sets of local operators that effectively capture the dynamics of a QFT. Notably, we are able to identify key similarities between the perturbative series and the component-based methods of growth operator construction. These correspondences enable us to reinterpret certain aspects of the perturbative series in terms of the underlying quantum field theory. Finally, our study suggests that growth operator construction is a versatile approach that is applicable to a broad range of contexts, including non-interacting systems and those defined by random matrix models. Conversely, we are also able to employ growth operator construction to shed new light on the inherent structural properties of these systems. Notably, our analysis indicates that certain interaction-mediated operator processes are inherently impossible in non-interacting systems. Ultimately, our study demonstrates that growth operator construction is a valuable tool for the theoretical and applied study of quantum field theories. It can be used to effectively map out the local operator structure of a QFT and illuminate the underlying mechanisms driving the dynamics of a system. The essence of this advancement is the successful application of phase-field method to model fracture energy and its associated length scale. Studies have demonstrated that the phase-field method can reproduce various fracture instabilities. However, the source of the inherent spatial and temporal scales embedded in the phase-field model remains unclear. In this research, we numerically investigate the effects of different bond breakage lengths and time scales on fracture instability. The results indicate that both the bond breakage length and the visco-morphic time influence the critical frequency for oscillatory instability, while only the bond breakage length affects the critical amplitude for tip-splitting instability. Consequently, accounting for the inherent spatial and temporal scales in the phase-field model is crucial for accurately computing fracture instability. Furthermore, this research provides a methodology for determining model parameters based on material properties. The critical analysis of frequency and amplitude thresholds for tip-splitting offers an in-depth understanding of the roles of different scales. Additionally, the research explores whether the phase-field model can accurately represent the inherent material dynamics and whether the critical scales are inherently embedded within the model when the material's length and time scales are not explicitly defined. If this is the case, the inherent critical scales would depend on the specific material being studied and would require experimental input from dynamic fracture tests. This study examines the completeness of sample sets for finite state channels with feedback, given that the encoder has access to the encoded state. We demonstrate that any sample set for this type of channel, which is capable of achieving arbitrary levels of mutual information, can be transformed into a set of channel inputs with specific output sequences. More specifically, even without feedback, simply knowing the encoder state allows us to achieve this transformation. We find that this property holds not just for discrete states but also for continuous states, and it applies equally to channels with non-decreasing capacities. Furthermore, this result is utilized to analyze the complexity of identifying finite state channels with feedback. We also investigate whether knowing the encoder state as part of a feedback loop is sufficient to achieve this transformation, and find that in the case of discrete states, this condition is necessary as well. To prove these results, novel geometric and topological analysis methods are employed to characterize the properties of channel input output relationships. These techniques have the potential to be utilized in a broader range of cryptographic contexts. Additionally, the fact that state knowledge is sufficient to achieve this transformation raises questions about the security of any system that discloses this information. Since any system that discloses this information can be exploited by an adversary, this raises concerns about the completeness of sample sets in such cryptographic contexts. Consequently, it can be concluded that state knowledge should not be assumed to be publicly known. Furthermore, this result implies that in cases where state knowledge is restricted, incorporating this knowledge into the definition of the channel does not increase the channel's capacity. Also, the fact that state knowledge is restricted can be proved to be equivalent to a type of restriction on input output relationships. These relationships are of a type known as weakly collection, and can be identified through a type of coverage, also known as delta coverage. Additionally, it has been found that determining whether a given channel is collection, or a type of partial collection, is a decision problem that is in the class known as coNP. This study presents the results for SEM-TAB-FACTS, a new fact validation and evidence finding task focusing on tabular data, undertaken by a group of researchers from the University of Michigan. The goal of SEM-TAB-FACTS was to identify key information needed to create automatic systems for fact validation and evidence finding related to tabular data. In quantum mechanics, the application of complex numbers is thoroughly justified. However, the necessary use of complex numbers in formulae and methods is not always adequately understood. This lack of understanding can lead to confusing and misleading interpretations of quantum mechanics. This paper aims to clarify the essential complex aspects of quantum mechanics and provide a clear explanation of the complex formalism, hoping to alleviate common confusions and promote a more precise discussion of quantum mechanics.

This work has investigated the potential of integrating an ozone O3 and ultraviolet (UV) light system for eliminating sulfur dioxide SO2 in flue gas emissions. The study's aim is to identify the most responsive UV lamp configuration to minimize energy consumption while achieving European Union SO2 emission standards. The research involved reacting O3 with SO2 in flure gas using different UV lamps of various powers and combinations to determine the most effective setup for optimal emission removal. The results showed that using two 12W lamps was as effective as using a single 30W lamp and outperformed a 54W lamp, with the two 12W lamps requiring only 40% of the power needed from the 54W lamp to meet EU emission standards. Furthermore, increasing the O3 dose in the flue gas allowed for the reduction of UV power by as much as 70% without compromising performance. Additionally, the research identified key factors that influence SO2 removal kinetics, including the O3 dose and reaction time, and provided a newly developed equation to model flue gas conditions. As interest in neuromorphic computing grows, researchers require accessible platforms for testing and evaluating their algorithms, making available hardware and simulated environments crucial for the community. Current simulation tools have limitations, such as compliance issues, restricted concurrency, and inefficient power analysis capabilities, hindering further development. To address these issues, we present NMP4SC, a concurrent SystemC-based virtual platform for neuromorphic computing architectures. It integrates multiple interfaces for dynamic behavioral descriptions and provides efficient resource sharing, distinct from traditional SystemC methodologies. NMP4SC also incorporates a novel power analysis framework, allowing for accurate analysis of energy consumption. Our experiment using a parallelism-based simulation demonstrates NMP4SC's efficacy in testing complex algorithmic challenges and evaluating the energy efficiency of synapse reconfigurations. The open-source NMP4SC code is now available online. It is expected to become a standard resource for the neuromorphic computing community, supporting evaluations of various computing paradigms and accelerators. Furthermore, it enables energy-aware algorithmic optimization, a significant step towards developing energy-efficient neuromorphic computing systems. Our source code can be accessed at https://github.com/yujiang-virup/nmp4sc. Additionally, we are demonstrating NMP4SC as a tutorial at IEEE MICRO-2022 <https://ciera.rpi.edu/NMP4SC>. This virtual platform can be utilized in research and development through collaborative efforts. We aim to expand NMP4SC's functionality by incorporating multiple topology connections, reconfigurable synapses, and enhanced power analysis features. It is our expectation that NMP4SC will become a valuable standard tool for the neuromorphic computing community. It is easily extensible and adaptable to various computing paradigms and architectures, making it an essential resource for evaluating and comparing different implementations. Currently, we support Spiking Neural Network and Neurocore architectures, but we plan to incorporate multiple topology connections, reconfigurable synapses, and other models based on community feedback. Machine learning algorithms are incorporating more and more sophisticated decision-making components but often overlook key factors like uncertainty quantification in their predictions. This quantification is crucial as it enables uncertainty to be communicated effectively, thus guiding decision-makers to make informed choices. Moreover, numerous learning algorithms have been found to be flawed in their ability to model argumentation - a key component of many decision-making processes. This paper addresses these pressing issues in machine learning by developing a novel framework that learns to perform argumentation while quantifying uncertainty in its predictions. This new model, referred to as an Indecision Forest, is inspired by argumentation frameworks and draws from the field of belief function modeling to account for different forms of uncertainty. This innovative approach has several benefits, as evidenced by our experiments, which demonstrate that an Indecision Forest can improve decision-making outcomes and facilitate more accurate risk assessment. Ultimately, this model's ability to communicate uncertainty in a qualitative manner through decision graphs further reinforces its potential to address real-world challenges. This research is the first of its kind to utilize quantified uncertainty in the context of argumentation-based decision-making, thereby expanding the scope of machine learning to address more complex decision-making tasks. The research outcomes can be accessed via the neuraluncertainty repository: https://github.com/neuraluncertainty/indecision_forests. This research will be presented at the 34th International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence in July 2021. A shorter version of this research will be presented at the 19th Spanish Conference on Artificial Intelligence in November 2021. We examine the core graph convolutional operation in neural networks and find it to be an under-specification, leading to similar outcomes with distinct graph convolutional networks. This 'over-blurring' issue occurs because the core graph convolution operation is too flexible, enabling numerous interpretations. Our findings suggest that the choice of graph convolutional network is not critical and graph-based models can produce comparable results to existing node-wise multi-layer perceptron models. Notably, we discover that graph-based models have advantages in resource-constrained settings and highlight their potential for addressing data sparsity issues. Our code is publicly available. Keywords: graph-based neural networks, over-blurring effect, node-wise models, sparsity.

Internet Service Providers have long requested that Content Providers contribute financially towards improving network infrastructure, a demand that Content Providers have been reluctant to meet. This study suggests that an equitable settlement can be achieved if Content Providers compensate ISPs on a per user basis, through fees charged to users during the initial stage of connection. This leads to the concept of a new business model, where Content Providers offer their services on a fee-per-user basis, with these fees subsequently being distributed to the ISPs, effectively making them stakeholders in the Content Providers' company. This model comes with a guarantee that the market value of their investment will increase as the Content Providers' popularity grows. In this study, a fee-per-user model is developed for YouTube, where it is determined that the YouTube division of a company would pay ISPs a fee for every user, while also setting aside a portion of the company's profits to compensate the ISPs. This is comparable to existing practices where companies set aside a portion of their profits to compensate suppliers, a common practice known as "retrospective profit sharing". Simulation results of this model demonstrate that the YouTube division of a company can achieve higher net profits for the company if they choose to compensate the ISPs through a fee-per-user model, rather than through the traditional model of paying ISPs a fixed fee and hoping to increase profits through higher sales. This is because the fee-per-user model allows for a direct and positive correlation between the company's investments in improving network quality and the company's net profits, a correlation that is absent in the traditional model, where companies invest in improving network quality without seeing direct results in the form of increased profits. A deeper analysis of this model reveals that this business model's effectiveness is dependent on certain conditions, such as the company's pricing strategy, the characteristics of the content, and user behavior. By formulating the mapping between the categories of quantum states and observables as an equivalence, we demonstrate that the mapping is bidirectional and preserve certain properties. This framework is versatile enough to be applied to both finite and infinite quantum systems. Furthermore, the approach allows us to extend the mapping to inclusion preserving functors, resulting in a 2-categorical connection. This development leads to a deeper understanding of the mapping and its potential applications in computational quantum physics. By formulating the mapping in this abstract way, we are able to generalize it to various formulations of quantum theory. We also show that the mapping can be applied to subcategories of quantum states and observables without covering the entire spectrum. Consequently, this raises questions about whether the mapping can be used to construct a universal categorical representation of quantum theory. Ultimately, this research holds the potential to unlock new computational tools for quantum physics. This study enhances cross-sectional expected return models by utilizing a novel, flexible method of portfolio return estimation. The conventional method of calculating benchmark portfolios often leads to biased results that favor certain stocks. To address this issue, the research proposes to estimate returns based on stocks that can be precisely matched to the benchmarks. The analysis demonstrates that this alternative approach has several advantages, including minimizing measurement error and mitigating the influence of illiquidity. By applying this modified method, the research finds stronger evidence to support the size premium in empirical tests. Furthermore, the study establishes that this enhanced approach can increase the accuracy of backtesting linear short-selling constraints. Overall, the results suggest that benchmark portfolio allocation methods can introduce biases in empirical research, and that alternative techniques may yield more reliable outcomes. Early detection of heart conditions is crucial, and point-of-care methods like cardiac auscultation are vital for this purpose.  However, accurate abnormality detection using cardiac auscultation is challenging due to background noise interfering with the signal.  To address this issue, this study develops a signal processing method to prioritize the foreground heartbeat sound over the background noise.  Following this step, a predicted classification accuracy of 90% is achieved for identifying normal and abnormal heart sounds.  To validate the efficacy of this proposed method, simulation tests were conducted using various noise types and levels to mimic a real-world clinical environment.  Additionally, the study evaluates how different types of noise affect the accuracy of cardiac auscultation, and finds that both background noise and signal distortion negatively impact the ability to identify abnormal heart sounds.  Finally, this study involves comparisons with other baseline classification methods and demonstrates that its proposed approach surpasses these methods in terms of predicted accuracy.  The numerical data and simulation codes for this study are publicly available for others to reference.  The proposed method involves two distinct processes: separating the foreground heartbeat from the background noise, and identifying normal or abnormal heart sounds.  First, background noise is removed from the cardiac signal through a band-stop filter, and then a foreground-to-background ratio is calculated to prioritize the heartbeat.  This method, known as the Fourier Domain Foreground Extraction Method, is validated through simulations involving both clean and noisy signals. Twists can be categorized into distinct types: group twist, Swann twist, and Eilenberg-Rees twist. 
The Torus twist, an infinite loop of the Eilenberg-Rees twist, can be represented geometrically and algebraically.
This paper explores the Torus twist in relation to the 2-dimensional space group symmetries.

This study offers the first empirical assessment of a trust-building mechanism in online auctions, specifically the second-price auctions widely used for keyword auctions. Through a controlled lab experiment, we evaluated whether a trust-building mechanism, introduced by Haering and Klaus (2017), increases participant trust and, as a result, improves auction performance. Our results confirm that this mechanism boosts short-term trust among both buyers and sellers, but only translates to better outcomes for buyers, not sellers. Moreover, we found that the underlying theory requiring participants to make intertemporal choices is flawed, as they primarily focus on short-term gains. Finally, we observed that our experimental design did not elicit as strong a sense of loss aversion as expected. Leveraging the unique capabilities of online labs, we conducted this study with a larger and more diverse group of participants, resulting in a higher completion rate compared to traditional lab experiments. The study's online appendices include additional information, such as a full description of the design, a complete dataset, and a more in-depth analysis of the results. The field of Neural Painters is a subfield within the broader Deep Learning field, where models are trained to create paintings primarily using stroke-based representations. Recent research has led to significant advancements in this area through the development of new neural network architectures and the aggregation of datasets, ultimately resulting in neural painters producing visually appealing paintings that rival those created by human artists. Notably, a recently proposed GAN-based architecture has demonstrated superior performance compared to earlier models, and our analysis suggests that further refinement of this model is achievable. We sought to capitalize on this progress by applying the Delight Network, a GAN-based architecture that excels at generating pleasure-inducing content, to the Delight of Neural Painting. Our goal was straightforward - to determine the potential of neural painters to create more delightful paintings. Through our experiments, we found that the Delight of Neural Painting model produced paintings with higher delightful scores and also pushed the upper limit of the Delight score, establishing a new standard. Our findings were further validated by examining the correlations between Delight scores and expert-based aesthetic scores, revealing that the Delight of Neural Painting model was capable of capturing both content and aesthetic aspects. We demonstrate the practical value of the Delight of Neural Painting model by utilizing it for the induced generation of paintings that prioritize aesthetic appeal. In addition, we explored the prospects of neural painters making a significant contribution to the development of the neural asthetic field by analyzing the results of a peer review experiment, where neural painters showed the potential to produce more delightful content. Academic research paper readings are essential for both professionals and non-experts, 
but the diverse nature of papers makes it difficult for readers to grasp the main 
points. Current systems that utilize research papers are hampered because they rely on 
oversimplified assumptions: the main objective is to comprehend the paper's content 
rather than identifying specific areas that require further investigation. To overcome 
these limitations, we have developed a new dataset that consists of questions aimed 
at uncovering hidden connections between unrelated concepts. Each of these 
knowledge-seeking questions is linked to answers from existing studies in our domain 
of interest. Unlike other datasets, our collection does not rely on pre-labeled data and 
instead comprises questions and answers derived from research papers through 
automated processing. We have tested the efficacy of BERT in responding to these 
questions, only to find that it performs significantly worse compared to established 
models that summarize papers. We believe our dataset can serve as a useful resource 
for the development of more effective and informed open-ended question-answering 
systems that utilize academic research. It is currently accessible online at https://www.asearchdemo.org. BERT-based models that utilize our dataset can be found on GitHub under the repository name'researchquest'. A corresponding video can be found under the ID '2021.08.09.646'.03'.

Acronyms and abbreviations serve as common shortcuts for lengthy phrases, with
many having multiple possible expansions, sometimes conflicting with one another.
While there are numerous tools and websites specializing in acronym definitions,
few offer detailed, accurate, and comprehensive information regarding identification
and disambiguation guidelines.  MadDog is a web-based platform designed to address
this deficiency by providing guidance on acronym identification and disambiguation
through an interactive interface.  Developed using Python and MySQL, MadDog features
a range of functionalities, including an intuitive database-driven search engine
and customizable datasets for data mining applications.  Currently offering guidance
on 238,000+ acronyms spanning across 14 domains, MadDog is set to become a valuable
resource for Natural Language Processing researchers and practitioners.  Additionally,
its open-source code and database are freely accessible under a flexible CC-BY
license, enabling users to upload their own datasets and tailor the platform according
to their specific needs.  MadDog is poised to become a leading knowledge base, providing
essential information to software developers, researchers, and educators on identifying
and interpreting acronyms within various contexts.  Furthermore, its comprehensive
dataset can be utilized in machine learning training and testing activities.  In contrast
to existing knowledge base databases, MadDog is unique in offering identification and
disambiguation guidance, making it an indispensable resource for the Natural Language
Processing community.  Developed over the course of a semester through the IFT6136:
Advanced Topics in Human-Computer Interaction course at Birkbeck, University of London,
MadDog is an innovative, interactive, and comprehensive platform catering to the
needs of the NLP community.  In this paper, we delve into the platform's conceptualization,
design, and development, highlighting its distinctive features and showcasing its
potential to address real-world challenges in NLP practices.  Furthermore, we outline
possible directions for enhancing MadDog and its applications in data mining, machine
learning, and software engineering, in particular.  Lastly, we document the
open-source resources, enabling developers to build upon and adapt the MadDog platform
in accordance with their specific requirements.  In the future, we envision MadDog as a
leading knowledge base, providing essential information to researchers, developers, and
educators on identifying and interpreting acronyms, as well as guiding software
development and facilitating machine learning and NLP applications.  Additionally,
its comprehensive dataset can be utilized in machine learning training and testing

Quantum interference, evident in low-dimensional systems, is one of the most notable manifestations of quantum physics. Historically, quantum interference has been observed in charge transport; however, recent findings indicate that it also significantly affects thermal properties. This has created a basis for designing highly efficient heat management devices. This study focuses on heat transfer in complex systems, specifically quantum Hall junctions, where an electrostatic control enables instantaneous shifts between contrasting transport states. We discover that, in these systems, an equilibrium charge current can be triggered through the adjustment of a single control voltage. This process occurs in conjunction with substantial heat generation or absorption. Furthermore, due to interference-induced thermoelectric activity, heat rectification is also achievable. In particular, heat rectification can be realized even in the absence of thermoelectric activity, thereby offering a simplified approach to this phenomenon. Our theoretical model is validated through detailed comparisons with available experimental data. Moreover, our analysis indicates that, in certain cases, heat rectification and intense heat emission can coexist. We believe that this understanding will contribute to developing innovative heat management and energy harvesting devices featuring unprecedented performance.

Our work addresses the challenges of DNA storage accessibility by developing a method to efficiently organize and update large DNA file collections. Current approaches using hierarchical organization are plagued by long sequence lengths that lead to numerous index sequences, exacerbating issues with sequence fragmentation and indexing complexity. To mitigate these problems, our method utilizes hierarchical data storage with fixed height and efficient updating of file metadata through a balanced binary search tree structure stored within DNA. This approach requires only logarithmically more base pairs per file compared to non-hierarchical systems, and allows for rapid updating of file metadata by decomposing longer changes into smaller, easily introduced mutations. This innovation leads to a significant reduction in the number of required DNA writes. This work is illustrated through simulations utilizing data from Internet Archive, and the results show that our method enables rapid upscaling of DNA storage capacity without compromising data organization or the efficiency of DNA file retrievals. This approach can be realized with currently available DNA sequencing and editing technologies. Moreover, our work provides guidance for constructing effective hierarchical organizations in DNA storage systems. Hospitals encode patient and visit information into text reports, which are then translated into standardized International Classification of Diseases (ICD) codes by coding specialists. The increasing demand for patient data has led to a corresponding rise in the need for coded data. Manual coding is labor-intensive and expensive, rendering a large dataset unaffordable for many institutions. The need has given rise to semi-supised learning techniques for coding automation, though existing methods using full supervision or unlabelled data without incorporating clinical notes are inadequate. Researchers have employed various transformer-based models for coding, yet their reliance on extensive supervised learning data limits their practicality. To develop a more effective and practical solution, we propose utilizing clinical notes, even those that lack proper coding, to create a simplified coding system. By applying supervised learning to this reduced coding system, we can leverage self-supervised learning techniques to utilize unlabelled data. The results of our proposed method demonstrate considerable improvement over prior semi-supervised methods. Additionally, our method reduces the complexity of the coding system, producing a more compact and straightforward code that also shows promising results.
