To ensure the accuracy of our findings, we utilized several validation procedures, including a random background model and a real-time follow-up system. Upon close inspection of the most probabilitily-hypothetical planet candidates, we eliminated three that failed to meet follow-up monitoring standards. Furthermore, we reviewed our dataset to assess the accuracy of the AnomalyFinder's planetary likelihood score, revealing a positive correlation with the probability of a planet being genuine. Recent research on transport networks has highlighted the need to account for uncertainty and reliability by modeling demand rather than assuming a fixed origin-destination matrix. This study addresses this challenge by developing an innovative framework for estimating probabilistic demand while minimizing errors in origin-destination flow reconstruction. Initially, a general probabilistic model is established, and then modified to accommodate constraints based on link and path flow balance. Next, this model is refined further by incorporating day-to-day transport data and a proposed error metric. Finally, this approach is applied using real-world data from the North Jutland region of Denmark. The results demonstrate that under specific conditions, the optimized solution corresponds to the global minimum, and through numerical analysis, the order of the covariance matrix can be determined without extensive computational burden. Furthermore, this approach is adaptable to accommodate varying demand probabilities without significant computational disruptions. The study demonstrates that origin-destination demand uncertainty and the order of the covariance matrix are crucial considerations in transportation planning. These findings are substantiated by numerical simulations and a comparison with existing methods. Ultimately, this framework provides a useful tool for transportation administrators and policymakers. Researchers investigated this transition in detailed numerical studies, focusing particularly on the role of intrinsic frequency differences. This work uncovered key insights into the system's behavior: beyond a fundamental coupling threshold, the oscillators developed stable, long-lasting patterns of coordination. Moreover, the phase of the oscillators within these patterns followed a symmetrical arrangement. The researchers found that this arrangement is unaffected by the strength of coupling beyond the threshold and that the patterns of coordination emerge at a rate inversely proportional to the difference in frequencies. This new understanding challenges existing theories and suggests a universal principle for achieving highly coordinated patterns in arrays of nonlinear oscillators. Potential applications include the design of synchronized heartbeats in arrhythmia treatment and the optimization of vehicle spacing on roads. Additionally, the researchers propose an innovative method using speaker equipment to create controlled patterns of sound synchronization in everyday environments. One major obstacle with using Linked Data is the barrier of technology accessibility due to a lack of user-friendly interfaces, as well as difficulties in searching and traversing vast datasets of interconnected data. To address these issues, we have developed a range of natural language interface tools that enable users to interact with Linked Data using natural language inquiries. These tools include a range of applications, such as question-answering systems and data visualization platforms, that incorporate visual representations and word embeddings to facilitate effective visual data exploration. Specifically, we have utilized Ontodia, a diagram-based data visualization tool, in conjunction with Wikidata and the DL4Odia visual data exploration platform to analyze the impact of leveraging word embeddings on user inquiry behavior. Our results reveal that word embeddings enhance Ontodia user behavior when compared to control groups, and also demonstrate a significant but decreasing benefit when compared to WordNet, a popular semantic thesaurus. Additionally, we have identified and verified several key factors contributing to these findings. Firstly, word embeddings improve Ontodia user behavior when the users' natural language inquiries align with the embeddings. Secondly, when users' natural language inquiries do not align with the embeddings, there is no noticeable impact on behavior. Lastly, when Ontodia users rely on structured queries, there is no noticeable impact on behavior. These findings indicate that word embeddings offer potential applications for enhancing Linked Data exploration, but only when the associated natural language inquiries match the embeddings. Conversely, when natural language inquiries do not match the embeddings, there is no noticeable benefit. Nonetheless, we believe that these results offer promising indications for the future integration of other, more advanced NLP natural language interface technologies to further enhance Linked Data exploration. Specifically, we propose that natural language interfaces incorporating NLP technology will ultimately contribute to a greater variety of user inquiries, in turn leading to more engaging and diverse interactions with Linked Data. To achieve this, we have developed and released a range of natural language interface demos, as well as Ontodia datasets based on word embeddings, for the benefit of the Linked Data community. These resources include a range of applications, such as question-answering systems and data visualization platforms, that incorporate visual representations and word embeddings to facilitate effective visual data exploration. Additionally, the Ontodia and DL4Odia platforms are now available for public use, with associated datasets based on word embeddings and Wikidata. These datasets offer a valuable resource for researchers and developers seeking to replicate our results, as well as provide a range of natural language interface tools that can be utilized for data exploration. In optical systems where the non-linear interaction is supported by a medium 
whose wave propagation characteristics depend on intensity, we investigated the 
stability of dark solitons. The research reveals that, unlike in systems where 
wave propagation characteristics don't depend on intensity, these solitons don't 
exhibit exact stability. Instead, we found that the stability of dark solitons 
involves a resonance of unstable modes. The specific conditions for soliton 
stability, as well as changes in its spectral properties, were mapped out in the 
process. The study also demonstrated that increasing soliton density can 
enhance stability. The findings were verified using numerical simulations of a 
system where the propagation characteristics of light waves are supported by a 
medium whose properties vary with intensity. The study offers insights into the 
stability of dark solitons in optically-induced systems where the propagation 
characteristics of light waves are supported by a medium whose properties vary 
with intensity. The research is significant because it expands our understanding 
of soliton stability in optically-induced systems. The findings may also be 
utilized to create stable dark-soliton-based structures in optically-induced 
media, as well as to explore the properties of stable dark-soliton ensembles. 

Keywords: Optically-induced systems, dark solitons, stability, intensity-dependent 
dispersion, resonance of unstable modes, soliton density.

A detailed study employed rapid two-dimensional nuclear magnetic resonance imaging to monitor temperature distribution within a horizontal gas-solid fixed bed under varying gas velocities and heat fluxes. As expected, results showed that gas velocity and heat flux caused significant alterations in the mean temperature and temperature non-uniformity of the bed. Moreover, for low gas velocity, the mean temperature of the bed increased with rising heat flux, but exhibited a decline at higher velocities. Additionally, for a fixed velocity, the temperature non-uniformity of the bed decreased with increasing heat flux fluxes. Correlations were established between the temperature distributions and the Dittus-Boelter Nusselt number for the gas, which agreed well with existing literature trends. A theoretical framework suggested that the temperature non-uniformity of the bed could be solely attributed to particle clustering. However, since clustering was not directly measured, further study is required to verify this hypothesis. Overall, the study demonstrates that temperature distribution within a gas-solid fixed bed can be accurately predicted through physical means. Moreover, this research may be applied to other particulate systems based on their physical characteristics. Suggestions for future study on clustering are outlined. Please see the complete article in Journal of Heat and Mass Transfer, Volume 123, for further details.

We have developed a theoretical framework for modeling the self-assembly of aggregates containing shared components, based on the concept of "complexity elimination." This framework reveals a fundamental relationship between the free energy of aggregation and the system's entropy production, which applies broadly across different models. We have demonstrated that even when multiple detailed pathways coexist, the overall process still conforms to a simplified picture. From an thermodynamic perspective, the freedom to form aggregates is maximally harnessed, giving rise to thermodynamically well-defined equilibrium states. While thermodynamic stability is inherent in isolated systems, it can be compromised when interactions with the surroundings are considered. Despite these constraints, our findings still offer a solid foundation for studying aggregate self-assembly. Additionally, we have explored how molecular self-assembly rules might be different in closed and open systems. Our study provides a theoretical basis for understanding how molecules self-assemble and offers insights into the generalized principles that govern this phenomenon. Furthermore, it paves the way for applying concepts from non-equilibrium thermodynamics to biomolecular aggregates. Then, we translated the concepts to the context of rod-like aggregates. Our analysis reveals how closure affects aggregate formation and identifies key parameters influencing the thermodynamics of assembly. Our study demonstrates that even complex aggregate structures can be understood through thermodynamic analysis. Lastly, we have applied our theoretical framework to a model based on coassembly. Through our analysis, we identified key features of this interaction and elucidated how it affects the resulting aggregate structures. The researchers focus on how these preconditioners handle subdomains, either by selecting them randomly or by taking advantage of a given partitioning strategy. This is crucial because both the distribution of right-hand sides and the structure of matrices play significant roles in the efficiency of multilevel preconditioning. The study evaluates the outcome of different subdomain partitioning methods and analyzes their impact on the quality of hyperplane Smith's method, a complex multilevel preconditioner. The findings suggest that when coupled with a highly efficient linear solver, hyperplane Smith's method can lead to substantial reductions in solution time. What's more, by taking advantage of a given partitioning strategy, the performance of this complex preconditioner can be further enhanced. Although randomly assigned subdomains can still lead to acceptable outcomes, particularly when a highly efficient linear solver is used, the best results are consistently achieved when the domain is divided in an optimized manner. This optimization is found to be particularly beneficial for a wide array of test cases, from coarse to highly refined meshes. To gain deeper insights into these developments, researchers need to investigate the underlying dynamics of user interactions within these systems. In this paper, researchers focused on tags applied to user-generated content and related data to better comprehend current practices and future opportunities in the digital annotation space. Through an in-depth analysis of tags from systems representing distinct models of user interaction - collaborative, individual, and interest-based - researchers identified key patterns and characteristics. These findings, derived from an examination of twenty tag datasets spanning eight content types and ten domains, reveal important insights into user behaviors and the broader ecosystem of user-generated content systems. In particular, researchers found that user-generated content systems exhibit distinct patterns of tag reuse, usage, and interaction, influenced by factors such as user collaboration, individual activity, and the focus of shared interests. These observations have significant implications for the design and development of annotation systems supporting content exchange and collaboration. Furthermore, researchers highlight the potential of tag-based data exchange to facilitate the evolution of complex interconnected information networks driven by user needs. In this regard, researchers see great potential for tagging to play a more significant role in supporting not only content annotation but also various forms of user-driven collaboration and knowledge construction. These findings may encourage developers to reevaluate the design of current annotation systems and consider more dynamic approaches to supporting user interactions and the sharing of annotated content. Additionally, researchers point out that tagging can be utilized as an inexpensive and effective means of testing novel ideas in collaboration, by promoting the dissemination and dissemination of annotated information across connected systems. In this regard, researchers see great potential for tagging to facilitate innovative forms of collaboration and knowledge construction. When conducting global sensitivity analysis of computational models, it's typical to assume that input variables are independent of one another, which isn't the case here since we're investigating the ranking and effectiveness of evolutionary algorithm hyperparameters. We've explored the application of three global sensitivity analysis methods – Sobol, iSb, and Generalized Sobol – to hyperparameters of four optimization algorithms: no replacement, proportional, exponential, and combinatorial optimization. By utilizing a comprehensive framework, we evaluated how these methods individually and collectively rank these hyperparameters in terms of importance. We also analyzed the consistency of these methods and how their results correlate with each other, revealing that the Sobol method often struggles with bias for certain types of optimization algorithms. We've further demonstrated that the ProGen method tends to perform better than the Sobol method, especially for certain parameters. Ultimately, we suggest using the ProGen method in conjunction with the Sobol method to gain a deeper understanding of the importance of hyperparameters in parallel evolutionary optimization. We've made our code available for public use.

Freiman's 3k-4 theorem generally asserts that if subsets A and B, of size k and comprised of integers, have a significant syntonic difference, then the sum of these subsets' elements, modulo k, exhibits near-arithmetic progression properties. Specifically, the theorem states that there exist elements a and b, such that the difference between the sums of A and B, modulo k, is respectively a and b, and the number of solutions that satisfy this condition is substantial. The present research aims to enhance the 3k-4 theorem by removing the requirement for a large number of solutions. It is demonstrated that if subsets A and B, of size k, have a significant syntonic difference, then for a non-negligible fraction of values of a and b, the pair (a, b) satisfies the original conditions of the 3k-4 theorem. Furthermore, under these conditions, the subset of B's elements that corresponds to the additive coset of a can be expressed as the translatation of A by the integer b, within an error bound of at most 4. It is also shown that any subset of B's elements that corresponds to the additive coset of a can be expressed as the translation of A by the integer b, with a maximum error of at most 6. The research utilizes the framework of Szemeredi's partition theorem to establish the new Freiman 3k-4 theorem. The work is inspired in part by the account of the theorem provided in the book'additive combinatorics' by the renowned mathematicians Alon, Shalev and Sweedeen. Additionally, the research demonstrates that the Fourier decay lemmas can be viewed as a direct consequence of Freiman 3k-4 theorem. The application of the theorem in particular yields a simplified proof of the k-ramsey theorem. The research also examines the relationship between Freiman 3k-4 theorem and the structure of finitely generated finite nilpotent groups. The theorem's connection to the inverse conjecture for the k-ramsey theorem is also explored. The research also yields a simplified proof of the gowers norm version of the k-ramsey theorem. This research addresses the problem of recovering a radially inhomogeneous medium's outer boundary in a sphere by using transmission eigenfunctions. Mathematical representation of this problem involves an internal problem with given coefficients, demonstrating that various transmission eigenfunctions correspond to specific Dirichlet eigenfunctions in a given domain. Utilizing this equivalence, we prove that any radially inhomogeneous medium's outer boundary can be effectively identified through transmission eigenfunctions by restricting ourselves to those with specific rotation symmetry. Our findings are further validated by numerical experiments designed to recover boundaries using both ideal and realistically noisy data. Although the problem of recovering boundaries without restrictions on rotations is specified as unsolvable, our study provides a theoretical framework for understanding the capabilities and limitations of boundary identification using transmission eigenfunctions. Moreover, our research offers a simplified method for recovering radially symmetric boundaries, and our numerical results demonstrate that under certain conditions, this method can achieve significant error rates even in the presence of noise. Ultimately, our research provides a theoretical understanding of the capabilities and limitations of boundary identification using transmission eigenfunctions and offers a simplified method for recovering radially symmetric boundaries. Furthermore, our results demonstrate that under certain conditions, this method can achieve significant error rates even in the presence of noise. Unlike existing methods, our approach doesn't rely on explicit unsupervised cross-domain information or significant modifications to existing dialogue models. It simply requires a small amount of unlabelled data and no special training data for new intents. Utilizing a pre-trained dialogue model as a universal message encoder, we've developed a straightforward two-stage process. First, we use a pre-trained model to compare old and new intent responses, identifying similarities and discrepancies. Second, we use a pre-trained dialogue model to assess the plausibility of newly discovered intents based on their context. To facilitate real-world applications, we've also developed an innovative strategy for dynamically updating our intent discovery algorithm over time. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of our approach, matching the performance of state-of-the-art methods with significantly fewer resources. Additionally, our code and data are freely available for research and development. It takes approximately 45 days to discover new intents in the MultiWOZ 2.0 dataset, while existing methods require around 120 days. We develop a framework for comparing the cost of quantum information in terms of entanglement. Initially, we examine the cost of selective measurements. Following this, we explore the cost associated with weak measurements. It is demonstrated that weak measurements can be achieved at a low cost of less than 1 ebit, under two distinct assumptions. When assuming the measured states are continuous, we can estimate the cost to be approximately 0.44 ebit. Conversely, when considering the measured states to be discrete, the cost can be estimated as approximately 0.81 ebit. Notably, we find that without making any specific assumptions about the measured states, the cost can be bounded by a value greater than 1 ebit. We also show that the entanglement cost of weak measurements can be influenced by the level of measurement field, as well as the level of quantum field, and that it can be estimated through weak light-matter interaction. Furthermore, we successfully applied our framework to model a quantum eraser experiment. The study contributes to an understanding of the quantification of quantum information and offers insights into the design of quantum information transfer protocols. The investigation also sheds light on the interplay between measurement and entanglement. Lastly, the research has potential applications in quantum science and technology. Optimized hardware is often required in embedded systems, leading to a common operation called Multiple Constant Multiplication (MCM) over integers. One efficient way to achieve this optimization is by replacing expensive generic multiplication with bit-shifts and additions in a multiplierless circuit. Our analysis shows that most integer values can be represented with fewer than eight bits, prompting the investigation of eight-bit MCMs. By conducting exhaustive searches for optimal circuits involving one to four additions and various bit-shifts within this domain, we derived comprehensive databases. Interestingly, adding one simple constraint to the hardware design sometimes leads to circuits requiring fewer hardware components than their existing counterparts. We provide a polynomial-time approximation scheme (PTAS) for a broad family of sparse optimization problems with general-valued objectives. Our PTAS relies on a simple underlying assumption: the problem's optimal solution can be concentrated in a subset of at most $q$ coordinates, with the value in every other coordinate being at most $O(q)$ times its counterpart in the optimal solution. Without any specific assumptions, our PTAS applies to problems with optimal solutions containing at most $q$ non-zero coordinates. This research explores a novel application of hyperspectral imaging in urban settings, focusing on semantic segmentation using hyperspectral images without additional labels. We propose HS2P, a hyperspectral image segmentation framework that includes two key components: (1) a label aggregation module and (2) a lightweight hyperspectral image adapter. These modules enable the HS2P system to combine aggregated labels from the adapter and a traditional RGB image, ultimately improving the accuracy of semantic segmentation. This system achieves superior performance compared to current state-of-the-art urban segmentation benchmarks and requires minimal additional resources. Our experimental findings demonstrate the HS2P system's potential for precise segmentation in complex urban environments. Additionally, we visualize the HS2P system's segmentation capabilities in an interactive visual demonstration. The code for this research is openly accessible on the CVC-UAB GitHub repository.

We demonstrate that in a RAM with a linear access pattern, all constant-time arithmetic operations are equivalent to multiplication by a constant. To tackle the data sparsity problem inherent in personalized recommendation systems, many graph-based approaches have been developed to effectively utilize structured data. Nonetheless, session-based recommendation systems pose an even more critical challenge due to the transient nature of user interactions. This paper presents a novel session-oriented recommendation graph co-training framework that combines the strengths of undirected and directed graph models to address this issue. The proposed approach utilizes user historical session data to establish two interconnected graph models, where unlabelled user profiles act as pseudo-labellers to aid model training. The experimental outcomes demonstrate that this framework achieves superior performance over existing graph-based recommenders on four real-world dataset benchmarks. The source code is available at https://github.com/huiyangwu(SSGCT). The empirical evaluation confirms that the proposed approach offers an appealing solution to addressing data sparsity in session-based recommenders. Furthermore, the results indicate that the undirected graph model serves as an effective source of knowledge to enhance directed graph model performance. The training time required for the session-oriented recommendation graph co-training framework is roughly equivalent to training individual graph models. Nonetheless, the approach yields substantially improved recommendation accuracy across the datasets examined. The proposed framework's focus on session-based recommenders sets it apart from existing graph-based approaches, which often fail to address this critical problem. The framework's core architecture can be easily adapted to develop new graph-based recommenders with comparable performance. Nonetheless, further work is needed to explore using the undirected graph model as a session-based pseudo-labelling source of knowledge for other graph model variants. Additionally, the framework's potential applications extend to addressing data sparsity in recommendation systems with diverse graph model variants. The directed graph model leverages user historical click data to develop a tailored recommender by determining the most likely items users may interact with following each clicked item. In contrast, the undirected graph model utilizes user profile embeddings to identify overlapping user interests, which serves as pseudo-labelling to enhance directed graph model performance. The proposed session-oriented recommendation graph co-training framework represents a new approach to addressing data sparsity in session-based recommenders by training two graph models in tandem. The framework's core architecture can be easily adapted to develop new graph-based recommenders with comparable performance. The undirected graph model's focus on user overlapping interests can be further developed into a new session-based recommender. In a complex visual environment, distinguishing between different objects relies heavily on various characteristics such as shape, color, size, and texture. A fundamental question arises regarding how recurrent neural networks (RNNs), designed for object categorization, utilize these traits to process and consolidate information. Through our study, we investigated the essential visual characteristics that RNNs capitalize on to achieve this goal. We trained RNNs on a robust dataset of image-classification tasks and, through systematic replacements of supporting information, identified three core object attributes: shape, color, and texture. Notably, these attributes were found to be interdependent and mutually exclusive, forming a stable hierarchy. Furthermore, we observed that RNNs typically encode different attributes with distinct temporal dynamics. Our findings imply that RNNs can effectively utilize various object characteristics to inform their internal state, thereby informing subsequent decisions in a task. Such behavior is unique to object categorization and cannot be replicated with simpler models like linear regression. Overall, our study sheds light on the critical role of distinct visual attributes in informing object categorization tasks trained with RNNs. Additionally, our analysis provides a comprehensive framework for evaluating the role of different sensory characteristics in informing higher-level cognitive processes. Lastly, our work offers potential avenues for improving the performance of recurrent neural networks in object categorization by selecting training data that covers a diverse range of object attributes. Additionally, our study may have broader applications and interpretations within the realm of artificial intelligence and cognitive neuroscience.

In non-commutative spacetimes, the definition of identical particles breaks down, causing confusion. The standard method of applying exchange statistics to wave functions fails due to increasingly complex transformations under space transformations. For an exchange transformation to be well-defined, the total degree of non-commutativity must be even. Based on the properties of coordinate algebra, we re-examine the identification of particles in non-commutative spacetimes and propose a new criterion for identifying bosonic and fermionic particles. Our results show that in non-exceptional cases, the exchange statistic is well-defined, and the identification of particles aligns with standard theory. However, in scenarios where the degree of non-commutativity is odd, the exchange statistic is only defined for part of the coordinate algebra, leading to a failure of particle identification. We conclude that in odd cases, it is not possible to identify particles as bosonic or fermionic. We also discuss how this identity crisis affects the application of cluster rules in non-commutative spacetimes and propose additional research to resolve the ambiguity of particle identification in such contexts. Additionally, our results demonstrate that in non-exceptional cases with an even degree of non-commutativity, the application of cluster rules and exchange statistics is consistent, thereby validating the application of quantum field theory to such spacetimes. Lastly, we speculate that in spacetimes with an infinite degree of non-commutativity, the exchange statistic is always well-defined, and the resulting theory reduces to a commutative spacetime model. Our model in such a limit case is conjectured to be equivalent to a theory of interacting bosonic particles. We present an illustration of our findings using a simple particle wave function and explain the implications of our results on the properties of any quantum field theory existing in non-commutative spacetimes. Moreover, our research presents an original approach to developing a quantum field theory for any spacetime, including those with non-commutative structure. By re-evaluating the properties of any quantum field theory, we uncover novel insights into the properties of field operators and their interaction under the influence of non-commutative spacetime, which may have broader applications in theoretical physics. Our work offers an innovative perspective that can broaden the understanding of quantum field theory and its future development. Moreover, our research presents an original method to generalize quantum field theory to spacetimes with non-commutative structure. We introduce a novel technique called TVT and utilize it to study charge transport in diamond single-crystals across three-dimensional space. The research utilizes a coherent source at 800 nm and detects resonance in a thin photoconductive layer created in a resonance cavity. By mapping the conduction pattern at varying depths in diamond, TVT offers an alternative to studying charge transport through measurement of photoluminescence in a scintillator. The research involves examining a 0.4 mm thick single-crystal diamond substrate with an intrinsic region followed by TVT analysis at 10.2 um layer thickness. TVT has the capacity to distinguish between high charge mobility in the intrinsic region and lower charge mobility in the substrate, encompassing both drift and diffusion components. Moreover, TVT can directly measure charge transport across the entire diamond thickness, an advantage compared to contact-electrostatic simulation measurements that may not accurately represent charge transport in the diamond's intrinsic region. Consequently, TVT can facilitate a deeper comprehension of the physical processes involved in diamond charge transport even without contact to the sample. By employing TVT in diamond and a 240 um thick silicon substrate, TVT showed promising results in different fields, particularly in particle detection and scintillation detection, and is expected to expand into further research in these domains. Social media platforms are facing significant problems due to the spread of toxic content like hate speech, off-color comments, and misogyny. These difficulties have caught the attention of the Natural Language Processing (NLP) community, driving innovative research in Arabic toxic speech specifically. In this study, we explore the utility of Deep Learning models in detecting and classifying misogynic content on Arabic social media. A large dataset of 13,000 sentences was collected and annotated by Arabic NLP experts. This work presents the results of thorough experiments conducted on the newly created dataset, comparing the performance of individual-task and multi-task models, as well as the impact of pre-trained language models and data augmentation techniques. The research demonstrates that a pre-trained BERT model can enhance the accuracy of the task and that a multi-task model can improve results by as much as 5.50%. The proposed approach prioritizes data efficiency and can serve as a baseline model for addressing toxic speech in Arabic. The dataset and code used in this study are publicly available for reproduction of the results and further investigation.

The intensity of data manipulation affects both methods equally. The safe policy, which is learned using the probabilistic approach, remains effective even after the system has undergone significant changes. In contrast, deterministic policies lose their optimality in both scenarios, whether due to data manipulation or system changes. Furthermore, we observed that probabilistic safe policies consistently achieved better outcomes compared to their deterministic counterparts in both normal and manipulated scenarios. Moreover, these safe policies demonstrated improved performance as the intensity of data manipulation decreased. The benefits of probabilistic model-based policy search were particularly evident in tasks where the intensity of data manipulation was low. Nonetheless, our findings also indicate that deterministic approaches can still provide some value, especially in scenarios where data manipulation is not a concern. Theoretical foundations for our experimental observations are an area that requires further research. The present study validates the concept that learning robust controllers using probabilistic model-based policy search can lead to significant and reliable outcomes. Researchers initially developed the quantum Fisher information to assess sensor precision in metrology applications. At the quantum level, this property has been extensively used to establish optimal control in various contexts. A recent study introduced a novel approach to generalizing quantum dynamics based on Fisher information. This work presents a new operator that encodes complex phenomena in quantum systems. To demonstrate its practical implications, the study focuses on a specific system - a Bose-Einstein condensate - and shows that its proposed operator facilitates the description of non-linear interactions among gas particles. Furthermore, the investigation indicates that the generated super-soliton states are stable and energy-minimizing states of the system. The study also reveals that these super-soliton states can be achieved through suitable control parameters in the system. A corresponding theoretical framework is developed to support these findings. The research offers a broader understanding of quantum dynamics based on Fisher information and provides a useful tool for controlling and analyzing non-linear quantum systems. The study as well paves the way for applying the proposed approach to other complex quantum systems. The results can be seen at the arXiv:2106.11423, and the research is supported by CONACYT, Mexico. Polynomial system solving plays a crucial role in various applications to extract useful information. The nondegenerate locus of a system is defined as the complement of its degenerate solutions and plays a significant role in parameterized systems to determine codimensions and topological invariants such as Betti numbers. While codimension is fixed and invariant to nonsingular transformations, it varies significantly among all possible degenerate configurations. The bounded prism construction is introduced as a tool to precisely calculate the nondegenerate locus of a polynomial system through a sequence of signature-based steps. The proposed method is demonstrated using the well-known Gelfand-Sargent-Gusevski\u{i} unfolding of the cuspidal cusp singularity. This approach leverages the prism framework and signs within the Newton polytope to determine the nondegenerate locus of the system and its topological invariants via pointwise computation. Prior computational methods have encountered limitations in their approaches to calculating the nondegenerate locus, either due to the complexity of general degenerate configurations or the difficulty in capturing codimension via outerwelds. The prism-based construction provides a novel and efficient solution to these challenges, showcasing the computability of codimension and and Betti numbers for the given system through a straightforward pipeline. Furthermore, this method exhibits potential applications in the analysis of singularity codimension and its relationship with rationality in nonlinear polynomial systems. Direct photons have been measured at $p_T<5$ GeV/$c$ for midrapidity and most central events of Cu$+$Cu collisions at $\sqrt{s_{_{NN}}}=200$ GeV. By calculating the $e^{+}e^{-}$ excess in the $e^{+}e^{-}$ mass distribution over hadronic contributions, the investigation has focused on the same phenomena as previous LiNi$+$Li and Au $+$Au experiments held at the same energy. Due to lower count rates from the Cu$+$Cu dataset compared to those obtained from LiNi$+$Li and Au $+$Au experiments, the new results reveal a decreased $e^+e-$ excess separation confidence. Nonetheless, the hadronic contribution was accurately calculated by a theoretical model, while the remaining $e^+e-$ excess confidence was attributed to radiative decays of hadrons. As a result, the investigation was unable to separate the direct photon and radiative decays of hadrons components, a distinction that is a hallmark of similar direct photon measurements. Although the investigation failed to separate direct photon and radiative decays of hadrons components, the $p_T<5$ GeV/$c$ and most central events of Cu$+$Cu collisions at $\sqrt{s_{NN}})=200$ GeV appeared to exhibit in situ conditions analogous to those found in $d$+Au collisions held at the same energy. Consequently, the investigation suggested that cold nuclear matter is influencing the $e^+e-$ production in Cu$+$Cu collisions at $\sqrt{s_{NN}})=200$ GeV. One major issue with neural network training is getting stuck in local minima.
The gradient descent method, used widely in machine learning, has a significant
shortcoming: it often falls back on suboptimal solutions. To address this, we
introduce an optimization technique known as the organic gradient descent (OGD)
algorithm, which builds on the generalized gradient descent (GGD) methodology.
OGD is grounded in Flory's theory and the entropic model of protein folding,
utilizing fundamental thermodynamic principles to improve model efficiency. By
maintaining connectivity between higher and lower energy local minima, OGD
helps break through energy barriers. To demonstrate its efficacy, we applied OGD
to optimizing neural networks, and our results reveal a notable increase in
training accuracy and speed compared to conventional methods like SGD and
Adam, especially on challenging double-scaled convolutional layers. With
its potential to overcome local minima bottlenecks, OGD offers a valuable
alternative to existing gradient descent methods. A Python implementation of
OGD is available on GitHub. OGD is also available as a public IPython notebook.

analysis. Additionally, we'll discuss the computational requirements of using LSTM.

We've developed an approach that enables a group of drones to maintain a defined shape through the use of a centroid-based framework for aligning their positions in three-dimensional space. This method leverages a registration technique commonly used for aligning point clouds, applying it to the tracking of environmental features and fellow drones to calculate a centralized centroid that represents the overall structure of the swarm. Each drone then adjusts its position to move closer to this optimized centroid, allowing the system to achieve a stable and compact configuration. To implement this structure-maintenance capability while avoiding collisions, we've incorporated a novel extended state observer, designing it to incorporate both structure-maintenance and collision avoidance components into the swarm's dynamics. Reinforcement learning efficiency can be significantly enhanced through imitation learning, especially when expert guidance is available. However, recruiting expert demonstrations is often impractical and costly. We suggest overcoming this obstacle by utilizing imitation training without requiring expert demonstrations, achieving this goal with our new framework. We define a novel approach where agents learn to mimic each other's behaviors. Since self-imitation is inherently reliable, we focus on boosting the agent's ability to learn from others. We implement this concept through self-supervised peer imitation learning, which involves leveraging the agent's interaction history to create diverse paths. This is then used as expert behavior in an imitation learning algorithm. As a result, our method empowers agents to learn from non-expert peers without needing expert demonstrations, demonstrating high performance in complex tasks. It also offers cost savings by eliminating the need for costly human guidance and facilitates the development of more training data without the constraints typically involved. This new capability could be crucial for the training of autonomous systems. We provide extensive evidence of our method's validity through a comprehensive set of experiments. These results, along with the capabilities of our method, are highlighted in the associated videos and code assets. Furthermore, we investigate the general applicability of our framework by evaluating its effectiveness on diverse benchmarks and comparing its performance to alternative approaches. This paper addresses the code distance calculation in PAC codes, providing a detailed metric definition and convex optimization method. Numerical examples demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach. Furthermore, an efficient algorithm is proposed to directly calculate PAC code distances under certain conditions, significantly improving computational efficiency. These methods can be applied to diverse PAC code types. Introduced terms include minmax distance, quasi-optimal normalizer, and generalized PAC codes, with the latter offering enhanced performance and efficiency in Gaussian channels. As a type of Gaussian codes, PAC codes have distinct characteristics, including a density spectrum that shifts towards lower densities as the channel capacity is approached. We also investigate the structural properties of PAC codes under diverse decoding protocols and offer connections to prior research on normal codes. These studies were motivated by the ongoing analysis of the density spectrum's behavior in Gaussian codes. Additionally, this paper provides a thorough characterization of the PAC code family's properties. These findings are anticipated to be valuable in future studies on Gaussian codes. Lastly, an algorithm is suggested to determine the optimal crossover probability for binary-input, continuous-output channels based on the PAC code's density spectrum. This approach may be applied to identify ideal crossover probabilities in various coding problems. Furthermore, the impact of crossover probability variations on density spectrum and decoding performance, particularly in binary channels with output hard-decoded as binary outputs, is investigated. We calculate density spectrum values and assess decoding performances, including those resulting from random and structured PAC code constructions, across different crossover probabilities. These experiments may guide practitioners in selecting optimal crossover probabilities to enhance PAC code performance. Finally, noise models, specifically white and colored noise, are studied in relation to the density spectrum's behavior and decoding performances. These studies may facilitate generalizing the observed phenomena and their applications beyond binary-input, continuous-output channels. All numerical computations were conducted using MATLAB, with example code available on GitHub at https://github.com/haroldow/harold_2022arxiv1239. Moreover, a publicly accessible tool called PAC_code_tool has been released on MATLAB for comprehensive analysis of PAC code properties. This tool includes functions for calculating density spectrum values, assessing decoding performances, and determining optimal crossover probabilities. It also offers a graphical interface for visualizing density spectrum and decoding performance results and has been applied to various coding problems, as demonstrated in the provided figures. Please note that some figures have additional annotations that can be toggled on/off using zoom functionality. This report was initially made available as an arXiv preprint 1239 and has now been published in the journal IEEE Trans. Inf.

A new approach is presented for simultaneously estimating the 3D positions and movements as well as the configurations of hand joints and held objects from unorganized point cloud sequences, captured using depth sensors placed in a common coordinate system. This task is referred to as hand-object tracking, and while significant progress has been made on reconstructing 6DOF hand and object poses from single views, it presents an inherently more difficult problem due to the need for considering point cloud temporal correlations. To overcome this limitation, an efficient recursive algorithm, known as HOTHUC, has been developed. By utilizing a specialized cylinder-based representation for single-hand joints and incorporating an interconnected recursive detection framework, HOTHUC achieves high accuracy performance even in highly challenging real-world conditions. Notably, HOTHUC has outperformed state-of-the-art methods on a recently released large-scale real-world point cloud sequence benchmark, achieving an average intersection over the mean average precision of 35.96%. The proposed approach has further demonstrated its effectiveness through experimental validation on a widely used dataset containing synthetic hand and object interactions. The proposed method demonstrates promising potential for applications in computer vision that involve analyzing and predicting human hand interactions. A novel deep learning approach is proposed to derive information necessary for 3D printing from raw video footage without relying on pre-established markers or cameras. The method employs a dedicated neural network, trained on simulated data, to estimate the position and orientation of a robot's end-effector from video frames, as well as calculate necessary adjustments to adjust a Depth camera's field of view to facilitate successful printing. The proposed approach outperformed a comparative method built using OpenCV, demonstrating better results for both prediction tasks. The proposed system has been successfully integrated with the Bristle Bot, a simple underactuated robot, to demonstrate its effectiveness in 3D printing applications without pre-established markers or cameras. The system's dependency on pre-established markers or cameras was eliminated through this work. The proposed approach offers enhanced robustness over existing methods due to its ability to predict noise. The proposed method's source code is publicly available on the GitHub repository: https://github.com/AslanyanGevorg/DeepLearningBasedRobotDepthCameraAdjustmentAndEndEffectorPoseEstimation. The system's performance was evaluated using the mean absolute error (MAE), as well as through visual analysis of prediction results. The MAE metric yielded predictive results of $[5.626, 5.266, 5.045]$ degrees and $[312.068, 13.043, 0.947]$ pixels for the main and secondary tasks, respectively. In certain treatment settings, participants can be influenced by each other - a phenomenon referred to as therapy interference. Research has traditionally relied on subjective assessments to detect and quantify interference effects, but these methods have significant drawbacks. A newer approach involves operating within an interference model, providing researchers with an objective tool to analyze treatment data and estimate interference effects. A simulation study was conducted to examine how effective statistical tests can be in identifying therapy interference, utilizing data generated under the K-Nearest-Neighbors (KNN) interference model. Results demonstrated that tests able to account for the impact of therapy interference can accurately detect it at various levels, whereas ignoring it leads to biased estimates of treatment effects and increased type II errors. Furthermore, a novel asymptotic result was established, showing that a specific statistical test is consistent and capable of detecting interference effects at an appropriate rate. These findings have important practical implications, advising researchers to utilize statistical tests that account for interference effects when analyzing treatment data under the KNN interference model. Additional resources, including a accompanying software package, are provided to facilitate the reproduction of these results and clinical trial interpretations. A corresponding technical report includes further details, including proofs and model extensions. The ongoing UNIONS project, the most comprehensive optical survey to date in the Northern sky, has partnered with CFIS for $r$-band data collection, with partnered weak-lensing analyses. We introduce ShapePipe, a fast and precise pipeline for generating multiple galaxy shape parameters from raw image data, utilizing the SCALAPROF framework. We assessed ShapePipe's accuracy against the CFIS pipeline, discovering a low systematic error of approximately 0.5 $\mu$rad in shear signal recovery. Ultimately, we applied ShapePipe to the interim UNIONS/CFIS data release, achieving improved galactic foreground reduction with more realistic galaxy shape distributions compared to the CFIS pipeline, resulting in optimized weak-lensing analyses. We utilized the reduced data to compute two-point shear correlation functions for $70,000$ square-degrees, with precision sufficient for comparing theoretical models with observational data in the future. We also prepared the data for cosmological parameter estimation through Bayesian analysis on the shear power spectrum. This research was funded by an ISF grant (Grant Number 1631/20). This new framework is connected to the behavior of exponents in partial quotients of continued fractions. Furthermore, our results provide a novel approach to applying Diophantine approximation techniques to non-Archimedean settings. We establish that for k-rational singularities of local complete varieties, the Du Bois classification coincides with the k-Du Bois classification. Moreover, for such varieties, having k-rational singularities or being k-Du Bois can be characterized by the presence of a certain finitary hyperresolution. Additionally, for k-rational singularities in dimensions at most three, we provide an equivalent condition to the k-Du Bois condition utilizing a form of Fisken's theorem. These findings rely heavily on Fisken's theorem and certain generalizations of K\"ahl's theorem. These results imply that for local complete analytic spaces of dimension two, the k-rational and k-Du Bois classifications coincide, a demonstration that k-rational singularities capture the essential essence of the k-Du Bois category. This proves a conjecture proposed by Corti and Nekrasov. Moreover, we expand upon their hypotheses, considering the case of non-algebraic spaces with analytic singularities. Finally, we offer an example constructed by Yin, contrasting k-rational and k-Du Bois singularities in dimension four. This raises the question of whether the k-rational singularities category is comparable to the k-Du Bois category in dimension four. This question is answered affirmatively for local complete analytic spaces with dimension four, as demonstrated in the accompanying paper. These results are conditioned by a previously unproven conjecture related to Fisken's theorem in dimension four. This conjecture has since been resolved in the accompanying paper. A highly mobile spin chain with weak inter-spin interactions is studied as a starting point.
It is established that in the case of a weak transverse magnetic field, this system exhibits
Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless behavior, characterized by two-dimensional Correlation length growth
proportional to (T/K_Beskin)*$(1/(T_\xi- T))$, with T_K_Beskin denoting the critical temperature.
Further investigation reveals that in the case of a strong longitudinal magnetic field, the system's
unpolarized state can be described by a modified 1D S=1/2 Heisenberg chain with a specific easy-axis anisotropy.
Additionally, an unexpected growth in the correlation length is observed for temperatures below
T_K_Beskin/anisotropy, where T_K_Beskin/anisotropy is a temperature ratio based on the easy-axis anisotropy.
The proportionality constants for T_K_Beskin/anisotropy and T_K_Beskin are found to be equivalent. 
The effects of both magnetizations can be quantitatively analyzed and controlled through magnetic field. 
The system's unique properties may be attributed to the competition and intertwining of antiferromagnetic
unpolarized state anisotropy and ferromagnetic vortex excitations facilitated by a transverse magnetic field. 
This research offers an original and experimentally verifiable 1D model that showcases a Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless
phase, traditionally present in two-dimensional systems only. 
The study also opens doors for exploring quantum spin liquids and realizing reentrant phases, with possible implementations
using techniques such as hydrostatic pressure, chemical modifications, and irradation. 
Lastly, the research suggests that similar effects could also be observed in other compounds like CeRhIn5.

The study focused on the early $K$2 window, capturing objects whose useful half-life is around seven days. The investigation utilized $g$-$r$-$i$ photometry data from the Asteroid Thermal Model Database and analyzed lightcurves with various functions to categorize objects and their characteristics. The findings revealed lightcurves with diverse shapes and functions, predominantly characterized by a basic linear model. The study further identified linear systems with notable system heterogeneity, and objects exhibiting periodic behavior, including RR Lyrae and Cepheids. To facilitate comparison, key lightcurve parameters were also presented. Ultimately, the analysis aimed to provide an overview of objects' characteristics across four $K$2 plates. To ensure accuracy, simultaneous photometry data from ZTF were consulted to complement the analysis. The research has crucial implications for understanding variable stars and asteroids, and the findings are expected to be instrumental in future ground-based and space-based observations. Generating truly random numbers is essential for numerous statistical simulations and cryptographic applications. Current methods for creating random numbers, particularly in integrated circuits, often rely on external sources like thermal activity or electrical noise. In this research, we present a novel approach based on utilizing electrical noise from underscaled transistors to create random numbers. This method leverages a reduced supply voltage to stimulate SRAM bitcells, collecting the resulting binary data to create high-quality random bits. To accomplish this, we developed a 130nm CMOS test chip utilizing 32 SRAM bitcells, demonstrating the practical application of this principle. Under normal operating conditions, the collected bits exhibited exceptional entropy exceeding 480bits/byte over a extended time frame of 100 seconds. Furthermore, our results show that the entropy rate is directly correlated with the bitflip rate of the SRAM bitcells. To validate the random number generation, we employed the NIST Standard 800-22 statistical test suite. The outcomes of these tests demonstrate the high quality of the random bits, with success rates comparable to industry-standard hardware random number generators. To provide context, our research incorporates relevant quantitative metrics such as energy efficiency, area, and the underlying physics of SRAM. The empirical findings suggest that the proposed generator has significant practical applications due to its exceptional performance, relatively simple design that can be implemented using standard CMOS technology and modest power consumption. The test chip has been prototyped and tested using the Digilent Adept Embedded System Studio, providing a user-friendly interface for observing the random number generation in action. In summary, our research presents an attractive solution for integrated circuits, capable of supporting background-based random number generation with high entropy, simplicity, and relatively low power consumption. The proposed method and associated test chip may serve as a feasible alternative to existing random number generators. The test chip is available for download on the Digilent website under the designation SRRNG-ACTN. Additionally, the associated board-level hardware has been incorporated into the Digilent Ad boards collection as board 'SRRNG-ACTN.' The research documentation, including the board user manual and the research paper, can be accessed via the following link: https://git.cs.rutgers.edu/u08090p/public/SRRNG-ACTN.git. The functionality of a molecular single-electron resistor switch depends on its capacitance, charging and discharging rates, and the energy gap between its initial and final charge states.  These properties can be modeled and optimized using a geometric layout that incorporates a gate electrode and a capacitance value determined by the gap width and lengths.  Our study shows that increasing the gap width for a fixed barrier height reduces the energy gap between charge states, but raises the initial charge threshold.  For a fixed gap width, raising the barrier height elevates the initial charge threshold and decreases the energy gap between charge states.  Our simulations indicate that modest barrier heights and gap widths offer the best compromise of these properties.  Furthermore, our model's assumptions about constant current flow during discharge and a stable equilibrium state after switching may not always hold in reality.  Ultimately, experimental verification of our theoretical predictions will be essential to informing the design of efficient molecular single-electron resistor switches.  Additionally, our model can be applied to a broader range of electrostatic transistor designs.

This is illustrated using the model of a laser-cooled atomic gas in a dissipative optical lattice, where the interplay between laser cooling, optical potential, and photon absorption leads to complex equilibrium statistics. Long-range correlations and anomalous distributions arise due to the entanglement of atomic excitations, resulting in intractable thermodynamic properties. Similarly, fluctuations of the particle number exhibit a power-law dependence on the system size, indicating an absence of thermodynamic stability. When laser cooling is predominant, the system undergoes a crossover from Gaussian to non-Gaussian behavior, whereas increased photon absorption gives rise to long-range spatial correlations and increased non-Gaussianity. In contrast, if the system is isolated from external influences, it exhibits purely Gaussian behavior, characterized by a stable thermodynamic limit. Nonetheless, it is demonstrated that coherent excitations can lead to atypical statistical phenomena, even in closed quantum systems. Furthermore, it is suggested that analogous phenomena could be observed in ultracold bosonic gases using in-situ imaging, thereby providing a viable pathway for experimental verification. In contrast, the center of mass distribution and the mean bond lengths of the molecules, obtained through the time-averaged mean positions, did not adequately account for the rapid quantum vibrations. Automated essay grading has been a persistent challenge in Natural Language Processing.  Despite years of research, it remains an only partially resolved issue, with notable practical applications and research implications.  A key strategy for overcoming this challenge has been the development of highly advanced language models, including Transformer-based models like RoBERTa and BART.  While effective, these models come with a significant research cost, requiring substantial datasets to achieve reliable results.  A practical approach for addressing data limitations is data augmentation, which can be used to increase the quantity of available data.  This research investigates the application of Transformer models for AEGR, focusing on two approaches: using these models both for class label prediction and for data augmentation.  We evaluate various data augmentation techniques, assessing their impact on performance in relation to both dataset size and complexity.  A novel, straightforward, and efficient data augmentation method proves particularly effective, enhancing performance without requiring a massive dataset to reach reliability.  This research makes several significant contributions, including introducing a new, efficient data augmentation strategy, achieving top-notch results on standard benchmarks with limited training datasets, and providing an open-source implementation. 

Keywords: Automated essay grading, Data augmentation, Transformer models, RoBERTa, BART, Open-source implementation.

A dynamic model representing the dynamic nature of choices and opportunities is also developed. We use this model to analyze data on educational and occupational choices in the US, demonstrating that the data reflects a combination of situation-dependent and dynamic decision-making factors. We establish methods to quantify the relative influence of these factors in shaping societal mobility patterns. This approach can be applied to other domains where dynamic choices and varying opportunity structures play a significant role. Our model also yields insights into the persistent social inequalities observed in the US, suggesting that situation-dependent and dynamic factors can contribute to a self-perpetuating system where lower socio-economic status individuals face less favorable opportunities, leading to a continuous decline in their socio-economic status. We also suggest policy interventions aimed at addressing educational and occupational inequality, as well as strategies focused on breaking the cycle of low socio-economic status, including direct assistance programs and incentives to encourage individuals to seek better opportunities beyond their local area. We introduce an upgraded RingCT protocol that supports stealth addresses in conjunction with Delegated Proof of Stake, resulting in a compatible implementation with Nano. The improved Delegated RingCT through Ring Signatures (d-RCT-rs) maintains the anonymity, untraceability, and double-spending resistance benefits, while significantly enhancing transaction processing speed. Specifically, it integrates a high-performance linkable ring signature scheme and adapts RingCT to use aggregated compact ring signatures and efficient provably secure verifiable random functions within Nano. Furthermore, it incorporates a prototype of a new lightweight linkable ring signature scheme, 'hybrid thread,' which is an optimized integration of ring signatures and a thread-based approach, showing great potential for improved performance without compromising security. The hybrid thread design offers promising insights for further research and development in the d-RCT-rs framework. The integration of d-RCT-rs into Nano is presented as a reusable module, featuring a new lightweight RingCT-based consensus layer, along with hybrid threads. The results demonstrate that this design can provide a suitable trade-off between security, anonymity, and transaction processing speed in Nano. Detailed technical documentation and source code are available on GitHub at <https://github.com/jim-anderson/nano-d-rct-rs>. Additionally, a research paper has been published in arXiv, <https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.02042>. We analyze the stability of linear system solvers for matrix spaces equipped with different norms, often resulting in varied levels of tolerance for perturbations. This research originates from testing linear systems with imperfectly precise data, a issue known as ill-determined systems, where existing theory provides too strict bounds for accuracy. We investigate whether imposing a minimum condition number for solvers, measured in terms of vector 1-norm or matrix 2-norm, is sufficient to maintain stability when solving linear systems under weak conditions. Notably, we find that such stability condition holds for matrix equi-rotation and some specific cases, but it does not hold universally. We further demonstrate that imposing a minimum condition for matrix 2-norm is not sufficient to guarantee stability for solvers, illustrating this with a counterexample. We also discuss relationships between operator norms and 1-norms, showcasing that imposing a minimum condition for operator norms can actually result in more accurate tolerance levels for linear system solvers. We also investigate minimum conditions for operator norms in testing linear systems, based on cut-off or integration techniques. We have investigated the production of three massive gauge bosons in association with jets at the Large Hadron Collider. Our analysis is based on a theoretical framework of next-to-leading order QCD. This includes precise calculations of signal processes such as $WW+\text{jets}$, $WZ+\text{jets}$, and $Wgamma+jet$ that feature heavy electroweak bosons, alongside up-to-date parton distribution functions. We have selected final states characterized by a distinct and separated lepton signature, and have considered the contribution of four-parton processes up to next-to-leading order in QCD. We demonstrate that for $1<p<\infty$ and given $\varepsilon>0$, there indeed exists an integer $n=$$\varepsilon$$^2$ and a sequence $x=(x_t)_{t=0}^n$ such that a subspace spanned by $x$ is $\varepsilon$-isometric and completely contained in $\ell_p$. This means that for any other sequence $y=(y_t)_{t=0}^m$, if the subspace spanned by $y$ is also $\varepsilon$-isometric, then $m=n$ and $y=x$. Furthermore, this result holds without compressibility in $\ell_p$; in fact, the subspace it generates is completely contained in $\ell_p$. This achievement is grounded in a newly established theorem stating that for every $z\neq0$ in $\ell_p$, there exists a sequence $x=(x_t)_{t=0}^\nu$ and a scalar $\delta \leq \varepsilon$ such that the subspace spanned by $x$ is $\delta$-isometric and contains $z$. This implies that $n\leq \varepsilon^2$. This study significantly extends upon the work from the research paper titled: Linear dimension reduction into nearly-isometric images has nearly linear query complexity, authored by K. Lopale and J. Racz, which was presented at STOC 2021. The study resolves this complexity issue by introducing a new concept called almost-isometric linear dimension reduction with a more forgiving error bound. This study is part of a broader research in almost-isometric linear dimension reduction with distinct notions of isometry. A key challenge in creating complex computer models lies in verifying their accuracy against real-world data, particularly in complex systems where this can be a highly laborious task. Researchers have developed a new approach in which artificial intelligence generates mathematical formulas for complex problems by using real-world data and demonstrating model accuracy through repeated experiments. This innovative method was successfully applied to create a detailed computer model of twin pregnancies, utilizing a vast dataset of medical records and incorporating expertise from medical professionals to ensure precision and reliability. The artificial intelligence was able to identify critical factors influencing twin pregnancy outcomes and accurately predict risks within established accuracy margins. The fully transparent model, encompassing all findings and algorithmic decisions, has numerous potential uses beyond research, including safety assessments and clinical decision-making consultations. Moreover, this method can be adapted for use in both predictive and descriptive modeling across a wide range of fields and research domains. Furthermore, this approach offers an unprecedented opportunity to gain a deeper understanding of the underlying processes driving twin pregnancy outcomes. Despite reaching high levels of model refinement, the research team discovered that artificial intelligence models often develop unique features and interpretations of clinical data, potentially altering the outcome predictions and insights gained from the models. Consequently, incorporating expert knowledge and medical professionals' insights proved essential for achieving the highest possible model performance. Nonetheless, this approach also presents a challenge in terms of integrating human expertise with the complex, hard-to-read predictions generated by artificial intelligence, particularly as this methodology is still relatively new to medical research. Nonetheless, this innovative method has opened the door to seamlessly combining human expertise with artificial intelligence and has paved the way for more advanced combinations of these two elements in the future. Lastly, this research successfully demonstrated how deep learning can be utilized for creating highly detailed, complex computer models from medical records without any prior knowledge of the underlying processes. The way bits within codes are connected through relationships of degree, has a significant impact on their performance when sent over noisy channels. This effect will be examined in this study, specifically in a channel that introduces random, partial data loss. By developing an mathematical approach that accounts for this performance under various types of correlations, it becomes apparent that traditional coding research may not fully apply in this scenario. This is illustrated by the discovery that higher density codes aren't always better in this environment. Through an in-depth analysis using complex network theory, it is determined how correlations impact the performance of codes. This knowledge is then utilized to create new guidelines for designing optimal codes. This is done by comparing traditional coding research standards with those required for optimal performance in the presence of degree-degree correlations. Finally, simulations are conducted to validate these findings and provide a framework for designing and evaluating degree-degree correlated codes. These results have broader implications, extending beyond traditional coding research. The study of codes with interconnected bits of varying degree correlations may lead to new insights in complex network research and distributed computing systems. Also, it is believed that this research may be applied to neural networks that experience random, partial data loss. The findings of this study are a stepping stone towards exploring these connections further. The code used to create the figures in this study can be found at https://github.com/molavi/DDC-research. This paper presents an innovative method to design a detectable and secure system, using a predictive security filter, by transforming an insecure system into a secure one. It is based on a novel application of system level synthesis techniques to hybrid systems. A security filter is created that prevents unauthorized inputs from reaching the controlled variable while allowing secure inputs to pass through, while a detectable security filter is designed that detects and differentiates between secure and insecure inputs. Under predetermined security requirements, a algorithm is developed that generates a security filter model, which is then implemented in a practical system through a hardware description language. It is shown through simulations that this method can effectively design security filters in power systems and predict intrusive inputs. It is also found that its ability to predict intrusive inputs makes it possible to prevent such attacks, which further enhances its security. A practical application of this framework is demonstrated using a digital signal processor. Extensive tests in a laboratory setup verify the effectiveness of this framework. It is also envisioned that this framework will contribute to the development of secure and reliable smart grid systems. A video presenting the test results is available at https://youtu.be/7x3b_SiB1kQ.

This study focuses on the effect of training corpora on in-context learning. We investigated four training sets, including books, Wikipedia, forums, and user-generated content, and compared their impact on a state-of-the-art language model. Galaxy cluster observations have primarily focused on the birth of cooling clouds, which eventually block star formation. Discrete, moving structures within these clouds have been postulated but never directly seen. We analyze the dynamics of a developing cool core using 3D magnetohydrodynamics simulations that incorporate realistic galaxy cluster properties. We studied the effects of a Strömgren sphere formation on a hot cluster core, which leads to the formation of rings and whips. As cooling proceeds, rings collapse and generate spiral patterns. When cooling stops, a whiplike structure forms, which later becomes unstable and produces small, moving structures. We found that a growing cool core with whiplike structure has a unique pattern of gas rotation. This structure enhances heat transfer from surrounding gas to the core, which slows down cooling. We found that a growing cool core with whiplike structure can persist for millions of years. Finally, we concluded that both buoyant and non-buoyant structures can lead to the formation of discrete, moving structures within galaxy cluster cooling clouds.

In the Standard Model of particle physics, a phenomenon called CP violation allows matter to exist even though its antimatter counterpart does not. Researchers have discovered this violation in certain particle interactions, but its underlying source remains mysterious. This research explores the feasibility of synthesizing speech without prior knowledge of phonology, using only audio examples and their transcriptions based on acoustic primitives. We overcome the limitations of transcription accuracy by developing a method to identify and replace unreliable unit synthesis components. Since human-generated transcripts are also unreliable, we create a dictionary of learned acoustic units through clustering and establish a dictionary-edit distance metric to compare this with the transcription-based unit list. We then utilize a graph-based approach to locate and replace inaccurate synthesis components in transcription-based synthesis. Additionally, to integrate the acoustic primitives into a neural convolutional synthesis model, we develop a dictionary-edit distance metric to guide the training process. Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach in synthesizing speech without phonology knowledge, revealing that a significant portion of synthesized speech originates from the acoustic primitives and that the proposed method surpasses state-of-the-art speech synthesis models in terms of synthesis length. However, its speech quality remains inferior, likely due to the low efficacy of the acoustic primitives in capturing complex linguistic nuances. Therefore, we suggest a hybrid approach that combines the acoustic primitives with a neural synthesis model, achieving improved speech quality while retaining the benefits of acoustic primitives for length limitations. The code and data used in this research are publicly available. \\
