We examine the distinction between physical and non-physical quantum states made by the energy availability condition (EAC) in quantum thermodynamics. By developing a controlled environment, we assess whether a given state is physically attainable through probabilistic transformations. Our findings demonstrate that EAC serves as a necessary condition for probabilistic convertibility, surpassing previous strict convertibility criteria. Furthermore, EAC imposes stringent limitations on probabilistic resource theory scenarios. Specifically, we investigate the implications of EAC in the context of bipartite quantum thermodynamics within the context of the central resource framework. In this context, EAC is linked to the notion of relative entropy bias and its connection to total quantum entropy. Bias serves as a precise physical manifestation of the entropy difference resulting from interactions between systems and its complement. Consequently, we define and apply the concept of convertible bias, establishing a clear separation between physically attainable and non-physical states. The removable entropy by EAC's standards correlates positively with the convertible bias, thus illustrating EAC's strength in constraining physical state attainability. Our analysis also highlights the practical significance of EAC in achieving maximum entropy from a quantum system and recovering maximum entropy from a quantum system and its environment. In both scenarios, the convertible bias acts as a limiting factor for achieving the desired outcome. Moreover, we establish that EAC leads to a more stringent outcome compared to the total entropy in both cases. Finally, we reflect on the broader theoretical and fundamental implications of our findings. Firstly, we validate the practical relevance of the energy availability condition in real-world thermodynamic systems. Secondly, we clarify that the entropy difference between a system and its environment does not necessarily determine if a state is physically attainable in a probabilistic context. Lastly, we demonstrate that the convertible bias offers a more precise and stringent limitation on probabilistic convertibility compared to the entropy difference between a system and its environment. In conclusion, we examine the specifications and features of the energy availability condition, including its connection to total entropy in a system and its environment, and the convertible bias. We utilize the concept of hydrodynamic attractors to establish a universal relationship between initial energy states and the number of produced particles in high-energy collisions. By incorporating an energy function that decreases with collision centrality, we are able to calculate the temperature and ratio of transverse to longitudinal momentum scales at the moment when the fluid becomes quasi-static, for any given collision event. This enables us to establish a relationship between initial energy states and the number of produced particles. Specifically, for collisions of protons with protons, we find that the average number of produced particles per collision, per unit rapidity, depends solely on the collision's centrality and not on the energy of the collision. This prediction is subject to validation against future measurements of collisions at the Large Hadron Collider at higher energies. Furthermore, we observe that the number of produced particles per collision decreases as the mass of the charged particles per unit rapidity increases. This prediction is currently being tested against measurements at the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider. We note that the principles underlying our predictions may also be relevant to the study of turbulence in complex fluids and other systems exhibiting hydrodynamic behavior.

However, achieving both performance metrics in a single system can be a significant challenge. By employing a linear parameter-varying (LPV) approach, researchers have developed an innovative motion control strategy, incorporating a sequential loop tightening technique to increase closed-loop system fastening rates. This control scheme has been successfully implemented and tested on a high-precision aerospace motion drive, demonstrating a dramatic enhancement of performance. Key outcomes include a substantial increase of nearly 50% in the speed of closed-loop system convergence and a notable improvement in high-speed positioning errors, amounting to as much as 75%. Furthermore, integration of the LPV technique facilitated the development of a more streamlined and compact controller design, featuring a reduced number of parameters, from hundreds to thousands, to aid in practical implementation. This work marks the first practical application of the LPV sequential loop tightening technique in motion control systems. As such, it offers groundbreaking insights into the deployment of this advanced control theory, commonly influenced by research, to industrial settings. We introduce a novel deep learning approach for aligning partial human scans.  Given two partial point cloud views of a person, our network produces a registration that maximizes agreement on both shape and texture, doing so in a self-supervised manner without the need for fully visible scans during training.  Our approach is particularly suited for within-person registration tasks due to its robustness against diverse poses, individual variations, and missing data.  As a result, it outperforms existing methods on two public benchmarks, surpassing their performance and achieving results closer to those of 2D medical segmentation networks.  Our implementation and benchmark are available online.  This research was published in [Chen et al., 2020a].  Our code can be found at https://github.com/cchen223/PRNet. We demonstrate that each generalized abelian Baumslag-Solitar group $\Gamma_n$ possesses the $R_\infty$ property, and as a result, so do its nilpotent quotients. Additionally, for $n \geq 2$, the group $\Gamma_2$ can be represented as a subgroup of the automorphism group of a countable, finitely generated nil-2 abelian group. Furthermore, for $n > 2$, the group $\Gamma_n$ can be represented as a subgroup of the automorphism group of a countable, finitely generated nil-3 abelian group. Lastly, the groups $\Gamma_2$ and $\Gamma_3$ do not satisfy the $R_{\infty}^{ab}$ property, which requires that the above-mentioned subgroup has a finitely generated nilpotent quotient. In medical image analysis, particularly in multi-modal image segmentation, handling unknown image modalities is a persistent challenge. The conventional approach in deep learning involves training models for specific modalities and then combining them, often resulting in poor performance for unknown modalities. We present a novel method called CD-GAN, which uses a single deep learning model to automatically identify and segment objects across various modalities. CD-GAN achieves this through a training cycle that includes an unsupervised division of a composite image into its constituent modalities and subsequently applies a segmentation task to the resulting images. By training a single model in an unsupervised manner, CD-GAN is applicable to object segmentation tasks in multiple domains. Experimental results demonstrate that CD-GAN outperforms state-of-the-art approaches in multi-modal image segmentation, showcasing its effectiveness and efficiency. The source code can be accessed at https://github.com/alibaba-incubator-alipy/InstanceSegWithoutLabels. Leveraging weakly paired data, CD-GAN trains with modalities having different resolutions as input and produces higher-resolution segmentation results, resulting in a notable improvement in segmentation performance. Metrics such as the dice score and sensitivity of segmentation results confirm CD-GAN's superiority over existing methods. Furthermore, CD-GAN successfully applies to segmentation tasks in multiple domains, including brain, animal, and agricultural images, demonstrating its broad domain applicability. However, we also identify potential drawbacks of CD-GAN, primarily due to its reliance on image synthesis for unknown modalities and potential mode collapse, which could impact its segmentation performance. Potential future research directions for enhancing CD-GAN's performance involve incorporating attention mechanisms and adaptive loss functions. Additionally, we propose a label augmentation approach called label flipping to improve CD-GAN's robustness to ground-truth labeling variations. Furthermore, we evaluate the efficacy of cyclic training and image synthesis on segmentation performance, revealing that both components contribute significantly to the improvement in segmentation performance. Moreover, we conduct ablation studies on the effectiveness of the proposed method in automatically identifying and segmenting objects across various modalities. Results demonstrate that CD-GAN surpasses several baseline methods in terms of segmentation performance. Furthermore, we assess CD-GAN's applicability to real-world datasets, showcasing its ability to successfully segment objects in multiple domains. However, we also identify potential drawbacks of CD-GAN, primarily due to its reliance on image synthesis for unknown modalities and segmentation performance variability. We carried out comprehensive photometric and spectroscopic observations of the star AD Leo during its significant flare on April 12, 1985, which showed a spectacular explosion of ultraviolet radiation. The rapid flare rose to an extraordinary peak that was nearly 70 times stronger than the star's normal ultraviolet brightness, occurring at a wavelength of 169 nm. The explosive growth was most pronounced in the near-ultraviolet range, reaching an impressive factor of 30 at a wavelength of 250 nm. The spectral distribution of the flare radiation varied as it evolved, shifting from a cooler distribution with increasing wavelength earlier on to a hotter distribution later on. The energy released by the flare was estimated at approximately 4.3 x 10^31 ergs, which is about 4.5% of the star's total lost energy per second. The flare's effects were to temporarily expand the star to a size of about 2.7 times its normal diameter in all directions. The flare's impact also caused the star's average surface temperature to rise by about 800 K for a brief time. The observed variations in the flare's near-ultraviolet emission over time can be effectively explained by using a model that includes the core gas photoionization and the contribution of recombination continuum from stratospheric helium clouds with electron densities ranging from approximately 10^10 to 10^12 cm^-3. The most plausible explanation is the occurrence of the helium cloud breaking through the star's atmosphere and resulting in the observed explosive growth of ultraviolet radiation. The time taken by the flare to reach its peak varied based on the wavelength, ranging from the longest at 250 nm to the shortest at 169 nm. The star's optical and near-infrared brightness returned to normal quickly but the near-ultraviolet brightness took significantly longer, taking about 10 hours to return to normal. During this time, the star exhibited rapid and irregular variations in brightness. The star also experienced another significant flare during this time, which showed some similarities with the initial flare in its explosive growth and spectral distribution, although it was less intense. Nonetheless, the second flare was noticeably different from the initial flare in several aspects, particularly its rapid and sudden onset, and in the considerable time that passed before it displayed its peak brightness, which was almost as strong as the initial flare's peak brightness at longer wavelengths. We are exploring the deformation theory of G2-instantons within the context of nearly G2-manifolds. A one-to-one connection exists between nearly parallel G2 structures and real Killing spinors, enabling the deformation theory to be formulated through the use of spinors and Dirac operators. We establish that the space of infinitesimal deformations for an instanton is equivalent to the kernel of an elliptic operator. Furthermore, for a regular instanton, this kernel is comprised of the instanton's kernel and image, ultimately resulting in a finite-dimensional space. In contrast, an irregular instanton yields an infinite-dimensional space of deformations. Additionally, we analyze how deformations affect the linking number and Chern classes, revealing that these quantities remain unchanged under one-parameter deformations. Lastly, our findings are extended to the combination of one-parameter deformations and G2-deformations. Our methods involve a detailed examination of the properties of the Dirac operator across the cylinder and a study of self-duality equations on cylindrical manifolds. A new approach utilizes radio frequency identification (RFID)-like ALOHA protocols to enable multiple continuous wave (CW) frequency-modulated continuous wave (FMCW) radar transmitters to share the same unregulated, crowded spectrum, thereby allowing multiple radar receivers to simultaneously detect moving targets within their respective areas of interest. Two protocols, ALOHA and carrier sense multiple access (CSMA), have been developed and evaluated through analytical modeling and simulation to determine their performance under different parameter settings and scenarios. A key challenge lies in the dynamic nature of wireless channels that may cause significant performance degradation during back-off periods. Consequently, using higher power transmitters or increasing the number of retransmissions can lead to higher energy consumption and increased interference levels. Nevertheless, this solution may not be suitable for radar applications due to restricted transmit power limitations. Notably, these protocols have been primarily demonstrated to enable multiple radar receivers to share the spectrum and augment existing spectrum resources, including microwave and millimeter-wave frequencies. Furthermore, this study lays the groundwork for a new paradigm in passive safety and security applications. Simulation outcomes reveal that both slotted ALOHA and CSMA protocols can achieve satisfactory target detection rates at the cost of slightly increased collision rates. Moreover, performance simulations using Python reveal that higher back-off levels lead to lower collision rates at the expense of prolonged waiting times, which may not significantly affect radar operations due to long back-off periods. Notably, these protocols can also be employed in non-radar applications such as environmental monitoring and animal tracking. Since these applications typically prioritize successful transmissions over high collision rates, the ALOHA protocol may be more suitable than CSMA for radar applications that require high target detection rates. On the other hand, the CSMA protocol may be more applicable than ALOHA in scenarios where high collision rates can be tolerated for brief periods. Ultimately, the ultimate choice of protocol depends on whether the application in question prioritizes high target detection rates or low collision rates. One key drawback of recommender systems is data scarcity due to an overwhelming number of user activities and a limited number of user and item reviews. To alleviate this issue, hybrid recommender systems have emerged, integrating various approaches to address data insufficiency. A particular hybrid system that has gained popularity is the context-aware recommender system. However, existing context-aware approaches primarily focus on utilizing review content from both users and items, overlooking the importance of contextual information from item-provided content. To build on this insight, we developed a new hybrid system called Context-Aware Content-Driven Recommendation System (CACDRS), which seamlessly integrates context-based and content-based methods. The latter method is inherently capable of capturing item-provided content. Thus, our system is grounded in the distribution of provided reviews. We utilized two main components: a context-based method and a content-based method rooted in latent semantic analysis. To validate our approach, we employed two metrics: accuracy and fairness, testing the system's performance on real-world data. Results showed that our system's stability in producing just and accurate lists of recommended items surpassed comparisons with similar systems that utilize user and item reviews alone. Additionally, we employed two approaches to improve fairness: calibration and preference-based, achieving satisfactory outcomes. Lastly, we assessed our system's responsiveness with a performance evaluation metric, achieving a reasonable time of 0.054 seconds per user. We examine $k$-Center variants in graphs with limited doubling or freeway dimension, leading to improved algorithmic solutions and proof strategies. Our work particularly focuses on the Guha-Thomson $k$-Center problem, yielding the following key findings: For graphs with doubling property $D$, we can solve the Guha-Thomson $k$-Center problem within a time complexity of $O(2^{CDk}\cdot (D + \log k) Dk)$, where $C$ is a constant. For graphs with freeway dimension $f$, we can solve the Guha-Thomson $k$-Center problem within a time complexity of $O(2^{Lf^2k}\cdot (L+ \log k) f^2k)$, where $L$ is a constant exponent. Our solutions surpass previously established time complexities, $O(2^{7k} D^{5k+1} \frac{\log k}{\log 2})$ and $O(2^{19k} L^{10k+1} \frac{\log k}{\log 2})$, which were specifically designed for doubling and freeway dimension graphs, respectively. Interestingly, our algorithmic approach appears to be sensitive to these dimension properties, as it fails to yield polynomial time complexity for either property. To confirm this, we provide an instance of a doubling graph for which the time complexity of our algorithm exceeds polynomial time. Furthermore, we can solve the $k$-Center problem with a fixed cover radius in graphs with limited freeway dimension, offering an $O(\log L k)$-factor approximation, a performance not achievable in graphs with limited doubling property. To confirm the limitations of our approach, we provide an instance of a freeway dimension graph for which the $k$-Center problem with a fixed cover radius cannot be solved within a constant factor of the optimal solution. Lastly, we investigate the Guha-Thomson $k$-Center problem with a fixed cover radius in graphs lacking any dimension bounds, yielding an $O(\log k)$-factor approximation, a performance also not achievable in graphs with limited doubling or freeway dimension. To confirm the limitations of our approach, we provide an instance of a graph without a doubling or freeway dimension for which the $k$-Center problem with a fixed cover radius cannot be solved with an $O(\log k)$-factor approximation. Interestingly, our findings reveal that the property of having a fixed cover radius can significantly distinguish between doubling and freeway dimension

In this paper, we explore solving polynomial linear systems with noisy answers, where each coordinate of the system's vector may be incorrect with a certain probability. Our research reveals that even with a relatively low error rate of $1-\frac{d}{2n}$ (where system size is $d$ and vector length is $n$), we can accurately solve the system almost certainly, provided $d$ is less than $n$ and the degrees of the system's polynomials do not exceed $2\frac{\log n}{\log \log n}$. The solver we present can be viewed as an extension of the Fourier Transform, and its analysis involves a new type of concentration bound for low-order multiplicative functions. Furthermore, we can modify our solver to quickly terminate with high probability when solving multiple polynomial linear systems simultaneously, such as in the context of random linear systems. This modified solver can be made to terminate after just a fraction of its total computation time, and its termination is not dependent on the system it's working on. We discover that this early termination capability can also be applied to previously known methods, and we demonstrate that doing so results in significantly faster computation times, especially for large system sizes. Finally, we investigate the computational efficiency of our new early termination technique and find that it can be highly beneficial, especially for small system sizes. In solving the initial conditions for numerical relativity, a challenge lies in fulfilling the constraints imposed by the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints. Researchers have developed various methods to address this issue, which, although crucial, remains understudied in the field. A recently introduced method called Conformal Unconditional Optimization (CUO) showed significant promise but has a drawback of its own; it produces a conformally deflated solution that may not meet the requirements of certain boundary conditions. This paper proposes a new approach called Conformal Transition Tensor Kinematics (CTTK), which offers an improved solution. CTTK is built upon CUO and incorporates an additional step that maintains a conformally deflated state while ensuring compatibility with prescribed boundary conditions. Through tests using both no-puncture black hole collapse and axisymmetric collapse scenarios, the effectiveness of the new method has been demonstrated. Furthermore, we discovered that CTTK performed better than CUO, particularly when dealing with prescribed boundary conditions. A key feature of CTTK is its ability to yield solutions with high Conformal Factor values, which is essential for generating high-quality initial conditions. It was found that PNS (purple/yellow/negative blue) conformal factor profiles can effectively accommodate most collapse scenarios, while white/stable blue profiles may also be beneficial. Through white/stable blue conformity, the new method was shown to produce initial conditions that lead to more accurate and long-lasting numerical solutions. To validate the findings, the same datasets were used to run simulations with the new method, resulting in even better outcomes. In particular, when employing PNS conformity, CTTK produced initial conditions that led to more accurate and long-lasting numerical solutions. Although increasing the Conformal Factor above a certain threshold did not significantly affect solution stability, it did lead to less conservative numerical solutions. Consequently, it is advised that a higher Conformal Factor should be used when generating initial conditions, particularly when it comes to more aggressive PNS profiles. On the other hand, when employing white/stable blue conformity, both stability and conservation were observed. Therefore, this new method is expected to greatly benefit researchers in the field of numerical relativity. Predicting time series data in complex systems, such as power and climate forecasting, often relies on models that account for multiple interacting variables. Traditional forecasting methods fall short when dealing with multivariate time series data, leading to the emergence of multivariate time series prediction. Advanced machine learning models have shown significant promise in tackling this challenge, with applications extending beyond dimensional limitations. Graph-based models, like Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs), have been successfully applied in time series analysis. However, these models are designed with static connections in mind, overlooking the adaptive nature of complex systems. Recent improvements have focused on enhancing GCN's structural limitations, resulting in variants that prioritize computational efficiency or claim superior performance. Despite these efforts, these improved models struggle to adapt to dynamic systems, where relationships between data dimensions are not constant. To address this issue, we present a novel Adaptive GCN structure, featuring multiple adaptive graph learning modules to capture complex interactions across multiple dimensions of the time series. To further this research, we compare traditional, adaptive, and efficient GCN variants, including recent innovations in multidimensional time series prediction, on datasets consisting of synthetic and real power systems. The results demonstrate the superiority of our Adaptive GCN model, showcasing significant improvement over industry-standard ARIMA and LSTMs, as well as recent research including LSTMs-MFGN, LSTMs-FFGN, and TimeSFCN. Additionally, our Adaptive GCN outperforms variants prioritizing efficiency or industry expertise, highlighting the importance of innovative graph adaptation for multidimensional time series prediction. With potential applications extending beyond power forecasting, our Adaptive GCN structure presents a new standard for multivariate time series analysis. Astronomical observations from ground-based telescopes can be distorted by Earth's atmosphere due to differential dispersion that varies by wavelength. This distortion can cause notable off-axis effects and reduce the quality of observations. To overcome these limitations, a device called an Atmospheric Dispersion Corrector can correct such distortions. To create an effective ADC, a comprehensive understanding of atmospheric dispersion is crucial, including customized atmospheric models. However, developing customized models from on-sky measurements is complicated due to the need for accurate fitting to observations affected by various factors, including measurement errors and the need to avoid overfitting. This process is further constrained by the necessity of matching our models to ones used in numerical simulations for the development of an ADC prototype. To achieve this goal, our team developed a set of standard atmospheric models that can be utilized for the development and testing of an ADC without relying on specific observation nights. These models are based on the knowledge of atmospheric dispersion and other on-sky measurements, including observations that took into account atmospheric conditions, including the atmospheric temperature, pressure, and Humidity, as well as the wind speed and direction. To ensure accuracy, our models are fit using an advanced, efficient fitting process that accounts for the errors in the observations. Additionally, these models are developed with the intention of being used as part of a software package called AtmosphericDispersionModel, which can be used to determine the best fit solution for various observation sets. Through a comparison of our models with on-sky measurements, our atmospheric models demonstrate an accuracy of about 0.00001 radians. A refined version of our models is then presented, showcasing improvements in accuracy. A description of our models is provided in more detail, including how they can be developed, refined, and used for the determination of off-axis points and off-axis images, as well as for determining which observation sets to use in the development of custom ADC models. To effectively manage the resources required for large-scale online learning platforms to label student responses, we develop a solution by applying knowledge distillation to multiply the output capacity. We propose a new method, PILE, which combines the insights of instructor supervision and student self-assessment to create a stronger and more reliable model. PILE works by first producing multiple initial base models, then repeatedly refining these models in pairs by adjusting their logits through multiple iterations. Throughout the process, PILE continuously uses instructor feedback to correct mistakes identified by self-assessment, thereby significantly improving performance. P4 has become the standard language for configuring reconfigurable programmable switches, with the V1Model architecture being the most widely used implementation. An open-source compiler for the P4 consortium allows for syntax analysis and translation of P416 programs into hardware-independent code, but a compiler backend to map this code to V1Model switch resources is needed. A freely available compiler backend for P416 programs and V1Model architecture-based switches has been missing until now. Commercial solutions exist but come with restrictive terms, hindering research into new mapping algorithms and custom instruction sets. Our work fills this gap with an open-source compiler backend for the V1Model architecture, utilizing graph-mapping and graph-coloring techniques to optimize P416 programs for different hardware resources. This allows for quantitative comparison of different mapping algorithms in terms of resource usage. Our compiler is based on the existing SPARTAN framework and incorporates new optimization techniques for better performance, including resource sharing and graph-coloring. Despite these optimizations, some P416 programs exceed the capabilities of our target V1Model architecture, so we developed a compiler plugin to generate simplified versions of these programs, preserving key flow control characteristics. The results show significant reductions in program size, enabling successful mapping of previously infeasible programs. The full source code is available on GitHub. Deep neural networks have seen significant success in various tasks, however their massive size often necessitates expensive memory costs and causes distribution shifts during training. The issue of large model size can be addressed by distributed neural networks where certain layers are processed in parallel on different devices. Despite this advancement, there is a significant knowledge gap regarding how to effectively replicate and distribute neural networks across multiple devices. In this paper, we propose regional critic training, a novel method that utilizes feedback from each device to assess the representation quality of the local neural network. Based on this feedback, a global supervisor selects the best representation and shares that information with the other devices through coordination, thus guiding them to improve their individual performance. Experimental results demonstrate that regional critic training surpasses current benchmark methods and achieves comparable performance with the baseline single-GPU training, all while reducing training time by a substantial margin. The code for this research is publicly available at https://github.com/CHJHUAI/Regional-Critic-Training. Speaking of datasets, we've incorporated four new ones into the research community, specifically SBU Captions, ILSVRC DetLabels, ImageNet Compact V2, and Stanford Action dataset. These datasets offer a range of challenging tasks, including image classification, object detection, and action recognition, with a total of 29 categories and 50,810,000 trainable parameters across the datasets. The regional critic training method is versatile and can be applied to a variety of learning paradigms such as supervised, self-supervised, and model-parallel learning. Furthermore, we've explored the relationship between representation quality and coordination frequency, revealing a critical threshold beyond which performance no longer improves. Additionally, we've analyzed the effects of coordinate layer positioning and the effects of particular layers in the local neural network. These findings have significant implications for future research in neural network training. Based on our research, we've implemented regional critic training in PyTorch and present the results of extensive experiments that confirm its efficacy. Finally, we identify potential areas for future research including the application of regional critic training to graph neural networks and the incorporation of regional critic training into neural network pruning methods. Overall, regional critic training offers an innovative approach to training large neural networks and provides new insights into the role of representation quality in model-parallel learning. With its proven efficacy and wide range of applications, regional critic training has the potential to greatly impact the community. This paper proposes a new computational approach to estimating thermal states and entropy in statistical systems, employing a method of nested sampling originally developed for cosmological applications. By leveraging this approach, we simulate the behavior of the Ising and Poincaré planes across various temperatures and magnetic field strengths. We derive key thermodynamic properties, such as the free energy, pressure, and specific heat, in addition to calculating the entropy from these simulations. The nested sampling method demonstrates exceptional accuracy in estimating entropy at high temperatures, in contrast to current approximation methods. Furthermore, we discover that the Ising model's entropy at zero temperature and in the pure paramagnetic limit can be accurately described by a logarithmic function of the system size. On the other hand, the entropy at zero temperature and in the pure ferrimagnetic limit exhibits a cubic relationship with the system size. Conversely, the Poincaré model's entropy is found not to converge as the system size increases. This research demonstrates that the nested sampling method presents a novel and valuable strategy for calculating thermodynamic properties. The findings presented can serve as a prototype for investigating modular circuitry in quantum spin systems. Lastly, the study highlights that the asymptotic behavior of entropy in closed Ising systems can be understood through logical extensions of Boltzmann's maximum entropy principle. The research presents a novel and valuable approach to calculating entropy and thermal states. In random systems, the scattering matrix converges rapidly to a universal state.
As a result, previous studies found that deposited energy tends to follow predetermined patterns.
To comprehend this phenomenon, we investigated the distribution of energy deposition in scattering systems.
Our analysis reveals that in two-dimensional systems, the distribution of energy typically exhibits one or multiple focal points.
Conversely, in high-dimensional systems, the deposited energy tends to be dispersed evenly.
Notably, our research also identifies certain conditions under ambient illumination that can lead to complete energy transmission. 
Our findings are further validated through experiments conducted in auditory perception. 
To broaden the applicability of our research, we developed two general theorems that can be utilized to evaluate the performance of coherent eigenchannels in scattering systems. 
These theorems quantify the potential gain from utilizing eigenchannels that are incoherent with respect to the active channel.
To implement these theorems, we devised two novel methods for calculating eigenchannel depolarization rates. 
Our research offers novel solutions for optimizing energy transmission in coherent eigenchannels and presents a framework for solving related problems across various fields. 
To demonstrate the universality of our research, we successfuly implemented and verified the findings theoretically and experimentally.

The Stable Roommates problem concerns pairing a set of agents according to their individual preference lists. A key variant involves three-dimensional lists, where agents prefer to form pairs within a group or solo. A special sub-problem, known as the 1-D version, Involves agents having linearly related preferences for each other. A corresponding three-dimensional version of this problem, known as the 3-D Generalized Stable Roommates problem, has been shown to have a tractable solution algorithm when agents' preferences are linearly related. In this study, we investigate the possibility of these favorable conditions extending to preferences that follow an additively separable model. Our results, however, indicate that this particular type of preference does not result in a tractable solution for the three-dimensional problem. In fact, we prove that finding a stable configuration is an NP-hard problem under this preference model, even when dealing with linearly related preferences for pairs. In an effort to mitigate this difficulty, we present an efficient, polynomial-time approximation algorithm for finding stable configurations in the three-dimensional problem with additively separable preferences. Our approximation algorithm is designed with the goal of maximizing the total satisfaction experienced by all agents. Furthermore, we show that under this preference model, the goal of maximizing total satisfaction is equivalent to the concept of maximizing joint satisfaction in a stable configuration, known as the Max-JS problem. In this context, we present an efficient, polynomial-time approximation algorithm for solving the Max-JS problem. Developed solutions for this study were inspired by applications involving matching groups of individuals according to their preferences for group activities. In particular, these solutions have potential applications in organizing medical research participation and advising students in finding group living arrangements. The designed antenna has a significant bandwidth of 13.1%, operating between 34.1 GHz and 38.9 GHz, facilitated by the combination of a slotted microstrip patch with multiple resonances and an optimized microstrip matching circuit. Constructed using the low-cost RO3003 substrate with top and ground layers, this design accommodates simple integration with other microstrip and frontend components via top-layer microstrip coupling gap feed. The achieved wide beamwidth of 100-125 degrees is primarily due to strategically designed parasitic patches for the primary resonant frequency and inherently wide beamwidth for the second resonant frequency within the specified bandwidth, making this a highly efficient microstrip patch antenna for operation over a ground plane. The input impedance and radiation pattern observed over a 3.5-D sphere were consistent with expectations, showcasing six distinct resonances across the specified bandwidth. The input impedance remained stable within a 2 Ohm range throughout the specified frequency bandwidth. To mitigate these issues, a reliable quantum computing architecture has been developed using fault-tolerant quantum circuits. However, constructing such circuits is both computationally challenging and costly, especially when implemented using existing quantum information processing tools. Moreover, our approach allows for the development of domain-specific compilers that can optimize circuit construction for distinct quantum algorithms. To validate our architecture, we conducted extensive simulations of fault-tolerant circuit construction for a range of circuits and found that our method surpasses current state-of-the-art compilation techniques. The underlying structure of data often presents inherent cross-training opportunities, 
which can significantly improve model performance when recognized. 
Research has shown that an ensemble model trained on diverse individual models can achieve better results 
if those models are similarly trained, i.e., all trained on similar data. 
Conversely, if each model is trained on unique data, their combined ensemble tends to demonstrate better generalization. 
Therefore, constructing an optimal training "wealth" becomes crucial - one that balances individual model diversity during training to enhance ensemble generalization capabilities later on. 
In this research paper, we introduce three novel wealth construction methods, 
including one based on data partitioning, another grounded in information theory, and a third rooted in the core principles of statistical mechanics, all designed to complement existing approaches like path-wise and semi-scheduled training and anchor scheduling. 
Through experimental validation on CIFAR10 and ImageNet datasets using residual networks, we successfully conceptualize wealth space, demonstrate scalable generalization trends and successfully identified key training parameters that influence both performance and generalization capabilities. 
Ultimately, we show that an optimally constructed wealth space yields significant improvements in generalization performance.

Achieving the formation of intricate structures and rapid concentration of light within or through disordered mediums is an arduous endeavor due to variations in refractive index, unpredictable light scattering, and speckle noise generation. To address these challenges, we've developed a novel weighted-magnitude-based iterative control approach for ferroelectric liquid crystal (FLC) waveplate-based phase modulators, facilitating the simultaneous formation of multiple complex structures in three-dimensional volumetric samples. Utilizing a commercial SLM, we've demonstrated through experiments that our designed control approach enables the creation of up to three intricate structures with high fidelity and stability, even in the presence of disordered mediums and biological tissues. Furthermore, our results reveal a balance between resolution and speed, allowing for the creation of detailed structures at high speeds or precise high-frequency details at faster rates. This iterative control method offers a cost-effective and versatile solution for optimizing existing binary-amplitude SLM systems and has vast potential applications in micro-resolution microscopy, tissue imaging, and laser tissue interaction. Additionally, we've ensembled the code for controlling the formation of optical structures, which can be accessed via the link: https://github.com/Obajikan/Iterative-FLC-SLM-Control/blob/main/index.py. However, these sensors have limited functionality due to the use of thin high-resistivity epitaxial layers during fabrication. In this study, researchers investigate the active sensor depth through the study of p-type Czochralski substrate CMOS sensors. The Fast Atmospheric Self-coherent camera (FASTSC) technique enables accurate identification of atmospheric turbulence patterns beyond the limit of conventional image resolution through the exploitation of speckle interferometry properties. This method does not rely on traditional sensors like Shack-Hartmann, which measures the global effect of turbulence on a larger scale. The effectiveness of this approach has been supported by various studies using numerical simulations. This research paper presents the first experimental results of implementing FASTSC on the Santa Cruz testbed. The test involved projecting a laser beam through a turbulent medium and capturing images using a high-resolution CCD camera, which were then analyzed to demonstrate focal plane wavefront control of the remaining speckles. This novel demonstration of focal plane control from intensity images marks a significant breakthrough in the field. Additionally, we found that FASTSC can provide data at a rate 100-1000 times higher than what is currently achievable with current adaptive optics systems. This significant advancement in speed will greatly contribute to the optimization of adaptive optics systems for high-speed applications, including astronomical imaging and laser communication systems. The test successfully demonstrated the functionality of FASTSC and found that the technique's performance is directly related to the pixel size of the CCD camera. The experiment's results showed that the implementation of FASTSC results in a loss of speed by a factor of 10 compared to the ideal theoretical value. This loss is attributed to the slow response time of current image processing technology. Further refinement of the technology is needed to achieve both high speed and high resolution, which is within the capabilities of current technology. The projected outcome is a fast ACS system capable of responding dynamically to the rapid changes in atmospheric turbulence at speeds exceeding 1000 times the current capabilities. The test also highlighted the considerable potential benefits of FASTSC for various applications, including a significant increase in the collected signal and improved image resolution through speckle diversity techniques. Furthermore, we found that FASTSC is capable of detecting even the subtle movements of a star image with high precision, which is an essential feature for speckle imaging and laser communication systems. The successful outcome of this experiment has paved the way for an upcoming test where a FASTSC system will be implemented outside the laboratory to demonstrate its capabilities in real-world settings. The anticipated outcome is a vast improvement in the performance of adaptive optics systems. The test also marked the beginning of a collaboration between the University of Arizona and the Santa Cruz testbed to develop a FASTSC system for use in the MMT telescope. The project aims to leverage FASTSC's capabilities to optimize the performance of adaptive optics

This study presents a novel exogenous model designed to explain negative interest rates, known as the DCIR model. The DCIR model's dynamics are driven by a combination of stochastic and deterministic movements in the term structure of interest rates. The analytical solver for DCIR appears to be computationally challenging, hence we introduce a numerical solution method, implementing an Euler-Maruyama scheme. Furthermore, we conduct a thorough global-to-local stability analysis of the DCIR model's stochastic differential equation, focusing on the impacts of discretization errors. Additionally, we evaluate and test the feasibility of the DCIR model through estimations, using two common estimation techniques: maximum likelihood and GMM. Finally, we conduct comparative simulations to assess the predictive power of both the DCIR and the standard CIR models. The research indicates that the DCIR model outperforms the CIR model, as evidenced by superior fit and predictive capabilities. Various specifications of the DCIR model are then applied to estimate the interest rate process. Interestingly, the results suggest that the DCIR model's parameters exhibit reasonable and meaningful values when estimated using certain specifications, further validating the model's theoretical framework. Lastly, we conduct a series of simulations to examine the effects of numerical methods on the predictive power of the DCIR model, revealing that the use of Euler-Maruyama steps can slightly diminish the model's fit compared to the actual data. Nonetheless, the difference is relatively minor, as the DCIR model still demonstrates superior performance. Interestingly, the findings also point out that the applicability of the local stability analysis to the DCIR model is limited, as its analytical nature makes the model's discretized version more amenable to analysis. To overcome this limitation, we rely on the global stability analysis, focusing on the impacts of discretization errors. Ultimately, the research contributes to a deeper understanding of the DCIR model's theoretical and numerical properties, as well as the interest rate process itself, while also shedding light on the DCIR model's predicative capability. The study also explores the intersection of the DCIR model's local stability and the general properties of the CIR model, as described by Barndorff-Nielsen and Schirmeyer. To this end, we conduct a thorough examination of the DCIR model's stochastic differential equation, focusing on its analytical nature and implications. To simulate the collision of particles that are typically encountered in complex mixtures, engineers often employ artificial methods due to the extremely short timescales involved. To address this, researchers have developed and tested a novel integration method that combines the accuracy of molecular collision models with the practical limitations of computational simulations. This method was successfully applied to resolving particle collisions in flows with timescales on the order of microseconds. Compared to standard simulation techniques, results have shown that the new method can accurately model collisions without relying on artificially extended collision times. Furthermore, simulations have revealed that very short-lived collision events are indeed temporary entities called "soft collisions." Additionally, researchers have discovered that very close approaches, known as "hard collisions," account for the majority of particle collisions. To improve the new method's performance when dealing with soft collisions, researchers incorporated a multiple-time-step integration strategy. This integration strategy can selectively advance time steps based on predicted collision events, prioritizing harder collisions that require more precise modeling. As a result, the overall simulation time is optimized, and when hard collisions occur, the time step is readjusted for a smoother experience. This integration technique has opened up the door for more efficient particle-resolved simulations with faster computational times. To confirm this, researchers have conducted drag-chaining and cluster-formation experiments using single-phase and multiphase flows. High-performance computing systems rely heavily on checkpointing to ensure the reliability of parallel programs by storing program states in memory. However, the increasing use of non-volatile memory in computing systems poses difficulties for checkpointing, as NVM's characteristics can lead to data corruption and consistency issues during recovery. Specifically, the potential for memory substitutions during checkpointing and data corruption after resuming execution from a checkpoint, along with the need for crash consistency, present significant challenges. In this paper, we introduce novel algorithms to address these issues under the context of shared-memory programming. Our experiments using the SPLASH-3 benchmark suite show that near-full efficiency can be achieved for checkpointing, resumption, and verification tasks. Additionally, the proposed algorithms demonstrate favorable outcomes in terms of page allocation, memory management, and page recycling operations. Notably, these results are unaffected by the degree of parallelism involved. Furthermore, we find that using a fixed-page allocation approach can further enhance efficiency in high-parallelism scenarios. The strength of our proposed solution lies in its ability to simultaneously address both checkpointing and crash recovery problems without compromising performance. Our work offers a performance-optimized solution for managing memory during checkpointing, resumption, and recovery operations, thereby setting a new benchmark for algorithms in this domain. Additionally, we identify areas for future improvement and provide suggestions for further optimization. Lastly, we estimate that our algorithm would achieve near-full efficiency for such levels of parallelism. Suicidal individuals are a pressing concern, requiring effective detection to ensure their safety. Research has shown that combining behavioral data with clinical information from Electronic Health Records can pinpoint individuals at risk of self-harm. Building on this finding, our study takes a step further by integrating behavioral data with text from EHRs, incorporating time-aware deep sequential models to integrate multi-source data. We demonstrated that incorporating behavioral data along with clinical text enhances the predictive power of traditional clinical data alone, effectively capturing the intricate connections between clinical data, suicidal thoughts, and relevant contextual factors. Notably, our results also showed that incorporating behavioral data increases the predictive power of models utilizing clinical text alone. We achieved Accurracy scores of 0.83, 0.80, and 0.92 for macro F1-score, Accuracy, and Purity score respectively, using a combination of time-aware deep learning models, including BiLSTM with time-embbeding, Time distributed LSTM with dense layers, and Bidirectional Graph Attention Model, all trained on clinical EHRs. Furthermore, our models preserved patient anonymity in accordance with HIPAA standards. The integration of behavioral data and clinical text holds great promise for enhancing safety predictions, underscoring the importance of preserving and linking patient data across diverse sources to inform clinical decisions. The code and datasets for this research are publicly available at https://github.com/cagdarozsu/SafeSUICIDE. We will make our anonymized dataset of suicidal individuals available, subject to HIPAA regulations, at a later date.

Our investigation focuses on how a spatially confined, freely vibrating harmonic oscillator's state changes over time, with particular attention to its initial state, which is a coherent state. As the oscillator is compressed and shifted, the characteristics of the initial state are analyzed in terms of a new set of number-state coordinates. It's found that these transformations modify the distribution of photon likelihood across the Fock space, resulting in either a more even distribution or a shift in the dominant photon number. For example, compressing a coherent state and then displacing it leads to a new state with a higher average photon number, where the photon number distribution is now more evenly spread among the Fock states. Additionally, it's discovered that Mirzabekov-Solomonovic transformations can be used to create odd photon number states by compressing and displacing even photon number states in a specific way. Finally, it's shown that erasing the photon information via Compton scattering for certain parameter values can result in a perfectly symmetric, high-photon number state, which is close to a classical limit. These research findings may have implications for real-world applications involving the preparation and manipulation of high-photon number states. Lastly, the utility of the proposed method could be evaluated in an experiment using modern atomics physics techniques to produce and study the described states. Ultimately, it's believed that this study will contribute to the development of high-photon number state preparation methods that may be useful in practical applications. To conclude, the research presented here is a theoretical investigation of a freely vibrating oscillator, which is an important fundamental system in physics. As such, the presented work is not motivated by an applied problem but rather by a fundamental inquisitiveness about the characteristics of a photon number distribution in a certain state. However, it's possible that the described concepts could be applied to other systems, such as those involving magnons, that may be of interest in both theoretical and experimental research in the field of condensed matter physics. We present the latest findings from Belle II regarding the branching ratio of $B^0 \to \rho^-\ell^+\ell^-$ and $B^+ \to \rho^0 \ell^+\ell^-$, where $\ell$ represents either an electron or a muon. These conclusions are drawn based on data from high-energy $e^+e^-$ collisions collected at the Belle II detector, operating at a KE of 4.9 GeV with a luminosity of 50.6 $\mathrm{fb}^{-1}$. To determine the branching ratios, researchers focused on specific final state kinematics from hadronic decays of the recoil $B$ meson, enabling them to reconstruct $\rho$ mesons close to threshold. To eliminate background, a machine learning-based algorithm was employed, leading to the detection of $B^0 \to \rho^-\ell^+\ell^-$ and $B^+ \to \rho^0 \ell^+\ell^-$ decays at frequencies of $4.65 \times 10^{-5}$ and $3.96 \times 10^{-5}$, respectively, with a confidence level exceeding 5 standard deviations. The measured branching ratios for $B^0 \to \rho^-\ell^+\ell^-$ and $B^+ \to \rho^0 \ell^+\ell^-$ are found to be in the ranges $[1.1(2) \times 10^{-6}]$ and $[0.24(3) \times 10^{-6}]$, respectively, matching theoretical predictions based on SM models. Additionally, the practice of using hadronic reconstruction to study $B$ decays shows promise in Belle II's dataset, particularly in searches for non-SM signals in these decays system. A Population III star's intense birth cloud is initially on a rotating disk, 
which could fragment due to magnetic fields that halt accretion, 
resulting in the formation of planetary mass objects.

considering both the rotational and magnetic forces exerted by the star.

that wraps around the equator could form and potentially prevent fragmentation 
by blocking mass accumulation, 
which in turn could intensify the star's rotational velocity, 
creating a scenario where no planetary mass objects form. 
This intense magnetic field could persist if the star remains isolated, 
which in turn affects the environment surrounding the star. 
In contrast, a more gentle magnetic field results in disk fragmentation, 
leading to the formation of smaller objects. 
This intense magnetic field phenomenon is distinct from typical star 
formations and could result in no binary or multiple star systems 
forming around Population III stars. 
Lastly, this intense magnetic field could significantly impact 
metal-free binary star formations.

Radio map estimation is crucial for optimizing wireless networks but creating these maps is very time-consuming and expensive. Additionally, we use clustering to improve efficiency and our approach is capable of handling various types of maps without any modifications. Overall results show that Aerial Spectrum Exploration significantly improves map estimation efficiency while maintaining high accuracy. Achieving dependable data privacy involves ensuring that sensitive information remains confidential when querying private datasets. One-sided differential privacy presents a straightforward yet effective approach to maintaining data confidentiality, however its standard falls short in accounting for dependencies among data attributes, which presents a challenge for maintaining confidentiality. Research has demonstrated that when attributes are interdependent, releasing certain summary statistics cannot maintain the confidentiality of individual data entities. Furthermore, studies have revealed that when attributes are dependent, gaining access to certain data without restrictions exposes more information than anticipated under one-sided differential privacy. In an effort to enhance the confidentiality of query releases, this research develops an estimated boundary for information exposure when attributes are dependent. Specifically, this research investigates how releasing certain summaries affects information exposure when attributes are ranked and when attributes have a specific relationship. Results demonstrate that when attributes are ranked, more information is exposed than anticipated under one-sided differential privacy, while attributes with a specific relationship can be as much as twice as sensitive as anticipated under one-sided differential privacy. These findings highlight the significance of attribute independence in maintaining data confidentiality and illustrate that releasing certain summaries without ensuring attribute independence can result in excessive information exposure when attributes are dependent. Importantly, this research also demonstrates that releasing certain summaries without ensuring attribute independence can result in a privacy breach for individual data entities even when none of the attributes themselves are vulnerable to privacy breaches. Results show that such releases can maintain confidentiality more effectively than standard releases, while also remaining more effective than certain customized releases that account for attribute relationships. Leveraging an integrated approach with multiple thread management, ETA achieves high-speed processing of large data sets, incorporating advanced features like time-based data normalization, dynamic signal processing, and customizability through an integrated development environment (IDE). Furthermore, ETA facilitates collaborative analysis with seamless data merging and comparison functions. With its extensive modularity and IDE-based data analysis mechanism, ETA offers a versatile approach to time-stamped data analysis, with applications in diverse fields such as physics, biology, and industrial processes. Recent studies utilizing Gaia proper motions have re-evaluated the structure of stellar filaments in the Milky Way, focusing on a region spanning 56.25 square degrees in Ra and Dec. In contrast to earlier research that discovered long, sinuous structures, the authors found these features to be comprised of relatively straight lines, forming a web-like pattern. Through mock filament generation and statistical analysis, the authors concluded that these features are not statistically significant. Furthermore, the authors observed that these "filaments" are primarily formed by overlapping stellar clusters, which can create the appearance of elongated shapes even if they have random proper motions. The authors propose that these features are not distinct, coherent structures, but rather an illusion created by densely packed star clusters, which can be reconstructed through 3D spatial analysis. The authors suggest that these structures, known as stellar filaments, may actually be an essential building block for understanding the complex distribution of stars in the galaxy. However, the authors' findings indicate that these structures are not as substantial as previously thought and that the "filaments" are predominantly composed of these clusters. The authors discovered that disrupting these "filaments" using the Schutte-Koertve-Dicke test indicated that they were not physically connected. The authors also found no correlation between the estimated mass of the "filaments" and the density of the stars within the selected sample, which further suggested that these structures were not physically significant. The authors found that integrating the spatial distribution of moving stars, which can be achieved through the use of machine learning algorithms such as SiFi, did not reveal any distinct, coherent structure. However, the authors did discover that the 3D reconstructed structures, which were generated through the use of machine learning algorithms such as SiFi, exhibited more coherent and distinct shapes, which is reflected in their higher disconnecting values compared to the initial "filaments". For visually appealing outfits, individual garments must harmoniously fit together based on factors like style, type, and color. Current fashion artisanal approaches, however, don't adequately address the issue of identifying visually incompatible items. In response, we present VICTOR, a cutting-edge transformer-based model that learns to classify fashion items into compatible categories. To enhance the model's overall performance, we integrated a custom-made transformer-based layout analysis module. Moreover, VICTOR was trained using a vast, specially curated fashion dataset, consisting of 13 million images collected from real-world fashion artisanal sites. The proposed method's layout analysis phase relies on a innovative, elegant layout representation that simplifies feature extraction and analysis. Experimental outcomes confirm that VICTOR achieves superior results on evaluation datasets compared to existing baselines. Moreover, we substantiate the practical relevance of our approach by successfully applying VICTOR to a range of challenging fashion artisanal tasks. The source code for our model is freely accessible at https://github.com/skypotter/VICTOR. Additionally, the model's API services are deployed at https://victor-fashion.com. Further information about our work can be found at this address: https://skypotter.github.io/publication/VICTOR2022.

Light quantum states go beyond traditional descriptions of photons. Recent theories, such as non-classical illumination theory, enable a broader understanding by utilizing light's wavefront and photon packing in a manner analogous to classical light. This introductory review focuses on the mathematical framework and key concepts of generalized non-classical illumination theory, including verification methods and resource theories. It also explores the theoretical implications through the identification of non-classical resources and their applications in generating quantum correlations and violating classical limits. The article also discusses the consistency of non-classical illumination and classical descriptions, as well as essential characteristics, and it concludes by outlining possible future research directions. The review is primarily accessible to master's and PhD students in the fields of optics and quantum information. The appendix contains detailed mathematical derivations that may be of interest to postdoctoral researchers and leading students in the field. The review primarily utilizes recently published papers by the author and co-authors, with notable contributions identified. The review is largely self-contained, with selected key papers included in the bibliography for further exploration of the subject. The review is divided into nine sections, with the first section introducing the concept of light quantum states and their applications in quantum information and optics, the second section discussing non-classical illumination and its generalized applications, and the remaining sections reviewing recent research in the field. The review is an introductory version, with a longer and more advanced version available, titled 'Light Quantum States: theory and application' (arXiv:2106.04069). The latter includes more research and is targeted at an advanced level. The two versions were written simultaneously, with the shorter version revised in July 2021 and the longer version revised in April 2022. The main sections of this review are the abstract, introduction, a brief review of classical illumination theory, a review of non-classical illumination theory based on non-classical light, a review of non-classical illumination theory based on quantum light, a review of resource theory of non-classical illumination, a review of generalized non-classical illumination theory, a review of quantum correlation generation, a review of limit violations, consistency of non-classical illumination and classical descriptions, and future research directions. As the user base of Federated Learning grows, encompassing both mobile and PC users, it's crucial to address the issue of slow aggregation. Mobile users may experience slow internet connections or device shutdowns, while PC users may have varying internet speeds. To resolve this, using a buffer to store communication data and combining it asynchronously is a viable approach. However, this method's effectiveness relies on having a reliable way to update buffered data when a new user submits their information. Current solutions for updating buffered data are limited to gradient updates, but this can lead to slow convergence or unreliable results, especially if users are still idle. To address these challenges, we introduce a number of innovations. Firstly, we demonstrate that using a buffer to store communication data is equivalent to using a quasi-Newton method. Secondly, we show that updating buffered data using an approximate Hessian matrix yields better results. Thirdly, we introduce a new way to update buffered data using quasi-Newton vectors, which outperforms gradient updates. Finally, we introduce a new communication schedule, where we update and communicate buffer entries simultaneously, minimizing communication cost and efficiently using bandwidth. These innovations are tested in FedADAGD, a new FL protocol that updates buffered data using a combination of quasi-Newton vectors and an approximate Hessian matrix. Test results on 6 datasets show that FedADAGD outperforms other existing protocols, including FedADAG and Prox-SGD. Specifically, FedADAGD significantly improves communication efficiency while achieving comparable test accuracy. To address potential issues with the new FL protocol, we update FedADAGD to handle user shutdowns during FedADAGD. This involves using a more robust update rule for buffered data and combining the results of ongoing communications. These innovations are also tested in "FedADAGD with recovery'". This research explores the algebra of polynomial tempered distributions, a branch of multivariate distribution theory. We prove that the derivatives of polynomial distributions are extensively defined and fulfill a significant differentiation theorem. We also establish functional equations for sums, products, and composition of polynomial distributions. Furthermore, we identify the necessary and sufficient conditions for the inverse of a polynomial distribution and show that the composition of a polynomial distribution with a smooth function admits a vast generalization. To achieve this, we devise a novel method of differentiating polynomials with symbolic variables, treating them as indeterminates, even in cases of graded algebras. This analysis provides a thorough justification for the algebra of polynomial tempered distributions. We also illustrate the practical applications of these results with several examples. We strived to make the content highly accessible by explaining the underlying concepts of Littlewood-Polya theory, degree of a polynomial, distributive extension, and graded algebra. Additionally, we offer a comprehensive list of frequently used notation and key concepts in the appendix. This research was partially presented at the 2020 UNED Mathematics Conference. Recent studies have highlighted the significance of viral interactions with marine cyanobacteria, which have implications for the health of aquatic ecosystems. This review delves into the complex world of viral relationships with aquatic cyanobacteria, examining the current understanding of this interaction and its impact on aquatic cyanoblooms. We investigate the effects of environmental factors on viral attachment and the implications of this attachment for the health of aquatic ecosystems affected by cyanobacteria. Furthermore, we explore the potential for viral manipulation of cyanobacterial metabolism, which could be exploited for the development of novel bioconversion technologies. The future research landscape is also mapped, focusing on the necessary advancements required to fulfill the projected goals of viral-cyanobacterium interaction research for applied applications. This area of research holds immense promise for addressing critical challenges related to aquatic biotechnology and ecosystem management. It is placed at the intersection of fundamental scientific investigation and practical, applied research that can benefit society. Understanding the interaction between viruses and aquatic cyanobacteria is crucial not just for fundamental knowledge, but also for the development of technologies that could improve food security, promote sustainable practices, and protect human health. Research in this field can significantly contribute to addressing critical issues related to aquatic biotechnology and ecosystem management, which can have far-reaching economic, social, and environmental implications if adequately addressed. We analyze potential areas of support and necessary research developments that can help fulfill our envisioned applications for viral-cyanobacterial interaction research. This area of research is critical for addressing fundamental challenges and providing practical solutions to improve food security, promote sustainable practices, and protect human health, while also promoting a resilient and sustainable ocean economy. We evaluate the progress made so far and map out the necessary research developments required to fulfill our envisioned applications for viral-cyanobacterial interaction research. Our study focuses on achieving p-type conductivity in GaN using lattice-matched binary compounds.  Upon analyzing strain's impact on the electronic properties of gallium nitride, we discovered that an in-plane compression of ~6.6% increases the hole concentration by over six orders of magnitude.  This significant improvement leads us to evaluate ZnGeN$_2$ and MgSiN$_2$ as potential donor materials for the same lattice constant.  Our research indicates that incorporating these materials into GaN via molecular beam epitaxy, via both co-epitaxy and superlattice growth, results in heavily hole-doped gallium nitride with concentrations exceeding 10$^{20$ cm$^{-3}$.  Through strain-free samples grown on silicon substrates, we demonstrate the potential for GaN to serve as a common substrate for III-V nitride p-type materials, offering an advantage over GaN itself due to reduced hole activation energy.  This technique may also be applied to other materials, such as AlN, by matching to CuN and MgN.  Finally, incorporating GaN's features into ZnGeN$_2$ could form a heavily doped p-type insulator with a bandgap of ~1.2 eV, or a p-type semiconductor with a bandgap of ~1.0 eV in combination with CuN.  Additionally, integrating MgSiN$_2$ and GaN, which has a larger bandgap, would yield a p-type material with a bandgap of ~1.6 eV and potential ferroelectric properties.  This research significantly expands the possibilities for achieving p-type conductivity in wide bandgap semiconductors.  It also suggests a new strategy for the common lattice strain-induced ferromagnetism in III-V nitrides, as previously reported.  This study presents new perspectives on the ferromagnetic properties of these materials, which could be useful for spintronic applications and are significant at concentrations greater than 10$^{16$ cm$^{-3}$. Our research focuses on developing a novel technique to facilitate the guided navigation of underwater robots using learning from web data, which is essentially pre-recorded robot trajectories. This is crucial as collecting paired teacher-student data in underwater settings is extremely costly and impractical. Leveraging Gaussian Process regression and the Temporal Difference learning framework, our approach enables the teacher to create a predictive map of optimal actions, which informs the student's search for the most efficient path. However, current implementations are hindered by high computational and memory costs associated with large datasets. Our contribution addresses this limitation by introducing a sparse version of the existing method, which achieves superior performance without sacrificing accuracy. Comprehensive simulations using real-world data demonstrate that our approach outperforms existing undersea navigation techniques, whereas a practical underwater trial validates the method's efficacy in actual underwater settings. Details about the code and data can be accessed via our website at https://spgtl.github.io. A video showcasing the results of our method can be found on YouTube at https://youtu.be/6hGoY__DM4k. The authors are currently conducting further testing to demonstrate repeated successful applications of the method in underwater settings. Knowledge graph completion, which involves predicting missing links based on existing information, has become a highly competitive field in natural language processing. Despite the superiority of models that utilize both relational path-based and multigraph techniques, their high computational requirements make them difficult to execute in real-time applications. In contrast, models relying solely on attribute-based templates have lower computational costs but tend to yield lower accuracy rates. In this paper, we explore the utilization of traditional attribute-based models for real-time link prediction in large-scale knowledge graphs by leveraging real-time knowledge graph maintenance systems to update template models frequently. Our proposed approach demonstrates comparable performance to state-of-the-art models, with notable improvements in real-time scenarios. Additionally, we discuss the advantages and limitations of combining our method with the maintenance of temporal knowledge graphs to enhance link prediction accuracy. Our source code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/seyedmahmoudk/Real-Time-KGC. Experimental evaluation shows that incorporating the temporal dimension significantly improves the accuracy of real-time link prediction. Furthermore, we investigate the feasibility of applying our knowledge graph maintenance method to existing real-time KBP benchmark datasets, including the Yelp dataset. Our study highlights the versatility of our method, encompassing various knowledge graph maintenance techniques, to serve as a versatile tool for real-time applications. Lastly, we prioritize addressing the pressing issue of evaluation fairness in neural knowledge graph completion, particularly in the KBC-Fair benchmark dataset, by proposing a straightforward technique to achieve comparable performance with established models without utilizing sensitive attributes. Our source code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/seyedmahmoudk/KBC-FAIR. Moreover, we successfully applied our method to real-world datasets, including the Yelp dataset, and achieved notable improvements in evaluation fairness. In particular, we achieved a 14.44% average increase in accuracy and a 16.33% average rise in fairness score, demonstrating the versatility and efficacy of our approach. In summary, our study contributes several novel methodologies, including the utilization of traditional attribute-based models for real-time link prediction, the integration of temporal maintenance techniques, and a straightforward technique to enhance evaluation fairness, all while providing versatile knowledge graph maintenance tools. Moreover, we successfully evaluated these methods on established benchmark datasets and real-world data, showcasing their efficacy and practical value. Lastly, our source code is openly available on GitHub at the specified repository links. In particular, the code for real-time link prediction is available at https://github.com/seyedmahmoudk/Real-Time-KGC and the code for fairness

Two directed graphs, D and E, are considered equivalent under a robust shift transformation if there exist infinite paths in both graphs that closely mirror each other, regardless of the starting point. When applied to the C*-algebras built from these graphs, this notion of equivalence ensures that the algebras are Morita equivalent, meaning they share common properties. Researchers have previously demonstrated that shift equivalence is preserved when applying certain covering mappings, but we now show that not all coverings have this property. Specifically, we constructed an example where the covering mapping is not robustly shift equivalent, which has significant implications in its use of Teichmüller space. Moreover, this example allowed us to demonstrate that the shift equivalence class of a graph is not necessarily topologically invariance, but can become so under a particular divisor. Finally, we investigated the stable version of shift equivalence and found that it remains topologically invariant. Notably, we were able to establish a connection between stable shift equivalence of graphs and Morita equivalences between their C*-algebras through the use of Teichmüller theory. This new theory aids in the study of stable shift equivalence using techniques from C*-algebra.
