Our approach has allowed for precise mathematical calculations via a heat-bath method and Feynman diagrams at next-to-leading order, enabling us to map out the complex diffusion tensor and the effective heavy quark mass for various magnetic field strengths. It is interesting to note that at a finite magnetic field, the imaginary part of the self-energy, which acts as a collision broadening in momentum space, exceeds the corresponding temperature broadening. Furthermore, our results suggest that diffusion and mass modifications are sensitive to the direction of the magnetic field. A notable phenomenon observed is that the imaginary component of the self-energy can achieve values much higher than would be expected from a simple sum of the temperature and magnetic field broadening effects. Our research provides comprehensive and accurate information about the anisotropic diffusion rate and effective mass of a heavy quark as a function of temperature and magnetic field. Additionally, our results imply that the anisotropic diffusion rate and effective mass of a heavy light quark, such as a strange quark, would require a more sophisticated analysis due to the significant role played by light quark exchange. Therefore, our results cannot be directly applied to heavy light quarks. We anticipate that our research will contribute meaningfully to the study of heavy quark physics and heavy light physics under high temperature and magnetic field conditions. with current Rydberg atom techniques, limited by their resolution and sensitivity. 
We've improved this capability by integrating Rydberg atom detection with deep 
learning, utilizing a convolutional neural network (CNN) to analyze atomic spectra. 
In a laboratory test, our Rydberg atom-cnn system successfully detected 
difficult cases, such as MW frequencies exceeding 10 GHZ, and resolved MW 
patterns narrower than 10 MHz, achieving resolutions five times better than 
current Rydberg atom methods. We've applied this improved sensor to a tricky 
problem in MW measurement, precision detection, and rapid frequency scanning, 
demonstrating its effectiveness. We believe this innovation will greatly enhance 
the capabilities of Rydberg atom-based MW measurement and control technology. 
Furthermore, integrating Rydberg atom physics with other cutting-edge technologies 
has the potential to drive significant advancements in science and industry.

public to download at https://github.com/LIPAN Rydberg MW. This will enable 
researchers to access and use the source code of our deep learning algorithm.

The objective of this research is to leverage visual information to control the generation of audio signals. The challenge lies in directly mapping images to audio spectra, which often results in audio outputs that are subpar in quality. To address this issue, we propose utilizing pre-trained image encoders and audio generators to translate images into audio spectra. However, simply combining these elements does not suffice to produce high-quality audio outputs. To boost audio quality, we developed two innovations: multi-layered feature alignment and visual attention-based audio encoding. The former involves aligning image and audio features at multiple layers of the network, while the latter employs a self-attention mechanism to allow the image encoder to transmit relevant information to the audio encoder. The results show that our proposed method outperforms previous baselines in terms of subjective metrics. Furthermore, our results indicate that incorporating aligned features and using visual information to guide audio generation are crucial to producing high-quality audio outputs. To facilitate replication of our findings, we released our implementation on the GitHub platform and recorded demos showcasing the effectiveness of our proposed method. Additionally, the proposed method demonstrates promising applications in generating audio outputs that are tailored to the visual characteristics of input images. To exemplify this capability, we developed a simple example of an image-to-music generator model. While this research does not represent a breaking point in the field, it does represent a notable improvement in visually guided sound generation, which has far-reaching applications and implications. To combat a pandemic, governments are forced to make the difficult decision between saving lives and preserving their economy. Our research reveals a straightforward method to achieve both objectives simultaneously by controlling the pandemic's pace using a timely and predictable flow of funds. This approach guarantees both the minimal amount of economic disruption and the minimal number of pandemic-related deaths. By modeling the pandemic as a fundamental economic process, we derive the fundamental laws governing it and derive exact solutions for both short- and long-term scenarios. Our analysis considers two distinct payment schemes and models the movement of people as an interconnected network. Furthermore, we apply our results to the specific context of the COVID-19 pandemic. Our calculations demonstrate that a timely injection of funds can mitigate both the economic impact and the mortality rate resulting from lockdowns. Our research shows that an extended lockdown is always necessary if funds are not provided, but also indicates that an infinitely large payment can replace an infinitely long lockdown. Our models also include predictions for the number of pandemic-related deaths and the magnitude of economic disruption. These predictions are comparable to real-world data for the COVID-19 pandemic. Our research uncovers two distinct phases of pandemic development: an initial growth phase and a decline phase. Correspondingly, we derive two distinct mathematical equations to model these phases, along with their solutions. Our analysis also includes an equation for the optimal payment amount needed to prevent either an economic disaster or a high death toll. This analysis further reveals the critical importance of timing in making either economic or life-saving investments during a pandemic. An investment made too late can result in an economic disaster or a high death toll. Conversely, an investment made ahead of schedule can result in not only improved economic outcomes but also a lower number of pandemic-related deaths. Our research includes an extensive discussion of the fundamental concepts underlying our models, including the critical parameters that govern a pandemic's development. Furthermore, we derive two distinct types of solutions for our equations, including one general approach that allows for the simultaneous minimization of economic disruption and pandemic-related deaths. This solution can be applied to any payment scheme. Our research also includes an analysis of when an infusion of funds can replace an extended lockdown. Additionally, we derive an equation for the optimal payment amount needed to prevent either an economic disaster or a high death toll. Our point-by-point comparison of various payment schemes reveals that an infusion of funds predictably flows through the economy. Our research shows that certain payment schemes can mimic the predictable infusion of funds. Furthermore, we derive exact solutions to two distinct equations that model pandemic development during different payment scenarios.

The development of end-to-end machine learning systems presents an complex issue 
as debugging these systems necessitates an in-depth understanding of both the 
algorithmic logic and the data used to train them. This data, which is often 
large and unwieldy, cannot be manually reviewed, requiring automated analysis 
instead. Our research develops an approach where the impact of each data point 
on the model's output is measured using the Shapley value, allowing users to 
identify and remove data points that excessively dominate the model's decisions 
and implement changes upstream in the pipeline. Our tool, MLMind, serves as 
a user interface that connects Shapley analysis to ML flow, a widely-used 
pipeline management system, enabling users to streamline the data debugging 
process. MLMind's effectiveness has been demonstrated in practical applications, 
resulting in a 17% improvement in model robustness and a 200x decrease in data 
size, all while maintaining data representation quality. Ultimately, MLMind 
facilitates the execution of a data debugging strategy within large-scale machine 
learning operations, an area it continues to improve in. An available

This study provides an in-depth examination of how high pressure influences the chemical and structural properties and the anomalous Hall effect (AHE) of Mn$_3$Sn, an antiferromagnetic compound with a triangular structure. At low pressure, Mn$_3$Sn exhibits a structure characterized by hexagonal symmetry with snowflake-like arrangements of atoms, which gives rise to an AHE due to its lack of inversion symmetry and the presence of spins that contribute to the effect. Upon increasing the pressure to 1.25 GPa, the material undergoes a transformation from this hexagonal phase to one with a coordination number of 10, exhibiting linear symmetry, in which AHE is not observable because of diminished conditions facilitating the effect. Analysis based on first-principles calculations indicates that this new phase features a type of magnetic arrangement called Scandi phenomenon, which is consistent with experimental findings on the material's pressure-dependent AHE behavior. In this research, the connection between a specific pressure-driven transformation and AHE behavior is explored, revealing that both exist within the same pressure range, thereby enabling a deeper understanding of how this phenomenon works. Additionally, this research reveals that both conditions essential for AHE, namely a lack of inversion symmetry and quantized circular magnetization, are absent in the higher-pressure phase of Mn$_3$Sn, thereby providing insights into the underlying physics of this phenomenon. Finally, this research suggests that Mn$_3$Sn, an compound exhibiting AHE, can be converted into a Heusler compound through a high-pressure process, and this property is applicable not just to this material but also to other compounds exhibiting this phenomenon, thereby paving the way for the creation of materials with desired properties. This paper rectifies a mistake in a previous study linked to Steklov-Robin eigenvalues and spectral gaps. The error concerns a problem involving a right-hand side partial differential equation with $m>0$ and $\beta \geq 0$ in a smooth, bounded domain. The research aims to find the principal eigenvalue $\lambda_1^m(\beta)$. However, the prior study contained an error in calculating the Steklov-Robin eigenvalue, particularly for $\beta > 0$, and as such, the main eigenvalue $\lambda_1^m(\beta)$ was inaccurately determined. Through further investigation, we first establish the lower limit of $\lambda_1^m(\beta)$ under the condition that $\lambda_1^0 \geq \lambda_1^m(\beta)$ for any non-negative $\beta$. Moreover, we prove that for $m > 0$ and $\beta = 0$, the Steklov-Robin eigenvalue is equal to the first eigenvalue of the standard Laplacian, andally, we provide an example that confirms that the upper limit of $\lambda_1^m(\beta)$ is not restricted when compared to $\lambda_1^0$. Finally, we introduce another problem and propose several hypotheses that require verification to extend the present findings, and subsequently, we derive the asymptotic behavior of $\lambda_1^m(\beta)$ as $\beta$ approaches either $0$ or $\infty$. Lastly, the research concludes by discussing the potential connection between our research and the 'triple phasic' behavior in spectral gaps identified by R. S. Strichartz in a different study. The last part is concluded by observing the described phases in the graph of $\lambda_1^m(\beta)$ for $m = 0.5$ and $\beta$ varying between $0$ and $\infty$. Improving the accuracy of brain disease detection through diffusion magnetic resonance imaging (dMRI) is a critical concern. To achieve this, researchers are developing new methods based on a simplified model that represents dMRI data through directional weighted graphs. However, real datasets often exceed the capabilities of graph-based models, requiring the use of more complex structures like hypergraphs to effectively analyze the data. Yet, the development of hypergraph-based methods is hindered by the limited availability of suitable algorithms and frameworks. A new technique, guided hypergraph reconstruction, has been developed to enhance the accuracy of disease detection by utilizing the effectiveness of hypergraphs. This approach involves constructing a pair of hypergraphs from diffeomorphism-aligned brain images and using their connection to identify and locate disorders. It has been successfully applied to dMRI tumor and multiple sclerosis lesion detection, demonstrating improved performance compared to graph-based methods. Furthermore, it has the potential to be integrated into established graph-based frameworks, as seen in its implementation using DTI-Probabilistic-AK, a widely used software for brain disease analysis. This integration has led to enhanced results and could potentially be applied to other existing frameworks. In addition, a comprehensive evaluation of the proposed method has been conducted using data from various sources, including publicly accessible datasets and an extensive collection of tumor lesions. This review has served to demonstrate the effectiveness of hypergraph-based approaches and guided hypergraph reconstruction in particular. It has also highlighted their potential to improve the accuracy of disease detection and awareness of their advantages in the field of dMRI and hypergraphs. This knowledge could potentially be utilized to develop more accurate brain disease detection algorithms. Several code segments and other required resources have been made available, including hypergraph reconstruction code, to facilitate the reproduction of this research. Important information on the used software, used data, and other relevant resources can be found in a previously published paper focused on reviewing hypergraph-based methods. This ensures that the necessary information is easily accessible and that others can draw upon this knowledge, as recently asked, by providing relevant details. Since 2017, there has been an increased interest in the use of hypergraphs to improve the accuracy of dMRI-based brain disease detection. This interest follows earlier concerns, also present since 2017, about the limited capabilities of graph-based models and the need for more complex structures, such as hypergraphs. This has led to a published review of hypergraph-based methods and guided hypergraph reconstruction, a new technique that utilizes the effectiveness of hypergraphs to detect tumors and lesions from dMRI and MRI images.

Radiologists' readings of chest X-rays include beneficial insights that can lead to accurate diagnoses. However, their full potential is not being leveraged due to outdated reporting methods. To unlock this information, we need to create detailed annotations for machine learning models. Current annotation procedures rely on standardizing and simplifying radiologists' reports, which hinders their effectiveness. We take a distinct approach by employing computed tomography (CT) projections to capture the intricacies of chest X-rays more effectively. We gathered a large dataset of 181,079 paired X-Ray and CT images from various hospitals and developed a unified system for annotating X-Ray reports using the ProReport tool. With deeper understanding of radiologists' writing, we designed Path-R, an automatic recommendation system that suggests reports and annotations based on pathologies identified during image analysis. Ultimately, we created a massive dataset of 52 million detailed annotations, enabling natural language processing models to comprehend radiologists' writing and empowering these systems to generate more accurate medical documents. To showcase our success, our team achieved a 44% relative improvement in semantic similarity between the generated and human-provided reports. The ProReport system and the annotated dataset are both publicly accessible resources. Moreover, the effectiveness of our approach has been validated through 35 clinical applications and assessments in collaboration with 45 radiologists. We achieved average cosine similarity of $0.75 \pm 0.06$ on assessing the similarity between the generated and human-provided reports, with the cosine similarity reaching as high as $0.85$ when the similarity between the two was strong. We observed that the similarity between the two increased over time, with the similarity at month $9$ amounting to $0.76$, in contrast to $0.69$ at month $3$. We established a threshold of $0.60$ for the similarity between the two, which proved to be challenging to achieve. Nonetheless, radiologists found the task rewarding and considered the annotations useful for their daily documentation tasks. Moreover, the ProReport tool facilitated radiologists' understanding of the task by providing a visual representation of the radiologists' writing and the recommended annotations. We developed Path-R, an AI-driven annotation tool that suggests reports and annotations based on pathologies identified during image analysis. With deeper understanding of radiologists' writing, we created a massive dataset of 52 million detailed annotations, and achieved a 44% relative improvement in semantic similarity between the generated and human-provided reports. We introduce a novel method for evaluating directional emission in microcavity lasers, utilizing the maximum entropy principle and comparing two configurations: a microcavity with and without an aperture. The entropy assessment technique enables a straightforward connection between experimental measurements of radiation pattern and anisotropic emission properties. This approach facilitates a deeper understanding of the relationship between the particle's degree of directionality and its entropy in both cases. Our study focuses on microcavity lasers to establish entropy as a versatile tool for evaluating directional emission in various scattering scenarios. Research in micro-photonics has shown that entropy can distinguish between highly directional (laser-like) and wide random emissions. We found that including an aperture, which introduces anisotropy, leads to lower entropy and increased directionality in comparison to a microcavity without an aperture. Directionality is directly proportional to the entropy's negative correlation with emission pattern anisotropy. This method's efficiency can be enhanced by multiplying entropy by the cavity's anisotropy. Our findings indicate that entropy effectively measures directionality in various electromagnetic scattering situations. This study's results are expected to broaden the application of entropy not only in micro-photonics but also in other research fields that involve directional emissions. Moreover, this entropy-based method may pave the way for entropy-powered innovations in active laser technologies. Please see our related patent applications for more information.

Our framework for assessing cryptocurrency stability joins two primary considerations: functional stability and value stability. Functional stability refers to the consistency of transaction processing rules, whereas value stability encompasses two aspects - the relative value of the cryptocurrency versus time and its volatility. This framework allows us to evaluate both the likelihood and severity of failures in a cryptocurrency's medium of exchange. By analyzing the Gaussian distribution of price fluctuations, our metrics can quantify stability using widely recognized statistical measures, such as the z-score formula. Applying this methodology to major cryptocurrencies, our results show that their value stability often falls short of gold's, suggesting that existing cryptocurrencies may not provide adequate functional and value stability for efficient money transfers. Furthermore, our framework's framework's ability to evaluate functional stability suggests that incorporating stabilizing mechanisms, such as decentralized treasury funds, could enhance a cryptocurrency's overall stability. Interestingly, our analysis also suggests that pairing a stable base cryptocurrency with a highly volatile derivative can create a more stable overall cryptocurrency, effectively effectively utilizing the stable base cryptocurrency's value stability. Ultimately, our proposed framework offers a comprehensive approach to assessing cryptocurrency stability and serves as a starting point for systematic testing and comparison of cryptocurrencies. We plan to expand our dataset and increase the frequency of data updates to reflect recent developments in the cryptocurrency market. In SASE FEL schemes, short pulse durations are commonly limited by the coherence time, typically measuring in hundreds of attoseconds for hard X-rays and femtoseconds for softer ranges. This paper introduces a modification to the chirp-taper technique, allowing for overcoming coherence time restrictions and enabling the production of attosecond pulses in the XUV and soft X-ray frequency band. A detailed analysis is provided for an envisioned setup within the BESSY IV project, utilizing a 0.2 T undulator with a center wavelength of 6.5 nm, and yielding over 1E-6 pulses per bunch at a rate of nearly 100 per second. These attosecond pulses exhibit a duration of approximately 250 attoseconds, along with a notable gain in average pulse power. This improvement is anticipated to significantly impact applications in chemistry and biology, enabling precise investigation into molecular and cellular structures. Additionally, this technique will facilitate the creation of a dedicated attosecond pulse user line, supporting a broad range of applications from vacuum and by:storm physics to nonlinear spectroscopy of matter. A subsequent upgrade to a slotted undulator is also discussed, demonstrating the generation of sub-femtosecond pulses in the range of 2-10 eV. This concept for attosecond pulse generation is considered to be a breakthrough, opening up new avenues at FEL facilities worldwide. This work has been partially supported by the EU's Horizon 2020 research and innovation programs. Moreover, simulations in relation to this research utilized the InfraMecs computing cluster at the HZB. Lastly, the authors would like to express their gratitude to Christian Gerth for his invaluable input.

This method involves calculating scattering residues across various frequencies as a high-frequency wave passes through layers with varying thickness. Our calculation demonstrates that low-frequency wave interactions are largely eliminated in a weakly viscous environment, and that at high frequencies, the nature of the flow becomes largely deterministic. Conversely, at intermediate frequencies, the nature of the flow is largely chaotic and viscosities play a significant role in these dynamics. To effectively utilize reinforcement learning in tasks that require visually-guided manipulation, it is essential to create robust representations of observed data that can withstand changes in visual content. Existing techniques using regularization often rely on pre-defined objectives which may not be aligned with the agent's learning goals. This study proposes a novel method that leverages information-theoretic regularization based on the mutual information between observed data and agent actions. By directly optimizing this mutual information, our framework dynamically develops a representation that is closely linked to the agent's decision-making processes. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach through successful application to a basic robotic task using observed textures, as well as as empirical validation of our framework's performance under varying levels of noise in the sensory input. The study's findings illustrate that the proposed framework can produce a more adaptable and flexible representation, resulting in improved performance and increased resilience to distortions in the sensory input. The study's code is publicly available at https://github.com/yoderlab/RLITR. Experimental videos are available at https://yoderlab.github.io/RLITR.adasel.html. Research on black hole growth via accretion has led to a question: what happens to the energy that, according to the black hole's potential well, should be transferred back to its surroundings?  Theoretical work has shown that a portion must be lost to entropy, but the rate at which this mass loss occurs has not been well understood.  By treating the process as a quasi-equilibrium expansion, researchers have now set a limit on the rate of mass loss relative to the black hole's accretion rate.  The limit appears to be around a few percent, with the exact value dependent on the black hole's potential shape.  The result has been verified through both analytical and numerical methods.  While the overall rate of mass loss may seem small, it could have significant effects over long periods of time, potentially shedding light on long-standing problems in black hole growth research.  Further study is needed to determine if this mass loss could provide the necessary cooling to explain the observed distribution of black hole masses.  Additionally, researchers propose that a similar mechanism could be responsible for a similar phenomenon observed in star formations, where a portion of the star's energy is transferred back to its surroundings.  The mechanism could provide a solution to the long-standing problem of how the star's initial contraction is eventually halted.  Further investigation is required to determine the relevance of this mechanism in these phenomena.  The study offers a new understanding of the black hole's growth process and its connection to the laws of thermodynamics, potentially paving the way for a new theory of black hole growth that is consistent across all scales.  The black hole's potential well is a powerful tool that can be applied to phenomena ranging from galaxy evolution to star formations and provides a universal connection point for further research.  Future studies can build on these findings by further examining the relevance of this mechanism to black hole growth and other energetic phenomena.  The work also raises questions about the connection between black holes and the observed phenomenon of galactic outflows, where large-scale matter loss occurs.  The study's results are based on a simplified model, and researchers are working to develop numerical tools that can accurately model the black hole's potential well and its interaction with its surroundings.  The development of these tools could significantly advance our understanding of black hole growth and its connection to the surrounding environment.  The work is part of a broader research initiative focused on black hole growth research and has led to new insights and a pending patent.  The study's results are expected to be published in a research paper soon.

We examine the emission of gravitational waves from the initial stars' remnants, specifically from the clusters' cores, using a detailed network of high-resolution simulations for nuclear star clusters' formation and evolution. Our analysis considers the diverse properties of the initial clusters and the movement of stellar remnants, including black holes and neutron stars, within a 10-pc radius around the central black hole with masses ranging from $\mu=10^{-4}$ to $10^{-2} \msun$. The merger rates of compact objects are significantly higher than previously estimated, especially for lower-mass clusters, due to their greater abundance. The most abundant type of merger is neutron star-black hole collisions, accounting for approximately 40-60 percent, with black hole binary mergers constituting an additional 20-50 percent. The merger rates increase rapidly with lower cluster masses, leading to an order-of-magnitude increase in merger rates for $10^{-4} \msun$ clusters compared to $10^{-2} \msun$ clusters. Most mergers originate from clusters with masses less than  $10^{-3} \msun$ and are associated with the initial stars' distribution, whereas higher-mass clusters primarily produce from the cluster's core. Consequently, the lowest-frequency mergers come from the lowest-mass clusters. This work highlights the significant potential of nuclear star clusters as sources of gravitational wave research, provided the clusters' properties align with observed phenomena. We establish categories that represent quadrics and establish isomorphisms between these categories and the category of finite dimensional commutative associative algebras. Additionally, we demonstrate how this description generalizes to higher dimensional analogs, known as secant quadrics. We utilize categorical methods such as functorial geometry to arrive at this description. The isomorphism between the category of quadrics and the category of finite dimensional commutative associative algebras is shown to be equivalent to the established correspondence between smooth quadrics and the tensor algebras of hyperplane line bundles, as previously studied by Eylem Zehl and the second author. We further prove that this description extends to the category of singular quadrics by establishing a correspondence between singular quadrics and the quotient of the category of finite dimensional commutative associative algebras by the tensor algebras of line bundles, for specific line bundles. The results presented here build upon previously published work of Eylem Zehl and the second author, which itself built upon the work of Yurii Prokhorov and Mikhail Schneider. The effectiveness of interaction forces and stability analysis for human-robot collaborative tasks depend on accurately positioning the robot's end-effector in line with human joints. However, due to differences in geometry, this alignment is often skewed and must be corrected, a process known as manipulability domain scaling. This paper introduces an innovative method using a data-driven approach to determine the optimal scaling factor required to realign human and robot manipulability tensors. The approach employs point cloud registration techniques, which we adapted to work with the complex manipulability domain by incorporating curvature information. Additionally, we carried out parallel computations during robot motion planning to streamline this process and tested it successfully in demonstrations. The proposed solution facilitates interactive tasks that benefit both humans and robots. For example, we demonstrate that the proposed scaling method enables robots to follow human joint movements accurately and efficiently. The integration of our manipulability domain scaling and parallel transport techniques allows robots to maintain a safe distance from human bodies while leveraging human interaction forces for improved task performance, representing an important step towards developing interaction forces that can accommodate varying levels of human-robot scaling. The developed methods can be useful for designing robots that are versatile and flexible in their interactions with people. Advancements in attosecond science hold great potential to unveil the core electronic behavior of matter, contingent on achieving two key advancements: attosecond pulse generation in isolation and boosting its intensity while maintaining its femtosecond laser pulse driver's coherence. This study demonstrates a novel approach to achieving this goal, where we increase the high-harmonic emission from a droplet-target plasma, driven by a powerful infrared laser. The generation mechanism is identical to that of conventional high-harmonic generation but the number of emitting electrons is substantially amplified. The isolated attosecond pulses displayed in this work show a record-breaking intensity of $3.8\times10^{10}$ Watts, with a pulse duration of 47 attoseconds, all of which occurs without compromising the controlling femtosecond pulse.

The proposed method of using plasma from droplets presents numerous benefits over conventional gas-based attosecond pulse generation, primarily due to its compatibility with low-energy drivers, enhanced pulse stability and a significantly broader spectral range, and the ability to produce extremely high recurrence phenomena. The success of this approach places attosecond science within reach, even when coupled to low-energy drivers, thereby making this field more accessible to a broader range of users. Furthermore, the technique offers opportunities to explore newly discovered, high-recurrence phenomena, which could significantly advance our understanding of matter. The approach also facilitates the creation of a highly stable, highly coherent X-ray source, which could have important applications in medical diagnostics, medical treatment, and materials analysis due to its high intensity and high energy stability. The combination of this source with the isolated attosecond pulses presented here could greatly expand the capabilities of each. The novel X-ray pulse characteristics can be attributed to high-density non-linear X-ray generation, an effect of reciprocal focusing, which is a phenomenon in its own right. The occurrence of high-density non-linear X-ray generation can lead to a significant break-through in the development and use of table-top, coherent, ultra-intense hard X-ray sources. The experimental results are consistent with one-dimensional model-based predictions, indicating an exciting future for this research area. One significant obstacle to using machine learning in scientific research lies in accurately assessing its uncertainty. This challenge is compounded by the lack of a well-established framework for evaluating uncertainty in learning algorithms. In this paper, we provide an in-depth examination of uncertainty quantification methods employed in recent literature and introduce novel metrics and adjudication guidelines that facilitate fair comparison of these techniques. Experimental validation using seven datasets from diverse scientific and clinical domains supports our proposed framework. Our study demonstrates that simple algorithms often yield accurate uncertainty predictions, thereby highlighting their value in scientific applications. Additionally, our research illustrates how algorithms' performance can be enhanced through data augmentation and demonstrates the efficacy of transferring knowledge from non-scientific datasets to improve scientific model accuracy and uncertainty detection. Furthermore, our analysis suggests that combining multiple approaches can lead to more effective uncertainty quantification. Ultimately, our research provides a useful guide for scientists seeking to employ machine learning in their work, alongside resources that enable users to replicate our study and assess the utility of uncertainty quantification in various scientific contexts. Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) are fundamental models for autonomous decision-making in systems with uncertain outcomes. Solving MDPs typically involves finding the optimal policy by solving the Bellman equation, which can be computationally challenging for large state spaces. The Gaussiantime Relaxed Policy Iteration (GRPI) method is an efficient approximate algorithm for finding the optimal policy in finite MDPs. Building on GRPI, we have developed an iterative algorithm that generates a sequence of tighter and tighter approximations of the optimal policy. This new algorithm is inspired by the Generalized Monotonic Policy Iteration (GMPI) method and is known as the Imprecise GMPI (IGMPI) algorithm. By leveraging a novel error analysis, we have demonstrated that IGMPI is capable of solving large-scale MDPs more effectively than GRPI. To illustrate the capabilities of IGMPI, we have applied the algorithm to a real-world scenario of autonomous driving. The results show that IGMPI accurately determines the optimal policy in under 2 seconds, while GRPI takes over 4500 seconds. Moreover, IGMPI is capable of solving larger-scale MDPs that are beyond the reach of GRPI. With the ability to scale to larger state spaces, IGMPI is poised to become a leading approach for finding optimal policies in MDPS. To prove this, we have carried out a comprehensive study of the algorithm's behavior as the state space grows. The findings show that IGMPI is capable of solving MDPs with millions of states using a minimal amount of memory. The efficacy of IGMPI is further evidenced by a comparison with the widely-used Deep MARS tool, which failed to accurately determine the optimal policy in a variety of tests. This paper examines the outcome of applying Monte Carlo (MC) methods in computer simulators that produce time series data, resulting in an abundance of sample paths, which in turn facilitates the determination of unknown parameters through data fitting. Utilizing a multiple contour estimation technique, we establish an indirect method for estimating parameters that incorporate both path diversity and data accuracy. The approach is demonstrated through its application to a water transport model, where an optimization problem within a Bayesian framework is formulated to fit observed time series data. The proposed method showcases significant improvements when compared to traditional estimation techniques employing only path diversity, underscoring the importance of considering both path diversity and data accuracy in recovering the true parameter distribution. Additionally, we highlight that high frequency components in the posterior distribution are effectively captured via path diversity, while low frequency components are largely influenced by data accuracy. This distinction is consistent across various numerical testing scenarios. The method has been successfully tested in scenarios with up to 1 billion sample paths and can be further optimized for greater efficiency. The research presents an innovative solution for handling large datasets in computer simulators, providing a comprehensive statistical analysis that such methods typically lack. The research has far-reaching implications for predictive modeling and simulation (PMS) techniques. The theoretical underpinnings of the method can be found in a previously published research paper (Cutler, 2021). The Bayesian estimation framework proposed in this study can be applied to various applications, as evidenced by our test case involving a water transport model that utilizes a dynamic computer simulator known as SUMO. A fully functional implementation of the method, complete with pre-compiled software and documentation, is available for public use at https://github.com/GraduateStudentUMich/MCE_Bayes Estimation. The researcher has explored the applicability of the method to other widely used computer simulators, including SOFI, SUMO, OpenSees, and OpenStudio. Further details on these potential applications can be found in a companion paper (Cutler, 2022). This study investigates the benefits of local data inquiry in the context of robust machine learning, focusing on settings where a malicious adversary has control over the training dataset. We establish criteria that dictate whether local inquiry is more beneficial when a learning algorithm undergoes adversarial manipulation or when it relies solely on provided training data. Interestingly, our findings indicate that local inquiry is advantageous under two specific conditions: (1) when an algorithm is not influenced by the manipulated dataset but rather focuses on extracting general characteristics, and (2) when an algorithm has access to a large amount of high-quality test data that an adversary cannot manipulate. In both scenarios, local inquiry leads to improved generalization performance. Furthermore, our research also identifies a new form of robust machine learning, which we term "robust discovery," where an algorithm develops concepts based on data from multiple distributions without focusing on a specific target distribution controlled by the adversary. We demonstrate that robust discovery is possible through local inquiry and that it results in more generalizable outcomes compared to those of traditional machine learning. Additionally, our research shows that a specific implementation of robust discovery, which we term "Robust Active Learning," can be successful in real-world applications. Furthermore, our study establishes a theoretical connection between robust discovery and recent advancements in learning theory that focus on the discovery of universal concepts. Lastly, our research also evaluates the applicability of local inquiry to the specific task of learning halfspaces and provides new insights on the feasibility of teaching algorithms that can accommodate adversarial training. Moreover, our research shows that the particular training dataset controlled by the adversary has unique properties that distinguish it from any other dataset, which implies that teaching algorithms are unable to adapt to adversarial training. However, our research also demonstrates that there are certain training datasets, specifically those that can be represented by a small number of features, in which case teaching algorithms can be effective without undergoing adversarial manipulation. Finally, our study presents a comprehensive empirical analysis of local inquiry on real-world datasets, which includes results from MNIST, CIFAR-10, and Yahoo!'s search query dataset. Our research shows that local inquiry leads to improved test accuracy and reduced adversarial robustness but also demonstrates that there are certain cases in which it results in lower test accuracy compared to the provided training dataset. Researchers have studied the fragmentation of jets associated with a high-energy photon in lead-lead collisions at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). This study compares the fragmentation in lead-lead collisions to that in proton-proton collisions, using data from 2015 and 2016. It finds that in lead-lead collisions, there is a change in the fragmentation pattern, particularly at high values of the charged-particle transverse momentum. This change is seen to occur when the jet interacts with a large number of particles in the collision. To quantify the level of interaction, researchers used the charged-particle pseudorapidity density as a benchmark. Since photons do not participate in the collision, changes in the jet fragmentation pattern are attributed to the interaction between the jet and the collision matter. To minimize the influence of additional photons, researchers selected jets that were not produced in the collision center and used advanced tracking techniques to analyze the jet's internal structure. Using data from lead-lead and proton-proton collisions at the same energy, researchers found a lead-lead suppression of the jet fragmentation pattern at high charged-particle transverse momentum, which increased with the level of collision matter. This lead-lead suppression was seen to occur for jets that were produced on one side of the collision, but not in the collision center. To understand the effect, researchers compared the lead-lead and proton-proton collision spectra in various regions of the jet and found a lead-lead suppression of about 8% for the most forward region. This effect was seen to occur for jets that had an energy of more than 30 GeV and interacted with a photon pseudorapidity of about 2.2, whichcorresponds to a distance of about 5 millimeters from the collision point. To quantify the level of collision matter at this position, researchers used the charged-particle pseudorapidity density as a benchmark. This research provides the first measurement of the alterations in jet fragmentation caused by collision matter in lead-lead collisions at the LHC. It also offers a new observational level of collision matter effects on jet fragmentation and serves as a new tool to study the collision matter's effects on jet fragmentation. To understand the effect, researchers compared it to theoretical models, including the "Energy loss via collision loss" and the "Radiative loss" models. While the latter provided a better fit to the data, it did not fully explain the observed effect, which required the use of additional energies to fully comprehend the collision matter's effects on jet fragmentation. Specimens made from Martian and Lunar soil substitutes, mimicking real-life lunar and Martian regolith, were pressed and fired at various temperatures to study their structural properties. The effect of temperature on the physical and mechanical properties of these specimens was investigated using X-ray diffraction, scanning electron microscopy, universal testing machine, and Rockwell hardness tester. The analysis showed that optimal firing temperatures existed for both types of regolith for achieving the best structural results. Determining star formation rates is crucial for understanding galaxy evolution, but the various methods used have produced conflicting results. A popular technique involves fitting spectral energy distributions using templates or parametric models. Despite the uncertainty associated with these derivations, the rates derived in this way are generally lower than those obtained from other methods. Furthermore, the comparison of these rates to those derived from emission lines suggests that the problem may not be solely attributed to the uncertainty associated with these derivations, as the rates derived in this way should be less susceptible to the influence of emission from existing stars. In this study, we revisit the calculation of star formation rates by fitting the spectral energy distributions of nearby galaxies using the Jayet et al's 2008 models and the Jayet et al's 2009 codes, applying the techniques developed in Starlight software to analyze the spectra of 39 galaxies. We calculate the star formation rates based on the masses of dust and gas as well as the luminosity of the continuum at specific wavelengths. We find that the rates derived in this way are consistent with those obtained from the analysis of the line Brackett-$\gamma$. The study provides a new framework for the calibration of the star formation rates derived through the fitting of spectral energy distributions against different parameters or models, and it offers a promising approach to utilizing galaxies with known star formation rates as reference points for the calibration of this technique. The comparison of this study to previous works on the calibration of star formation rates highlights discrepancies that suggest that the rates derived in this way may be specifically underestimating the rates in galaxies that are actively forming stars. Potential explanations for this underestimation include the influence of dust, the accuracy of the models, and the activation of the rates in galaxies that are actively forming stars. Furthermore, the study highlights concerns about the reliability of the rates derived from the analysis of the line [NeII] and suggests that the technique may be specifically underestimating the rates in galaxies that actively form stars. On the other hand, the study's findings are in agreement with other works that suggest that the rates derived in this way may be specifically underestimating the rates in dormant galaxies. The study's findings are based on the rates derived at specific wavelengths and it remains to be seen whether they will also be applicable to other rates derived through different methods. Additionally, the study highlights concerns about the reliability of the rates derived through the fitting of spectral energy distributions and the use of emission lines, and suggests that the problem may not be solely attributed to the uncertainty associated with these derivations.

This paper introduces an innovative method for generating synthetic speech durations in English, based solely on actual speech data rather than predetermined probability distributions. A non-parametric approach creates duration medians from sequences of adjacent speech units called footed sounds. The underlying assumption is that these footed sounds are the fundamental building blocks of speech. When a model is trained on a large corpus of transcribed speech, it can efficiently produce synthetic durations for any given utterance. This method is especially suitable for speech synthesis systems requiring short lead times and low system overhead. Its effectiveness is illustrated through a comparison with a standard statistical model in a speech synthesis application. Both methods are integrated into the FestVocal speech synthesis platform. When evaluated on a dataset of spoken sentences, the new median-based method yielded an error margin for duration prediction of 20.6 milliseconds, whereas the traditional approach had an error margin of 24.3 milliseconds. Additionally, the new method demonstrated reduced computational complexity and facilitated the creation of synthetic speech within festVocal. Further details on implementing this method can be found in a supplementary festival module. Specifically, the festival module'synth_dur_median.fest' is available on GitHub at https://github.com/bradleymonson/festvocal-dur-medians under the terms of the permissive BSD license. Additionally, the associated festival configuration 'festvocal_dur_median.sh' can be found on my GitHub repository at https://github.com/bradleymonson/festvocal-dur-medians. This code is compatible with festvocal version 2.4 and later. If you encounter any issues with the installation, you can contact me via email at bradley.monson@gmail.com. I look forward to hearing from you.

The primary goal of the Skincare initiative is to create an interactive deep learning system capable of visually assisting dermatologists in accurately diagnosing skin cancer more effectively. To accomplish this, the initiative combines machine learning algorithms with clinical expertise to produce training data for a model that can learn and adapt to clinical decision-making patterns. By integrating the interactive deep learning system with the initiative's data set, the Skincare project enables the development of a decision support tool capable of providing actionable and transparent reasons for diagnostic decisions, ultimately enabling more effective and accurate diagnosis of malignant skin lesions. 

Key Features of the Skincare initiative include:

- A large, standardized data set for machine learning analysis 
- A rich set of relevant clinical data 
- Expert input from dermatologists 
- Pluggable machine learning algorithms 
- A versatile decision support tool 
- A user-friendly interface for clinical operations 
- A comprehensive set of reasons for decisions 

Through the Skincare initiative, the feasibility of using machine learning to support clinical decision-making in complex conditions has been demonstrated, providing a framework for other medical specialties to adapt and modify the initiative's approach for their own use. 

Key Challenges faced by the initiative include 

- Standardizing clinical data across multiple locations 
- Maintaining objectivity in machine learning algorithms 
- Ensuring the trustworthiness of reasons for decisions 
- Combining the initiative's methods with existing electronic health records 
- Addressing issues related to diversity and equity 

Future Developments of the Skincare initiative include 

- Scaling up the available data set 
- Developing new algorithms and applications 
- Implementing the initiative on mobile devices 
- Integrating the initiative with other decision support systems 

In conclusion, the Skincare initiative provides a pioneering approach to using machine learning in clinical settings, offering a forward-looking solution to the complex problems surrounding the implementation of AI technology in medical practices.

To enhance the reliability of cosmological distance measurements, we've developed a deep learning approach for extracting key features from type Ia supernovae spectra. The method treats feature extraction as an unsupervised learning problem, using a probabilistic autoencoder trained on combined temporal series of spectral lines. By accounting for redshift, velocity, and time, our model can identify intrinsic feature patterns and compensate for spectral distortions. We demonstrate that relying solely on temporal series is sufficient for accurate feature extraction, obviating the need for magnitude data. Furthermore, our approach is robust against potential biases inherent in type Ia supernovae data. We've tested our model using realistic simulations of approximately 5000 type Ia supernovae events, covering a redshift range of $0.00525$ to $1.62$. The feature extraction method we've developed is an essential component of our preceding research on improved cosmological distance measurements. However, assuming only pair-based interactions oversimplifies the complex human interactions seen in everyday life, neglecting the role of group meetings in disease spread. To address this shortfall, we introduce a more comprehensive model, exploring disease transmission on hypergraphs, a type of network that accounts for interactions among groups of individuals. Focusing on the transmission of diseases that spread quickly at the outset but slowly thereafter, we investigate the boundaries of extinction and highlight the importance of considering multi-person interactions in understanding epidemic transmission. Although significant advancements have been made in multimodal learning, existing deep architectures often train and combine vision and audio features in isolation, ignoring their inherent connections. The globally pervasive messaging app, WhatsApp, has become a key medium for disseminating information, including misleading rumors that often spark severe consequences. In an effort to curb the spread of misinformation, WhatsApp introduced limitations on the number of groups a single message can be shared with. In this study, we utilize WhatsApp's built-in programmatic interface to collect Philippines misinformation data during the 2020 presidential election period. We analyzed a dataset of 189,615 messages forwarded between one to three groups, focusing on news item similarities to gauge the effectiveness of WhatsApp's limitations. Our analysis indicates that these restrictions prevented the broad dissemination of certain misinformation items. However, we identify several shortcomings in WhatsApp's approach to combating misinformation, including its inability to combat rumors confined to single groups and its failure to address multimedia content, which frequently contributes to misinformation spread. Furthermore, our analysis highlights WhatsApp's inability to distinguish between identical news items, hindering its capacity to target specific misinformation stories. Ultimately, we conclude that WhatsApp's current measures are insufficient and suggest the implementation of a custom-built information quality assessment system to evaluate the credibility of received messages. While this system would likely face challenges arising from users' privacy concerns, we contend that WhatsApp could initially trial this system within a smaller group of users before expanding it to the entire user base if deemed effective. Additionally, WhatsApp could consider collaborating with existing fact-checking organizations to bolster its efforts to combat misinformation. In cases where WhatsApp's limitations prove ineffective, we suggest the deployment of a crowd-sourced fact-checking system or the integration of a neural machine translation-based information quality assessment system. In exceptional situations where WhatsApp's limitations prove insufficient, we propose a data-driven approach to target specific misinformation stories. The implemented programmatic interface, WhatsAppChecker, along with its dataset, can be accessed via https://github.com/SaharKdar/WhatsAppChecker, under the terms of a CC-BY-NC-ND license. Additionally, a video showcasing our method can be found at https://youtu.be/3QsOGLOL3Gk. In addition, an interactive visualization of our results can be accessed at https://bit.ly/3j4UFlo. The dataset used in this study can be accessed via https://bit.ly/3mYkH3M. This study analyzes data from an online monitoring system of U.S. local news to explore the correlation between COVID coverage, case and death rates, and audience size. For each week of 2020, the paper measures national COVID trends, average local news coverage volume, and audience shifts. Results indicate a significant increase in local news COVID coverage across the year, along with a notable decline in audience. It was found that areas with higher COVID death rates received more local news coverage and had larger audiences. Moreover, the paper reveals that local news COVID coverage was linked to broader media attention and systemic responses, rather than solely influenced by the immediate COVID situation in specific areas. Implications of these findings for understanding how local news responded to the pandemic and how it influenced public awareness and behavior are discussed. Data from the COVID period also enabled the reconstruction of a comprehensive database of local news coverage, spanning the 2010-2020 decade, which enabled the analysis of pre-pandemic trends and contexts. This allowed for a comparative examination of pre- and pandemic periods. Notably, it was observed that areas that received more local news coverage were also hit harder by the pandemic, with higher case and death rates. These areas typically had smaller audiences, indicating a shift towards 'pre-selection' where local news was already concentrated in places that were more inclined to consume COVID-related information. Ultimately, the paper highlights the significance of breaking down aggregate data into more granular'micro-place' categories to gain a deeper comprehension of local news systems and their COVID coverage. To comprehend how humans learn to count, we developed a cognitive model that leverages a multi-layer neural network with memory capabilities. This model utilizes the same principles as the renowned Teaching Machine hypothesis, which suggests that a network can master sequential tasks, including counting, through a systematic teaching process involving positive reinforcement. We demonstrated that the model, which consists of a network with attention-based memory and a specialized teacher, can learn to count accurately with a learning deficit, similar to that observed in humans. Furthermore, our findings reveal that the model requires a particular learning strategy, involving the gradual increment of sequence length, for successful outcome. Using cognitive modeling, we were able to quantify the underlying mechanisms of counting and explain the observed discrepancies between human and machine learning through the integration of theoretical and empirical approaches. Additionally, we conducted experiments to test whether the developed model and its variations could overcome the learning deficit, and our analysis suggests that combining the systematic teaching approach with memory capabilities can enable the model to master counting without training on individual numbers. These findings have implications for the understanding of counting as a cognitive ability and the design of artificial intelligence systems. Bloom filters provide probabilistic assurance that a membership query yields a negative response with high confidence; a similar function is provided by Bloom filters' cousins, such as Bloomier filters and Bloom filters with counters. A relatively recent addition to these tools are Bloom filters' opposites, known as Cuckoo filters, which often outperform their counterparts in terms of storage efficiency and filtering speed. Yet, despite their advancements, these algorithms can still be improved upon. We introduce a new concept, known as Xor filters, which can be viewed as an abstraction of both Cuckoo filters and Bloom filters combined with counters. By integrating features from both worlds, Xor filters can offer quicker membership query processing, greater element tracking capabilities, and higher confidence guarantees than Cuckoo filters, all while consuming less memory than Bloom filters combined with counters. In other words, Xor filters provide a compromise that strikes a balance between the quicker but less capable Cuckoo filters and the more capable but slower Bloom filters with counters. We also provide a detailed analysis of the newly designed Xor filters, along with an implementation-based validation of our design. Furthermore, we introduce a second variation of Xor filters, known as Xor filters with recursion, which can be viewed as an extension of our initial design; this variant can offer improved memory usage and faster membership query processing times than its predecessor, the standard Xor filter. Lastly, we introduce a third and final variation of Xor filters, known as Xor filters with hierarchical recursion, which can be viewed as an optimization of its predecessor; this final variant can offer even faster membership query processing times and improved memory usage efficiency than its predecessor, the Xor filter with recursion. Throughout our paper, we consistently evaluate the performance of our filter designs using the Netflix DVD rental service as a case study. It is our hope that these newly designed Xor filters will serve as a valuable tool for programmers and engineers tasked with implementing disk-efficient, Bloom-filter-based algorithms, including Cuckoo filters, Bloomier filters, and Bloom filters combined with counters. Additionally, we envision these Xor filters to be versatile enough to be applied to an expansive array of applications, ranging from networking to ransomware detection to DVD rental services. We develop a spiking neural network for sequence learning tasks, drawing inspiration from brain mechanisms. The model utilizes synaptic plasticity based on a competitive learning principle, enabling it to detect underlying patterns in sequence data. Experiment results demonstrate that our competitive learning Spiking Neural Network (CL-SNN) is capable of accurately learning and memorizing long sequences, a capability comparable to deep learning models, yet doing so in a biologically plausible manner. What's more, CL-SNN exhibits robust performance even in the presence of noise, showcasing its efficacy for real-world applications. To evaluate its biological feasibility, we analyze and visualize the network's weight dynamics, finding that CL-SNN can efficiently utilize synaptic connections to optimize sequence learning. Additionally, CL-SNN requires less synaptic connections compared to a traditional Neural Network, thus we conclude that CL-SNN is a feasible model of brain function. The source code of our study is publicly available on GitHub. Furthermore, the simulation results can be reproduced using the JNN simulator, a Python package developed by our team to simulate large-scale spiking neural networks. The JNN simulator is also openly sourced at GitHub. The parameter configurations for reproducing our results can be found at this repository. Furthermore, we employed the HPC resources at VTT's Valtori data center to carry out the large-scale simulations needed for our research. The CL-SNN framework holds promise for inspiring novel chip designs, with potential applications in computer vision and natural language processing, fields where learning from long sequences plays a crucial role. We define a homotopy invariant of finite homotopy theory for profinite groups by leveraging a previous extension of homotopy theory to compact monoids. A new action spectrum functor is created as a result, which assigns a sequential spectrum to each profinite group. This functor establishes a connection between the homotopy theory of profinite groups and that of actions on sequential spectra, preserving key properties like universality and distributivity. This framework leads to a method for constructing a universal profinite group representing a given homotopy type, and it also enables a generalization of a previous result showing that profinite groups can be embedded in a universal space. Additionally, a method based on simplicial presheaves is used to compute the homotopy groups of a profinite group's action spectrum, and it is demonstrated that these groups contain relevant information about the group's topology. A key example is provided to show that these homotopy groups can be more complex than initially anticipated. This new theory is applied to study the fundamental group of a space constructed from a profinite group's classifying space for torsors. Moreover, a method based on a generalization of a concept known as "pro-resolution" is devised to compute the total homotopy group of a profinite group's action spectrum, and it is shown that this construction generalizes a concept known as "pro-automorphic" action. Finally, a method based on a theory known as "non-abelian cohomology in homotopy groups" is used to study the second homotopy group of a profinite group's action spectrum and to establish connections between these groups and non-abelian cohomology classes. A key example is provided to show that these connections can lead to interesting topological invariants of the group. A future work will utilize these ideas to study the Galois group of a fundamental field. A preliminary version of these results was presented at a meeting of the London Algebraic Topology Seminar, specifically in sessions 54 and 55. In particular, theorem 0.1 was announced under the title "a universal profinite group for a given homotopy type" in session 54. Furthermore, a related concept known as "pro-finite homotopy theory" was introduced, which is a more general theory that encompasses both "pro-finite groups" and "pro-finite homotopy theory as a theory for compact monoids", and the relationship between these theories was also discussed in session 55. Document analysis, which involves extracting key information from scans of papers, is a labor-intensive process that requires each scan to be manually reviewed for accuracy. Given the high costs of manual review, training models on a small, high-quality dataset becomes ideal. However, these models often underperform due to their limited training data. To mitigate this issue, we propose an approach that uses standard document structure to efficiently label data for training, reducing costs by identifying and excluding irrelevant fields in each document. This allows us to develop a weak supervisory signal for a neural network, which can be trained without extensive manual labeling. Interestingly, our approach's benefits extend beyond data labeling costs to inclusion difficulties, as well. To validate our method, we analyzed a dataset containing over 1 million invoices from over 1,000 different classes, many of which had unusual structures that required adaptation. Without any training, our model achieved an initial accuracy of 40% in identifying relevant fields on randomly selected samples. After being trained on a small, high-quality dataset consisting of 1,500 labeled scans, our model reached an accuracy of 95%. Notably, our approach's results compared favorably to those of a strong supervised model, which had been trained on a larger, but more expensive dataset consisting of 42,000 labeled scans. Specifically, we demonstrate that any universe $\mathcal{U}$ satisfying Pawlikowski's First Principle relative to a countable universe $\mathcal{M}$ gives rise to a linearly ordered class of submodels within $\mathcal{U}$, and show that this ordering is comparable to the Turing-degree spectrum in $\mathcal{M}$. Moreover, we define a natural $\Sigma^0_2$-hierarchy on these submodels and prove that they contain a diverse collection of uncountable submodels within $\mathcal{U}$, and show that these submodels can be encoded through a complex system of sets of natural numbers. We also propose an alternative interpretation of Pawlikowski's Second Principle in a specific formal system, and prove its equivalence to a well-known undecidability hypothesis. Finally, we show that under a specific undecidability hypothesis, we can construct two distinct submodels of $\mathcal{U}$ which are not comparable to one another. These results expand upon Pawlikowski's work and show that it yields unique and undecidable consequences. Moreover, we show that our submodels can host a diverse collection of "non-computable reals" in a specific context. This expansion yields a substantial number of contextually related quantum systems derived from the $E_8$ root system, offering a potentially vast collection of context-sensitive correlations for experimental purposes. To gain deeper insights, we examine the face counting method used to define flags and establish a connection between this technique and quantum interference. This analysis not only contributes to an understanding of the interplay between contextuality and entanglement but also explores the potential for generating context-sensitive correlations without entanglement. To facilitate empirical investigations, we identify a set of non-entangled states producing context-sensitive correlations, deriving specific numbers for specific scenarios and proposing that these figures could be achieved experimentally. Additionally, we propose a method for generating context-sensitive correlations in laboratory settings utilizing a specific type of pyramid known as a simplex. This approach presents an attractive option for laboratory studies due to its connection with established techniques for creating entangled states. Furthermore, we investigate how quantum errors affect the measurement of contextuality and entanglement, utilizing a specific example to illustrate these effects. This discussion highlights the relationship between contextuality and entanglement but also considers the impact of errors that may arise in experimental studies, suggesting the use of non-entangled states producing context-sensitive correlations as a viable standard for such research. Lastly, we propose a new parameter, $C_{\rm min}$, which serves as a measurable indicator of contextuality and may be useful as a laboratory tool to distinguish entangled and non-entangled states producing context-sensitive correlations. This concept could have broader applications in testing quantum complementarity. To facilitate further research, we provide a detailed explanation of our methods and the results, accompanied by relevant technical annotations. We investigate a two-dimensional system composed of electrons interacting with a smooth topological band, devoid of corners or chiral edges. Through applied gate voltage or Coulomb coupling with a substrate, we demonstrate that this band can be folded into a flat band at the Fermi level, giving rise to local moments that can condense into a variety of orders at zero temperature. Under the influence of electron-electron interactions, we find that this flat band induces pairing in the electron cloud, leading to multiple intertwined superconducting orders. Notably, breaking symmetry by means of a d-wave pairing order does not require the presence of nodes in the gap function, and we propose an experimental verification of this phenomenon using scanning tunneling spectroscopy. Furthermore, we transform the electron cloud into a quantum link system, and find that interaction-mediated binding of electrons can result in quantum connections, a form of indistinguishable binding. The binding strength exhibits scaling behavior, and we identify regimes of parameter space where the quantum connection and the resulting bound charges exhibit non-Abelian statistics. We discuss the feasibility of observing this behavior in experiments. Ultimately, we establish that the coupling of electrons to a substrate is insufficient for inducing superconductivity, but can serve as a catalyst when combined with electron-electron interactions. Additionally, we demonstrate that the binding of electrons can result in a labile superconducting state characterized by non-local binding, and propose a strategy for achieving this state through experimental manipulation. Lastly, we establish that the coupling of electrons to a substrate is insufficient for inducing superconductivity, but discover that coupling to a substrate can serve as a mediator for electron-electron interactions when the substrate's dielectric constant exceeds a certain threshold. Consequently, the substrate becomes entangled with the electron cloud. We derive the threshold for the substrate's dielectric constant, and verify that this threshold is feasible with present-day technology involving graphene, and propose a strategy for verifying this phenomenon using transport measurements. Additionally, we establish that the binding of electrons can result in distinct forms of superconductivity, and propose a strategy for distinguishing between these forms through spectroscopy using a tunneling probe. Finally, we transform the electron cloud into a quantum link system, and find that interaction-mediated binding of electrons can result in a entangled state characterized by non-local binding, and propose a strategy for verifying this behavior through measurements in space. The study presents an in-depth analysis of how electron binding is influenced by electron-electron interactions and electron coupling to a substrate in a specific topological band structure. Presence-absence data are often analyzed using distance-based methods of classification.
Researchers compared six different clustering methods using 2230 observations and 599 variables from genetic data.
Principal component analysis was used to reduce the data's dimensions prior to the applications of both traditional and soft clustering techniques.
The findings suggest that when using traditional methods, the European populations grouped according to established categorizations, with Sub-Saharan, North African, and East European populations distinctively separated.
However, the clustering of the Berber and Bedouin populations was not consistently maintained across all analyses.
The applications of soft clustering revealed a high level of uncertainty associated with these assignments.
Surprisingly, the entropy rates did not clearly indicate which method was "best". 
The results suggest that the choice of method depends on the specific research objectives, with none being universally superior. 
Ultimately, ad hoc clustering and confidence intervals for population fixation indices may provide a simpler and more accurate approach to data analysis. 
We propose a future study incorporating functional data involving individuals with disorders, as well as one that employs novel multivariate multivariate statistical techniques like latent variable models and mixed membership models.

The integration of depth information in monocular images has led to improved performance in this task. However, current approaches typically incorporate depth data through the fusion of two separate neural networks, one taking in RGB images and the other depth images, with features then combined and processed together. The UM-IU@LING system for the 2019 SemEval Task 6 challenge focused on identifying aggressive language in Twitter. Our approach used a combination of machine learning and transfer learning with BERT. In particular, pre-trained BERT models were combined with various screening vocabularies, each corresponding to different annotation schemes (HS, Labeled, Agk). For the HS annotation scheme, our system applied a trained SVM classifier to select relevant tweets. When using the Labeled and Agk annotation schemes, our system employed an SVM classifier coupled with a screening function to identify aggressive content. Ultimately, our system yielded top-tier results across all metrics, achieving a moderate 57.5% overall accuracy according to the Seimeval metrics. A detailed analysis of our experiments revealed that the UM-IU@LING system's performance was most strongly influenced by the combination of BERT and the HS screen. Interestingly, our system's results were also found to be relatively insensitive to the choice of BERT hyperparameters. A comparable performance was also demonstrated with an SVM-based classifier that utilized a distinct set of screening features. Interestingly, our human annotators completed the Labeled and Agk datasets before the HS dataset without seeing each other, indicating a notable degree of consistency between the annotations. Consequently, our system's time complexity was kept relatively low by choosing the HS annotation and screening methods. A similar approach was successfully applied in the past to Natural Language Inference, where our team developed and utilized analogous datasets and screening methods. More information about our system can be found on our website. The source code and data used to generate the results are freely available on GitHub. Moreover, the Labeled and Agk annotation datasets have been posted on HuggingFace. The UM-IU@LING system's BERT-based classifier has also been uploaded to HuggingFace. In accordance with SemEval rules, our website includes a full explanation of our work, along with which HuggingFace entities have contributed to this research. HuggingFace has also recently launched a new BERT-based classifier that is remarkably similar to our earlier work. Naturally, our system was not trained on this later model, which is all the more impressive given its relatively recent release. Valued reviewers of our work have drawn attention to several potential areas for improvement, including incorporating more modern BERT variants, multi-task learning, and the utilization of BERT-like language models that are specifically designed for zero-shot learning.
