Computed Tomography (CT) is extensively utilized in both engineering and medical applications for creating detailed images of internal structures within various subjects and objects. Since most CT systems use X-rays emitted from a single source, the X-rays interact with the objects through diverse mechanisms, resulting in various energy spectra that are then measured by detectors. The reconstruction process typically involves transforming measured data into an image under a specific projection transformation, utilizing a weighted superposition of radionuclides with known attenuation characteristics. In a new study, we address three key challenges associated with polyenergetic CT systems:  first, we develop a non-convex variation framework to simultaneously remove high-frequency noise, separate materials, and determine energy-dependent attenuation coefficients; second, we rigorously prove that the proposed model has a unique solution; third, we provide a customized gradient projection algorithm for solving the non-convex problem, which is substantiated by a convergence analysis. Furthermore, we conduct extensive numerical experiments to validate the effectiveness of our approach, applying the method to both synthetic and real-world data, with remarkable results that demonstrate its superior performance compared to conventional techniques. The proposed framework not only denoises and decomposes materials but also recovers the energy-dependent attenuation coefficients, enabling more accurate double-exposure imaging. The study's findings are expected to contribute to the advancement of CT systems and radiography restoration. The code is openly accessible at https://github.com/tiepiying/Poly-CT-reconstruction. Additionally, the reconstructed images are hosted at https://tiepiying.github.io/Reconstructed-Images/. Handwritten Text Recognition (HTR) with limited resources is a complex challenge, largely due to the scarcity of labeled data and limited language knowledge (dictionaries and language models). The problem is further compounded by the presence of handwritten characters that can be difficult to decipher. We address these challenges by developing a novel approach for HTR based on synthetic data generation through a Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) trained on existing resources, and incorporating a compositional template framework for modeling handwritten characters. This template framework serves as a character-based language model, facilitating the breakdown of complex handwritten characters into simpler components. Leveraging the advantages of pre-trained Transformer models, our approach demonstrates exceptional performance on the datasets "TAO-2000" and "TAO-4000, even without fine-tuning. Notably, this approach achieves impressive results with generated data produced just once. We also present an innovative strategy for reducing generated data redundancy, which enhances the quality of produced data. The proposed method is now available on GitHub. This research develops a fully-integrated temperature sensor, utilizing a sub-micron CMOS process. The temperature detector incorporates a bi-metal thermal indicator, accurately simulating thermal expansion across a temperature range of -25$^\circ$C to 125$^\circ$C. The detector's compact design allows for operation over a voltage range of 0.6V to 1.8V. The indicator's thermal expansion is monitored by a digital counter, enabling the conversion of thermal expansion into temperature (^\circ}C) values. The indicator's counting sequence and resulting temperature values are established through thorough analysis and verification. To minimize power consumption while maintaining accuracy, a novel digital circuit technique is employed to generate the temperature counter code. The detector's micro-cellular design facilitates area efficiency. The temperature sensor's effectiveness is validated by comparing its values with standard temperature tables with minimal inaccuracy of $\pm$1.4$^\circ}C and 0.24$^\circ}C resolution accuracy. The detector's total power consumption is 1.5nW and 1.06nW per conversion at 100kHz and 50kHz conversion rates, respectively. The design meets specifications with a minimal power budget. Experimentation outcomes and temperature sensor performance statistics are available online at https://tinyurl.com/2022-IGARSS-abstract. We present a simple proof that in three or more dimensions, the Cauchy problem for the incompressible Euler equations has a critical issue in terms of stability, specifically when using Sobolev spaces and certain types of Lorentz spaces. This is achieved by developing a modified version of the well-known Berard-Aziz-Shadman example, which is now adaptable to various types of Lorentz spaces without requiring a condition on the Hessian. Consequently, the non-uniqueness in Cauchy problems is manifested through the creation of nearly homogeneous measures in different dimensions. Furthermore, the work includes a discussion on the extension of results to certain types of flow maps. From a mathematical structure perspective, the proof reveals that the cause of instability arises from a specific mathematical object known as a monogenic polynomial. In essence, it can be understood as a object that lacks a certain property that would make its components more orderly and predictable. From a physical perspective, the object in question can be thought of as a vector field whose rotation and gradient have certain predefined properties. When this vector field controls a fluid flow, it results in a fluid behavior that is nearly homogeneous in all directions. Interestingly, this nearly homogeneous property is reflected not only in the fluid itself but also in the forces acting upon it. These forces, which are ultimately determined by the shape of the surrounding environment, can be accurately described using certain mathematical constructs. Given the novel approach in the paper to establish the ill-posedness of incompressible Euler equations, it is expected that the results will significantly broaden the scope of methods, known as 'null spaces', which have various applications in the study of partial differential equations. Additionally, the findings of this study will likely have notable implications in the investigation of its nonlinear counterpart, the incompressible Euler equations. It is anticipated that the proofs of several conjectures in this field will be simplified by the results presented here. Specifically, the nonlinear version of the incompressible Euler equations, and certain types of equations involving the Laplace operator, are all expected to benefit from these new findings. Lastly, the work is expected to yield insights into the well-known and widely studied Helmholtz decomposition theorem, particularly in its applications to the incompressible Euler equations and the Laplace equation. Recent research has shown remarkable results by applying large language models to image creation, but the field faces challenges related to images' lack of semantic structure, making it difficult to incorporate prior knowledge and steer the creation process. To overcome these limitations, we propose the Stable Creator, a method that utilizes image segmentation datasets to guide latent space image creation in the context of text-to-image generation. By preserving the semantic structure of images, the Stable Creator enables users to create images from detailed prompts that would otherwise be difficult to generate. Additionally, we evaluate the Stable Creator's ability to produce images that align with specific classes and patterns when provided with corresponding prompts, demonstrating its capabilities. To facilitate wider adoption, we also offer pre-trained models for different image datasets, offering potential benefits. This work presents novel approaches for incorporating prior knowledge and steering the creation process, opening up new possibilities for text-to-image models to incorporate external knowledge and improve the diversity of generated images. The code for this project is publicly available on GitHub. Experimental results can be viewed on the DreamFruits webpage. Stable Creator-generated images can be found on DreamFruits and Imaginarium. Our research explores the implications of the $J/\psi$ decay into photons and invisible particles on dark matter models, particularly those involving Majorana or Dirac neutrinos, within the context of effective field theories. By examining the photon spectrum, we determine the limits on invisible decay branching ratios and derive new constraints for dark matter effective theories below an eV mass. The analysis considers four neutrino masses and shows that a certain type of neutrino decay forces the associated dimension-6 operator to be zero. The limits on invisible decays influence the neutrino-dark matter coupling, mostly when the dark matter mass is lower than the $J/\psi$ mass. However, this impact is most pronounced for a specific type of dark matter particles. Moreover, our research reveals that effective-field-theory assumptions may fail for certain types of dark matter particles. Furthermore, our analysis demonstrates that a future $J/\psi$ experiment can potentially detect invisible decays and may even surpass the sensitivity of collider experiments. Consequently, this could provide new insights into dark matter. Moreover, our research reveals that a future $J/\psi$ experiment can potentially detect invisible decays that involve neutrinos with masses greater than the W boson mass. Additionally, this could enable the direct determination of neutrino decay lifetime in a regime that is previously inaccessible. Finally, our research demonstrates that a future $J/\psi$ experiment can potentially detect invisible decays that involve neutrinos with masses equal to the Higgs boson mass, provided that a particular type of neutrino decay occurs through interaction with this boson. Moreover, this could enable the direct determination of neutrino decay lifetime in a range that is previously inaccessible. Finally, our research reveals that a future $J/\psi$ experiment can potentially detect invisible decays that are induced by the Higgs boson. However, this might be challenging in experiments where the dark matter mass equals the $J/\psi$ mass. On the other hand, our research demonstrates that a future $J/\psi$ experiment can potentially detect invisible decays that are induced by the Higgs boson when the dark matter mass is not equal to the $J/\psi$ mass. Moreover, this might provide new insights into the Higgs boson. Finally, our research reveals that a future $J/\psi$ experiment can potentially detect invisible decays that are induced by the Higgs boson at levels that are comparable to current collider experiments. Small, intensely bright features called "bright points" are pervasive in solar images, accounting for a substantial fraction of emitted light. They are thought to be a manifestation of highly concentrated magnetic fields on the solar surface, which give rise to intense emission regions. To better understand these features, statistical analyses were conducted on a dataset containing over 67,000 bright points, collected through the Solar Optical Telescope on board the Solar-B spacecraft. The results revealed a bi-modal pattern when plotting intensity distributions of these features. This finding was further substantiated by a study of the spatial patterns within a specific cluster of bright points. The observed patterns suggested that the majority of bright points can be described as a combination of two distinct components, each with its own characteristics. Consequently, it is hypothesized that these features are comprised of two separate entities, namely whitlight areas surrounding magnetic bright points, and those associated with granules. Based on this theory, two distinct mechanisms can give rise to the bi-modal pattern observed in the data. Ultimately, it is proposed that all bright points fall into one of two categories, namely Type I, which are surrounded by whitlight areas, and Type II, which are embedded within granules. A statistical test revealed that approximately 85% of bright points belong to the first category. Additionally, it was observed that magnetic elements of all sizes exhibit bi-modal intensity distributions, albeit less pronounced than larger structures. Consequently, it is concluded that small magnetic elements also contribute to the overall bi-modal pattern. Lastly, a theoretical model was developed to describe the physical characteristics of the two distinct components of magnetic elements. The two models proposed are namely the isolated magnetic element in a whitlight area (Type I) and the magnetic element within a granule (Type II). Minimal human films depict humans navigating through unfamiliar environments while ignoring irrelevant details, which is reflected in their quiet movements. Active vision theories propose that humans use active inference to filter out redundant information, but existing computational models often fail to replicate this level of selectivity. We examine whether minimal films can offer insights that can be utilized to develop more effective active inference models. By analyzing footage of humans navigating unfamiliar spaces, researchers can gain valuable understanding of how humans prioritize task-relevant information. This, in turn, can be used to create more selective active inference models. By incorporating local and global context insights derived from human behavior, researchers can develop more informed policies that integrate active filtering and prediction capabilities. This, as demonstrated through controlled experiments, leads to an improved active inference model that surpasses existing state-of-the-art methods. The study presents a novel dataset consisting of human films along with corresponding scene descriptions, which can be accessed through a dedicated website. The proposed model, along with the dataset and training code, is made available on request. Additionally, the study includes a comprehensive online supplement that provides further details on the dataset, training code and model, as well as key technical aspects. Key terms: active vision, filtering, inference, decision-making, minimal human films, dynamic recognition models, neural network training.

James and Serrano's angle-based metric for measuring similarity between sets has gained popularity in information retrieval research. However, this article demonstrates that their method is a specialized instance of the Tversky metric, which is a well-established measure of similarity. We examine the Tversky metric in detail, including its range of values and relationship to diverse set similarity measures. Our analysis shows that the Jaccard distance is connected to an analogue of the information distance used in quantum mechanics. Furthermore, we present a parametrized family of Tversky metrics that encompasses a range of similarity measures between sets. These results lead to two main implications: first, the choice of similarity measure depends on the specific use case; second, as more data becomes available, most similarity measures converge towards using the Jaccard measure. We also investigate the relationship between similarity measures and cardinality-normalized functions of set similarity. Our findings include characterizing the set of these functions and identifying the range of values for any function in this class. Moreover, we present a theorem establishing a convergence property for these functions. Our research identifies promising avenues for further exploration, as well as delving into the cohomology and critical points of these functions. Additionally, we investigate the properties of similarity measures that are invariant to specific transformations. Our analysis includes characterizing the set of these invariant measures and identifying a particular function that is both comprehensive and computationally efficient. Modern single-image deblurring methods primarily rely on deep learning techniques, which assume access to a dataset of blurred and sharply focused image pairs. The primary constraint of these methods is the need for paired data, which is scarce due to exposure variations, resulting in distorted and unrealistic blur patterns when paired examples are artificially created. The application domains of deblurring techniques are further restricted by their inability to handle motion-related blur, a prevalent type of exposure that affects both images and video. Understanding graph convolutional neural networks' (GCNNs) working principle is challenging due to the intricate manipulation of graph data. To address this issue, we introduce a new perspective on GCNNs, based on matched filtering, which simplifies the convolutional operation and makes it amenable to analysis. This analysis reveals that GCNNs rely on the graph's eigenfunctions, specifically using the first few principal eigenvectors to approximate the convolutional function. This simplification allows us to examine the effects of graph normalization and residual connections. Building on this understanding, we develop improved graph convolutional layers, including a new type of layer utilizing the graph's cross-covariance matrix, as well as a simplified residual layer component. Experimental results demonstrate that these new layers outperform standard GCNN layer components in several benchmark datasets. Notably, the proposed layer components exhibit notable performance improvements in settings where the graph is sparsely connected. Additionally, we introduce a general method for estimating the cross-covariance matrix from randomly sampled triads, which has broader applications than just GCNNs. This algorithm is particularly useful for large-scale graph data. Furthermore, we introduce a novel batch normalization technique, specifically tailored to graph data, which uses the graph's cross-covariance matrix to calculate per-graph channel means and standard deviations. This batch normalization technique is combined with our new GCNN layer components to establish a powerful baseline for comparison, which performs well on various benchmark datasets. The proposed methods and source code are available at https://github.com/alishajeb/GCNN-Analysis-and-Benchmarking. Experimental demonstrations can be found at https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1kx4pM9e4T0xkxkxkxkxkxkxkxkxkxk. We develop a new class of unimodal distributions called cyclic likelihoods, which share properties with the negative hypergeometric distribution. Cyclic likelihoods are characterized by a lack of transitivity, a characteristic also found in preference rankings. Furthermore, we prove that the geometric and negative binomial distributions are specialized cases of the exponential family formed by cyclic likelihoods. Using a distinct perspective on statistical models through ranking theory, we explore the intersection of likelihood and preference metrics, establishing the relationship between Fisher information and the discriminant information needed for optimal classification in ranks. Ultimately, we demonstrate that the maximum likelihood estimator is equivalent to the median rank estimator in the case of cyclic likelihoods. This novel approach to statistical models offers a fresh understanding of the underlying nature of these distributions, thereby providing a more comprehensive perspective. Key findings are exemplified through numerical simulations and practical applications in fields such as preference research and taxonomy bioluminescence. The typical approach of configuring software through a central hub can be vulnerable to security attacks and complications arising from misconfiguration. In response, several frameworks have been developed to automate the configuration process, but these solutions come with their own limitations and difficulties. This study proposes a novel method that leverages static analysis to optimize and fine-tune the runtime configuration environment of software systems. By reducing the size and complexity of the configuration space, developers can fix common issues and ensure the security of their system. To demonstrate the feasibility and effectiveness of this approach, we conducted extensive experiments using three software systems and a detailed evaluation of our results revealed significant gains in performance and efficiency. Specifically, we were able to reduce the size of the configuration space by an average factor of 8.13 and also identified potential security and security-related issues that other frameworks might have missed. Furthermore, our specialized configurations outperformed the default configurations used in widely recognized software systems in various evaluation metrics. Additionally, we verified that our customized configurations could withstand security attacks and provided a clear comparison with existing software systems for further reference. Lastly, we plan to expand our research by applying our approach to other software systems and plan to make our code available for others to use. This paper explores non-resonant Rabi oscillations in a complex system consisting of a two-level atom interacting with a qubit and a cavity in a specific configuration. It is discovered that contrast of Rabi oscillations in this setup can serve as a precise indicator of atomic-cavity interface strength. Notably, when the atom and qubit are initially in a shared entangled state before interaction with the cavity, a distinct transmission pattern is observed for entangled and anti-entangled states. Furthermore, it is found that for entangled states, a greater degree of entanglement between the atom and qubit results in enhanced transmission, whereas for anti-entangled states, a greater degree of entanglement between the atom and qubit results in decreased transmission. These findings have potential applications in fields such as quantum information processing and metrology. Additionally, the study examines the effects of detuning and anti-detuning in the system and reveals that anti-detuning leads to enhanced transmission compared to detuning, especially when the atom and qubit are in a shared entangled state. Lastly, the implementation of a non-resonant Rabi oscillation approach allows for the precise measurement of coupling strength with high accuracy, even in the presence of significant uncertainties in frequency. Such a method has potential practical applications due to its simplicity and effectiveness. Notably, the features of this system, particularly regarding transmission and entanglement, are reversed when compared to the Jaynes-Cummings model, and it is noted that entanglement in both scenarios is a result of distinct physical phenomena. Furthermore, it is observed that there are numerous applications of the anti-Jaynes-Cummings model that do not rely on Rabi oscillations, and proposals for implementing this model in experimental settings are presented. Lastly, the intersection of theoretical and experimental research is an essential aspect of advancing both areas. It is noted that future studies should focus on relating key findings from the theoretical model to corresponding experimental results. Additionally, the potential for observing distinct optical phenomena in experiments could be explored to verify key predictions of the theoretical model. It is also suggested that specific analytical tools, such as spectral analysis, could be utilized in conjunction with corresponding experimental results to deepen our understanding of the anti-Jaynes-Cummings model. Lastly, the capacity for entanglement in both the anti-Jaynes-Cummings and Jaynes-Cummings models could be the focus of numerous research opportunities. It is noted that one such possibility could involve investigating how to maximize entanglement in both scenarios over extended periods of time

Despite the growing need for language models in non-English markets, developing and training models for every language can be impractical, given the vast number of languages in existence. A feasible solution to this problem is cross-lingual transfer, where knowledge from a model in one language can be utilized to create a similar model in another language. However, this goal is complicated by discrepancies in character sets, the absence of similar words across languages, and differences in sentence structures. Researchers have addressed this challenge by utilizing neural machine translation to share representations across languages, or by developing sets of similar words within a single language. Our approach takes a different stance, arguing that knowledge transfer can be achieved through neural networks without relying on elaborate mappings. Instead, we define the task to be performed using vector representations and find correspondences between the input words and the task at hand, a task that can be accomplished through cross-lingual similarities. We evaluate our method by translating the representations into the target language using a model that can translate vector sets. Our experiments demonstrate that this method allows us to achieve successful model-to-model knowledge transfer in multiple tasks including part-of-speech tagging, named entity recognition, and dependency parsing, achieving results comparable to those achieved through neural machine translation, while also achieving successful knowledge transfer to languages for which there is limited data available. Additionally, we find that our method allows us to achieve successful knowledge transfer to languages that it has never been trained on, a feat that neural machine translation is unable to accomplish. We consider these results to be significant and believe that our method may allow for more practical applications of cross-lingual transfer. As such, we propose that knowledge transfer may be a more practical goal for developers and researchers, and encourage them to explore cross-lingual transfer as a means of achieving more practical results. Furthermore, we believe that our method can be adapted to utilize knowledge from multiple source languages, and suggest a number of possible approaches that could be utilized to achieve this goal. We consider these ideas to be part of a broader family of techniques that can be employed to facilitate knowledge transfer, and propose that researchers explore these possible avenues. We support our method with an open-source implementation, and invite fellow researchers to utilize our findings and join us in further exploring the possibilities of cross-lingual transfer. In multi-task reinforcement learning, using shared representations can greatly
benefit a learner when it comes to solving a variety of tasks. However, when
using model-based approaches, simply copying across tasks can lead to a problem
known as interference, where new tasks negatively impact learning progress on
previous ones. We've found that this interference is particularly harsh when
occurring in the same time frame (synchronous) as when learning is happening
immediately after first encountering a task (online learning). Our research
involves the application of modular networks to model-based multi-task reinforcement
learning and demonstrates that using separate networks for each task can avoid
this interference and yield better results. Moreover, combining this approach with
the use of experience buffers and second-order Taylor approximations, we've been
able to develop a new method that significantly improves performance in complex
multi-task environments. It's interesting to note that when the temporal context
is considered (sequential learning), the traditional model-based approach seems to
avoid interference and thus we've also introduced a new method that utilizes
temporal dependencies to boost performance in such scenarios. Our research
demonstrates state-of-the-art results on standard multi-task benchmarks and
opens-up new avenues for research using the modern deep learning approaches in
model-based multi-task reinforcement learning. Additionally, we've made our code
and models publicly available for the first time. It's observed that the
interference in multi-task reinforcement learning occurs primarily due to sharing
the model's weights whereas in representation learning, it's generally the
representation itself that benefits from sharing. Therefore, we've developed a
new method known as {\tt CIRL-MBM} which uses a model-based approach to learn
policies for both single and multi-task reinforcement learning tasks. Our
findings clearly show that this method outperforms the current state-of-the-art
in complex multi-task reinforcement learning benchmarks. Our research makes two
important contributions. Firstly, we've made the code and models publicly
available for model-based multi-task reinforcement learning. Secondly, we've been
able to demonstrate state-of-the-art results in the MROM benchmark by using
temporal dependencies to boost performance in multi-task reinforcement learning
tasks. It's observed that model-based multi-task reinforcement learning
distinguished from representation learning, as the latter generally benefits from
sharing the model's weights whereas the former generally benefits from temporal
dependencies. Therefore, we've developed a new method known as {\tt MBM-CIRL}

These constraints can take several forms, such as maintaining a stable internal temperature or avoiding sudden changes in control settings. Our approach allows for the precise calculation of optimal performance within these constraints, and we have found that under certain time-critical conditions, these optimal performance levels converge to their infinite-time counterparts. Furthermore, for certain constraints and in the limit of infinite time, our results confirm the optimal temperatures and work outputs determined by previous theoretical studies. To validate our findings, we have successfully tested them in a laboratory setup using a laboratory-scale heat engine designed to mimic a Otto cycle. Our study demonstrates the significance of considering both the time and control constraints in the optimization of heat engines. Additionally, our work highlights the potential for finite-time optimizations to be applied in a broader range of systems beyond heat engines. Although our study primarily focuses on thermal systems, the techniques and strategies developed here are versatile enough to be applied to the optimization of a wide range of systems with internal degrees of freedom. Lastly, our research also sheds light on the intricacies of defining thermodynamic universality, a key concept that requires further clarification. To achieve this, we have calculated the maximum work that can be harnessed from a system with an internal heat bath, an approach reminiscent of Jacobi's formula. Different image enhancement techniques tend to excel in specific domains. Neural based methods often produce more natural looking results but lack clear control over the style they are trying to replicate, whereas grammar based methods have better control over the style but their results appear more artificial compared to neural based methods. Recent research has demonstrated that style in these two categories can be bridged through a cross training approach called style distillation. However, this approach requires large amounts of paired data which can be expensive and time consuming to collect. This paper proposes a new method to train neural based models in an unsupervised style distillation approach that produces similar results to those achieved through supervised style distillation using extensive paired data. The method works by first establishing a correspondence between images through a bidirectional solver, allowing style to be extracted and applied consistently. A new forward mapping solver was also developed specifically for the popular CIEDE2000 metric, outperforming previous methods. A global forward mapping function based on neural networks was also improved upon using the newly established correspondences. The paper shows that the proposed unsupervised style distillation approach not only matches but surpasses the performance of traditionally supervised style distillation. Moreover, it combines the natural looking results of neural based methods with the grammar based control over style, representing a major breakthrough in the field. Optimizing wireless Device-to-Device (D2D) communication interventions to improve Age of Information (AoI) performance is a critical challenge in maintaining up-to-date network data. This study develops an Age of Information Age (AoIa) framework to gauge D2D system delay, enabling its utilization in reinforcement learning algorithms. Through analyses of D2D activated link durations and new packet arrival rates under various wireless channel conditions, this study's findings demonstrate that optimizing D2D interventions by maintaining two buffer sizes, namely a modest and a full buffer, suffices to maximize AoI. A deep reinforcement learning strategy, named AoI-Based Value (AV) network, is then proposed to resolve the optimization problem. Within this system, when a new packet arrives, a fully loaded buffer activates a D2D link while a modestly filled buffer waits for an appropriate D2D connection. This strategy successfully solves the real-time optimization problem, yielding an approach that can be quickly trained and yields superior results compared to the current best available solutions. Since these equations are formulated in terms of vorticity, which is no longer solely determined by the velocity's curl in compressible fluids, the verification becomes complex. In a recent study, the issue of verifying helicity conservation for the compressible Euler equations was resolved analyically. Characterizing colorectal polyps through histopathological examination allows clinicians to assess the polyp's potential to develop into a carcinoma and inform subsequent surgical decisions. However, Polyp Classification and Adenoma Grading are labor-intensive tasks that demand extensive pathologists' time. Given the rising demand for these diagnoses, we've developed UniToPatho, an annotated dataset consisting of 350 histopathological whole-slide images (WSI), designed to support Polyp Classification and Adenoma Grading tasks. These tasks were conducted according to the Vienna Classification system, which provides a solid foundation for further research on carcinoma evolution potential, surgical decisions, and clinical diagnosis. Our dataset promotes research in these areas, effectively bridging the gap between clinical diagnostics and computational assessments. Additionally, we've established the UniToPatho Challenge, an activity where machine learning experts can engage in tasks such as Polyp Classification and Adenoma Grading, using the provided WSIs, to test their methods and identify the most effective approaches. The UniToPatho resources, including the dataset and challenge details, can be accessed at https://unito-patho.github.io/. The dataset can be downloaded at https://doi.org/10.25825/20210114UnitoPatho.1/UNITO_PATHO_2021.1.zip. The challenge server will be maintained until December 2023, when the UniToPatho Challenge officially concludes.

Two adjacent piezoelectric crystals can efficiently transfer energy when placed close to each other, regardless of their cut orientation. When an acoustic wave reaches the first crystal, it generates a charge signal that can be effectively transferred to the second crystal, where it is converted back into an acoustic wave. Effective energy transfer relies on complete transmission between the two crystals. Research has been conducted to analyze this process using advanced mathematical techniques and numerical models. By applying these methods, the transmission efficiency between closely spaced, longitudinally cut zinc oxide crystals was studied. Numerical models confirmed that high efficiency transmission is achievable when the crystals are very close to each other. Interestingly, increasing the frequency of the acoustic wave actually results in improved transmission efficiency. This trend was observed across a range of different crystal spacings. It is hypothesized that these findings could be applied to other types of materials. Ultimately, understanding how to optimize energy transfer between materials holds significant potential for advancing technology.

The disintegrating or "grainey" sub-Neptunes offer a chance to study the process of destruction and creation of particles in space, however the exact mechanism remains to be determined. K2-22 b, a planet that undergoes rapid changes in size, is particularly interesting as it exhibits characteristics of both disintegrating and grainy planets. Two possible explanations are that the planet is consuming a ring of debris or that it is a massive planet losing mass heavily. To better understand the properties of K2-22 b, observations were taken using the Large Binocular Telescope with the CRIRES instrument, revealing the presence of large dust particles and mass loss in the vicinity of the planet.

Observations taken close to opposition showed a peak at 1.3 micrometers that can be attributed to dust, while a blue shift and lack of this peak at other phases suggest movement of small particles. This can be explained by a model involving high levels of mass loss from the planet, with smaller particles being carried away by Poynting-Robertson effect. Additionally, the absence of infrared radiation using SPITZER and WISE also supports this model, indicating that the planet's heat is being dissipated into space. Mass loss rates are found to be in the range of 10-100 times that of other disintegrating or grainy planets, with the exact rate dependent on the characteristics and location of the lost particles.

A second model that takes into account a ring of debris around the planet also failed to fully explain the observed properties, however it is possible that the planet could be consuming this ring which would explain the changes in its size over time. While a massive planet losing mass heavily is the most preferred explanation, further study using higher resolution telescopes such as the JWST and the ELT are needed to fully determine the properties of K2-22 b and distinguish between the two possible explanations. We establish a condition for the coherence of a Milnor fiber in terms of the dimensionality of the critical locus. Specifically, if the coherence of a non-degenerate polynomial f is intact after a quadratic monomial division, then the critical locus of f is at least two dimensions higher than the Milnor fiber. In the case of a hypersurface, this condition translates to a new criterion for coherence, based on an analogy with the flatness of the base locus in multidimensional discriminant theory. Consequently, this result yields a novel proof that a non-degenerate, homogeneous polynomial of degree d+1 possesses a coherent Milnor fiber when d is an odd number. Additionally, this notion of coherence in conjunction with multidimensional discriminant theory may potentially develop into a more comprehensive tool for studying singular polynomials and their fibered links in higher dimensional spaces. Finally, this research opens up the possibility of investigating flatness in the context of Milnor fibers and coherent polynomial singularities in differential topology and algebraic geometry, encompassing not only discriminants but a broader range of singular loci. Several examples are provided to illustrate these concepts and results, coupled with suggestions for future research. Alongside this text is a supplementary dossier containing further examples, additional proof details, and an extensive bibliography on the topic of coherent polynomial singularities and Milnor fibers. The analysis of magnetic reconnection, a collisionless process, can be approached through two main methods: global simulations that capture the full phenomenon but lack detailed particle insights, and local studies that provide in-depth particle information but are limited in their scope. To bridge this gap, an integrated method has been developed that embeds the Magnetohydrodynamics with Adaptively Embedded Particle-In-Cell (MHD-AEPIC) model. This method utilizes the MHD model to identify areas that require higher spatial resolution for reconnection, thereby adjusting the grid size and density to match the MHD-AEPIC model's settings. The integrated method is validated through an examination of the reconnection process at multiple scales, from global simulations to detailed local studies, all sharing the same framework. The analysis includes computational costs, reconnection rates, electron dynamics, and heat production. The integrated method proves to be an efficient and versatile tool for studying various reconnection scenarios. Due to its high flexibility, this method can be applied to a range of physical systems, such as astrophysical reconnections and laboratory-based experiments. The development of the integrated method paves the way for employing the MHD-AEPIC model in various research contexts. Additionally, the method demonstrates the potential for the MHD-AEPIC model to be utilized in adaptive simulations with nested domains, enhancing the understanding of reconnection and entropy production. The integrated method will continue to be essential for refining the models of magnetic reconnection, which it has played a crucial role in developing. The code, including its integrated model, is freely available at [https://github.com/PhysICS-LAB/MHD-AEPIC]. Future releases will incorporate an embedded fluid-in-cell component for comparing the MHD-AEPIC model to another existing approach. Furthermore, a recently integrated version of the integrated method will be released that employs machine learning to evaluate and potentially enhance reconnection, entropy production, and other computational outputs in various astrophysical settings. This version will be based on recent research described in arXiv:2205.08133. Both versions will be compatible with each other and can be used simultaneously.
